title: Foundations & Research Methods
subject: Psychology 101
description: What psychology is, how psychologists study it, and how to spot a solid claim.

questions.q: Which approach explains behavior through unconscious drives and early childhood experience?
questions.explain: Freud's psychoanalytic approach centers unconscious drives and early childhood.

questions.q: A researcher watches students in a cafeteria without interfering. This is:
questions.explain: Naturalistic observation means watching behavior in its natural setting without manipulating it.

questions.q: In an experiment, the variable the researcher deliberately changes is the:
questions.explain: The independent variable is manipulated; the dependent variable is measured.

questions.q: Which correlation shows the strongest relationship?
questions.explain: Strength is about distance from zero, not the sign: |-0.85| is the largest.

questions.q: A single, deep study of one unusual patient is called a:
questions.explain: Case studies examine one person or group in depth — rich detail, weak generalizability.

questions.q: Participants who unknowingly receive a fake treatment are in the:
questions.explain: A placebo is an inert treatment; the placebo group is the comparison for expectancy effects.

questions.q: Random assignment is used in experiments mainly to:
questions.explain: Random assignment distributes individual differences evenly so the IV is the likely cause of differences.

questions.q: The branch of psychology focused on mental processes like memory and problem-solving is:
questions.explain: Cognitive psychology studies how people perceive, remember, think, and solve problems.

questions.q: Which ethical rule requires explaining a study to participants afterward, especially after deception?
options: Debriefing is optional in all studies
questions.explain: Debriefing explains the study's true purpose and clears up any deception.

questions.q: Wilhelm Wundt is credited with:
questions.explain: Wundt opened the first psychology lab in Leipzig in 1879, marking psychology's start as a science.

rounds.title: Foundations & Research Methods
rounds.desc: What psychology is, how psychologists study it, and how to spot a solid claim.

title: Brain & Biological Bases
subject: Psychology 101
description: Neurons, neurotransmitters, brain regions, and how we sense the world.

questions.q: The part of the neuron that RECEIVES signals from other neurons is the:
questions.explain: Dendrites receive; the axon sends. Myelin speeds the signal along the axon.

questions.q: The fatty coating that speeds neural impulses is the:
questions.explain: Myelin insulates the axon; its breakdown (as in MS) slows signaling.

questions.q: The junction where neurotransmitters cross between neurons is the:
questions.explain: The synapse is the tiny gap where chemical messages cross.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is most associated with reward and movement (and Parkinson's when lacking)?
questions.explain: Dopamine: reward, motivation, movement. Too little → Parkinson's symptoms.

questions.q: The brain area most responsible for forming new explicit memories is the:
questions.explain: The hippocampus consolidates explicit memories; the amygdala handles fear/emotion.

questions.q: Phineas Gage's personality changed after damage to his ___ lobe.
questions.explain: Frontal lobe damage altered Gage's planning and personality — a famous localization case.

questions.q: Broca's area damage causes difficulty ___; Wernicke's causes difficulty ___.
questions.explain: Broca = speech production. Wernicke = language comprehension.

questions.q: The sympathetic nervous system:
options: Is the same as the somatic system
questions.explain: Sympathetic = accelerator (fight/flight); parasympathetic = brake (rest/digest).

questions.q: The minimum stimulus strength detected 50% of the time is the:
questions.explain: Absolute threshold: the weakest detectable stimulus, half the time.

questions.q: Weber's law says the just-noticeable difference is a constant:
questions.explain: JND is proportional: 2% for weight — heavier objects need bigger absolute changes to notice.

rounds.title: Brain & Biological Bases
rounds.desc: Neurons, neurotransmitters, brain regions, and how we sense the world.

description: Thresholds, vision, hearing, pain, and how the brain organizes sensory input.

questions.explain: Sensation is the raw detection of physical energy by sensory receptors (light hitting the retina). Perception is the brain's active organization and interpretation of that input into meaningful experience.
options: Sensation is conscious; perception is unconscious.
They are the same process with different names.
Sensation involves memory; perception does not.
Sensation is detecting stimuli; perception is organizing and interpreting them.
questions.q: What is the difference between sensation and perception?

questions.explain: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulation needed for detection 50% of the time — classically, a candle flame seen 30 miles away on a dark, clear night. "Smallest noticeable difference" describes the DIFFERENCE threshold instead.
options: The maximum stimulus we can tolerate
The point where sensation becomes perception
The minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time
The smallest noticeable difference between stimuli
questions.q: The absolute threshold is defined as:

questions.explain: Weber's law: the just noticeable difference (JND) is a constant PROPORTION of the original stimulus. You would notice 1 lb added to 10 lbs, but need about 10 lbs added to 100 lbs to notice — the ratio stays constant.
options: The just noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus
Sensation grows linearly with stimulus intensity
Thresholds are identical across all senses
questions.q: Weber's law states that:

questions.explain: In the famous Simons and Chabris study, viewers counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene — focused attention makes us blind to unexpected stimuli.
options: Failing to notice a gorilla in a basketball-passing video
questions.q: Inattentional blindness is best demonstrated by:

questions.explain: The retina lines the back of the eye and holds the photoreceptors: rods (dim light, peripheral vision) and cones (color, fine detail). The cornea and lens only focus light; the optic nerve carries the signal out.
questions.q: Which structure contains the photoreceptors (rods and cones)?

questions.explain: Trichromatic theory holds that three cone types — sensitive to short (blue), medium (green), and long (red) wavelengths — combine their signals to produce all color experience. It explains color mixing but not afterimages; that's opponent-process theory.
options: Three types of cones sensitive to red, green, and blue wavelengths
Opponent processes located in the thalamus
A single cone type that adapts to light
questions.q: The Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory explains color vision by:

questions.explain: Gate-control theory (Melzack and Wall) says non-pain signals can close spinal "gates" to pain input — which is why rubbing a bumped elbow reduces pain, and why distraction and placebos can modulate pain.
options: Pain signals can be blocked by neural "gates" in the spinal cord
questions.q: The gate-control theory of pain proposes that:

questions.explain: Bottom-up (data-driven) processing builds perception from sensory details upward — for example, assembling lines and curves into the letter A. Top-down processing instead applies expectations and prior knowledge downward onto the input.
options: Building perception from raw sensory input upward
Processing that always starts in the cortex
questions.q: Bottom-up processing is:

questions.explain: Kinesthesis (proprioception) tells you where your body parts are and how they are moving — letting you touch your nose with your eyes closed. Balance is the VESTIBULAR sense; internal organ states are interoception.
options: Body position and movement of muscles and joints
questions.q: The kinesthetic sense provides information about:

questions.explain: Perceptual constancy lets a door look rectangular whether open or closed, and a shirt look white in sunlight or shadow — the brain corrects for changing retinal images to keep objects stable.
options: We perceive the same stimulus identically every time
We perceive objects as stable despite changing sensory input
questions.q: Perceptual constancy means:

subject: Psychology 101
title: Sensation & Perception
Learning & Conditioning
subject: Psychology 101
description: Pavlov, Skinner, Bandura — classical, operant, and observational learning.

questions.q: In Pavlov's experiment, the food is the:
questions.explain: Food naturally triggers salivation — it's unconditioned (unlearned).

questions.q: After pairing, the bell alone causing salivation means the bell is now a:
questions.explain: Once learned, the bell is the conditioned stimulus producing the conditioned response.

questions.q: Salivating to a similar-sounding tone as well as the trained bell is:
questions.explain: Generalization: responding to stimuli similar to the conditioned stimulus.

questions.q: Removing an aversive stimulus to INCREASE a behavior is:
questions.explain: Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior by taking something unpleasant away (seatbelt buzzer).

questions.q: A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of pulls. That's a ___ schedule.
questions.explain: Variable-ratio: reward after an unpredictable number of responses — high, steady responding.

questions.q: Paying a worker for every 10 items assembled is a ___ schedule.
questions.explain: Fixed-ratio: reinforcement after a set number of responses.

questions.q: Reinforcing closer and closer versions of a target behavior is called:
questions.explain: Shaping builds complex behavior by rewarding successive approximations.

questions.q: Bandura's Bobo doll study demonstrated:
questions.explain: Children imitated an aggressive model — learning by watching, especially when the model was rewarded.

questions.q: Tolman's rats learning a maze without rewards, then using it when rewards appear, showed:
questions.explain: Latent learning: knowledge acquired without obvious reinforcement, stored as a cognitive map.

questions.q: If a conditioned response fades when the CS is presented alone repeatedly, that's:
questions.explain: Extinction weakens the conditioned response when the CS no longer predicts the UCS.

rounds.title: Learning & Conditioning
rounds.desc: Pavlov, Skinner, Bandura — classical, operant, and observational learning.

title: Memory & Cognition
subject: Psychology 101
description: How memory is built, stored, lost — and the thinking shortcuts that misfire.

questions.q: Short-term memory holds about how many chunks of information?
questions.explain: Miller's famous 7±2 chunks — expandable by chunking related bits together.

questions.q: Visual sensory memory is called ___ memory; auditory is ___ memory.
questions.explain: Iconic = visual (~0.5s). Echoic = auditory (~3–4s).

questions.q: Memory for facts (capitals, definitions) is ___ memory; memory for personal events is ___.
questions.explain: Semantic = facts. Episodic = events from your life.

questions.q: Old learning interfering with recall of new learning is ___ interference.
questions.explain: Proactive: the OLD material pushes forward and blocks the new. Retroactive is the reverse.

questions.q: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows forgetting is:
questions.explain: Most forgetting happens in the first hours — which is why early review matters so much.

questions.q: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind is the:
questions.explain: Availability: plane crashes feel common because vivid examples come to mind easily.

questions.q: Loftus's research showed that the wording of a question ('smashed' vs 'hit') can:
options: Alter memories and create false details
questions.explain: Memory is reconstructive — post-event information can be woven into what people 'remember.'

questions.q: Patient H.M. could learn new skills but not form new explicit memories, showing that:
options: Explicit and procedural memory are separate systems
questions.explain: H.M.'s pattern proved memory has distinct systems with different brain bases.

questions.q: Solving a problem by testing every possibility uses a(n):
questions.explain: Algorithms are exhaustive and guaranteed but slow; heuristics are fast shortcuts.

questions.q: The tendency to seek information confirming what you already believe is:
questions.explain: Confirmation bias: we search for, notice, and remember confirming evidence.

rounds.title: Memory & Cognition
rounds.desc: How memory is built, stored, lost — and the thinking shortcuts that misfire.

title: Development Across the Lifespan
subject: Psychology 101
description: Piaget's stages, Erikson's crises, attachment, and moral development.

questions.q: A baby who searches for a toy hidden under a blanket has mastered:
questions.explain: Object permanence (~8 months, sensorimotor stage): things exist even when unseen.

questions.q: A child who thinks the taller glass must hold more juice lacks:
questions.explain: Conservation develops in the concrete operational stage; preoperational children center on one feature.

questions.q: Piaget's stage for abstract, hypothetical reasoning is:
questions.explain: Formal operational (12+): abstract and 'what if' thinking.

questions.q: Erikson's crisis for adolescents is:
questions.explain: Adolescence is about figuring out 'who am I?' — identity vs role confusion.

questions.q: Erikson's crisis in infancy is:
questions.explain: Consistent, responsive care in the first year builds basic trust.

questions.q: Harlow's monkeys preferred the cloth mother over the wire mother that fed them, proving attachment depends on:
questions.explain: Contact comfort, not feeding, drove attachment — a landmark result.

questions.q: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, a baby who explores happily, is upset when mom leaves, and is soothed when she returns shows ___ attachment.
questions.explain: Secure attachment (~60–65%): the caregiver works as a secure base.

questions.q: Kohlberg's preconventional morality is based on:
questions.explain: Preconventional: right = what avoids punishment or gains reward.

questions.q: Vygotsky's term for what a child can do WITH help but not alone is the:
questions.explain: The ZPD is where good teaching aims — with scaffolding that fades as skill grows.

questions.q: Fitting a new experience into an existing schema is ___; changing the schema is ___.
questions.explain: Assimilation fits new into old; accommodation rebuilds the schema.

rounds.title: Development Across the Lifespan
rounds.desc: Piaget's stages, Erikson's crises, attachment, and moral development.

description: Drives, arousal, and the major theories of why we feel what we feel.

questions.explain: Maslow's hierarchy is a pyramid: physiological needs form the base and must be reasonably satisfied before safety, belongingness and love, esteem, and finally self-actualization can motivate behavior.
questions.q: According to Maslow's hierarchy, which need must be met FIRST?

questions.explain: James-Lange reverses common sense: we do not cry because we are sad — we FEEL sad because we cry. Bodily arousal comes first, and the brain's perception of that arousal IS the emotion.
options: We feel emotion BECAUSE of our physiological arousal
Facial expressions are irrelevant to feeling
questions.q: The James-Lange theory of emotion states that:

questions.explain: Schachter and Singer's two-factor theory: arousal alone is ambiguous, so we cognitively LABEL it based on context. The same racing heart becomes "fear" in a dark alley or "excitement" on a roller coaster.
questions.q: Which theory says emotion equals physiological arousal PLUS a cognitive label?

questions.explain: Intrinsic motivation comes from within — curiosity, enjoyment, mastery. Extrinsic motivation comes from external rewards or punishments. Overjustification research shows extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic interest.
options: Doing an activity for its own inherent satisfaction
questions.q: Intrinsic motivation is:

questions.explain: Yerkes-Dodson: performance peaks at MODERATE arousal and drops when arousal is too low (boredom) or too high (anxiety). Complex tasks need a lower optimal arousal level than simple ones.
options: A steady increase of performance with arousal
An inverted-U: moderate arousal maximizes performance
questions.q: The Yerkes-Dodson law describes:

questions.explain: The amygdala, part of the limbic system, is the brain's threat detector — central to fear conditioning and emotional memory. Damage to it impairs fear responses while leaving other cognition intact.
questions.q: Which brain structure is most central to emotion, especially fear?

questions.explain: Homeostasis is the body's drive to keep internal conditions — temperature, glucose, hydration — stable. Drive-reduction theory says hunger, thirst, and similar states are motivations to restore that balance.
options: The body's tendency to maintain a stable internal state
Avoiding all stress at all times
questions.q: Homeostasis in motivation refers to:

questions.explain: The facial feedback hypothesis says expressions feed BACK into feeling — forcing a smile can slightly lift mood, frowning can darken it. It's a weaker cousin of James-Lange, supported by pen-in-teeth studies (though effects are small).
options: We smile because we are happy, never the reverse
Facial expressions only communicate to others
Emotions are unrelated to facial muscles
Facial expressions can influence emotional experience
questions.q: The facial feedback hypothesis suggests:

questions.explain: Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory: autonomy (feeling in control), competence (feeling effective), and relatedness (feeling connected) fuel intrinsic motivation and well-being. Power/achievement/affiliation is McClelland's need theory.
questions.q: According to self-determination theory, the three basic psychological needs are:

questions.explain: McClelland's research: high need-for-achievement people choose MODERATE difficulty — hard enough to feel accomplishment, achievable enough to succeed — and they crave performance feedback.
options: Moderately challenging tasks with clear feedback
Impossible tasks, to avoid blame for failing
questions.q: A person high in achievement motivation (nAch) prefers:

subject: Psychology 101
title: Motivation & Emotion
Freud & Psychoanalysis
subject: Psychology 101
description: Id, ego, superego; psychosexual stages; how Freud thought personality is built.

questions.q: According to Freud, the part of personality that operates on the pleasure principle is the:
questions.explain: The id is present at birth and demands immediate gratification — the pleasure principle.

questions.q: The ego operates on which principle?
questions.explain: The ego mediates between the id and reality, delaying gratification when needed.

questions.q: The superego is best described as:
questions.explain: The superego holds internalized morals and ideals — it's where conscience lives.

questions.q: Freud's first psychosexual stage, focused on feeding, is the:
questions.explain: The oral stage (birth–~18 months) centers on the mouth: sucking and feeding.

questions.q: During which stage does Freud say sexuality goes dormant and children focus on school and peers?
questions.explain: Latency (roughly ages 6–puberty) is a quiet period — energy goes to skills and friendships.

questions.q: The Oedipus complex occurs during which stage?
questions.explain: In the phallic stage (ages 3–6), Freud claimed children desire the opposite-sex parent.

questions.q: When an adult gets stuck at a psychosexual stage, Freud called it:
questions.explain: Fixation is being stuck at a stage because of over- or under-gratification.

questions.q: Freud's method of having patients say whatever comes to mind is:
questions.explain: Free association lets uncensored thoughts reveal unconscious material.

questions.q: In therapy, when a patient redirects feelings about someone else onto the therapist, that's:
questions.explain: Transference is redirecting feelings from a significant person onto the analyst.

questions.q: Freud believed dreams were:
options: The royal road to the unconscious
questions.explain: Freud called dreams 'the royal road to the unconscious' — wishes disguised in symbols.

questions.q: The energy of the life instinct (libido) is said to drive which structure?
questions.explain: Libido is the psychic energy of the id's life instincts.

questions.q: Freud's three levels of consciousness were the conscious, preconscious, and:
questions.explain: The unconscious holds repressed drives and memories outside awareness (note: 'subconscious' is not a Freudian term).

rounds.title: Freud & Psychoanalysis
rounds.desc: Id, ego, superego; psychosexual stages; how Freud thought personality is built.

title: Defense Mechanisms
subject: Psychology 101
description: The ego's toolkit: spot each defense from a real-life scenario.

questions.q: After bombing an exam, Maya insists the professor 'has it out for her' and never considers that she didn't study. She is blaming her own failure on someone else — actually she's attributing her shortcomings to others. This is:
questions.explain: Projection: attributing your own unacceptable feelings or faults to someone else.

questions.q: A man furious at his boss comes home and snaps at his dog. This is:
questions.explain: Displacement redirects an impulse toward a safer target.

questions.q: An ex-smoker now lectures everyone about smoking and campaigns against it with unusual intensity. Freud would suspect:
questions.explain: Reaction formation: expressing the exact opposite of an unacceptable urge.

questions.q: A soldier recounts a traumatic battle in flat, purely factual detail, discussing strategy only. He is using:
questions.explain: Intellectualization avoids painful feelings by focusing on abstract, factual analysis.

questions.q: After a breakup, a student takes up boxing and channels everything into training. This healthy redirection is:
questions.explain: Sublimation channels unacceptable impulses into socially valued activities — Freud saw it as mature.

questions.q: A four-year-old who was toilet-trained starts wetting the bed after a new sibling arrives. This is:
questions.explain: Regression: returning to behavior from an earlier developmental stage under stress.

questions.q: A driver who caused an accident says 'well, the sun was in everyone's eyes, it could've happened to anybody.' This is:
questions.explain: Rationalization generates logical-sounding excuses to protect self-esteem.

questions.q: A woman cannot remember a genuinely traumatic childhood event at all — the memory is simply gone from awareness. The mechanism is:
questions.explain: Repression pushes threatening material out of conscious awareness entirely — Freud's foundational defense.

questions.q: A patient refuses to accept a serious diagnosis, insisting the labs 'must have mixed up the samples,' week after week. This is:
questions.explain: Denial is refusing to accept a painful reality.

questions.q: A shy student adopts the slang, style, and opinions of a popular athlete she admires, as if taking on his identity for protection. This is:
questions.explain: Identification: taking on the traits of someone more powerful or admired to bolster the self.

rounds.title: Defense Mechanisms
rounds.desc: The ego's toolkit: spot each defense from a real-life scenario.

title: Trait & Humanistic Personality
subject: Psychology 101
description: The Big Five, Maslow, Rogers, and the self — plus the biases that distort how we see ourselves.

questions.q: The Big Five factor 'O' stands for:
questions.explain: OCEAN: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism.

questions.q: Someone who is organized, dependable, and disciplined scores high in:
questions.explain: Conscientiousness covers self-discipline, planning, and dependability.

questions.q: According to Maslow, the need at the very top of the hierarchy is:
questions.explain: Self-actualization — fulfilling your potential — sits at the top, after basic needs are met.

questions.q: Carl Rogers believed people flourish when they receive ___ from others.
questions.explain: Unconditional positive regard — acceptance without conditions — lets the self-concept grow.

questions.q: The gap between your actual self and your ideal self, in Rogers' terms, produces:
questions.explain: Incongruence is the mismatch between self-concept and experience/ideal, producing anxiety.

questions.q: Bandura's belief in your own ability to succeed at a task is called:
questions.explain: Self-efficacy is task-specific confidence, built through mastery, modeling, and encouragement.

questions.q: Rotter's 'locus of control': people who believe outcomes depend on their own actions have a(n):
questions.explain: Internal locus = 'my choices drive outcomes'; external = 'luck and others decide.'

questions.q: The tendency to attribute your successes to yourself but your failures to outside forces is the:
questions.explain: Self-serving bias protects self-esteem: wins are mine, losses are circumstances.

questions.q: Feeling like a fraud who will be 'found out' despite real accomplishments is the:
questions.explain: The imposter phenomenon: high achievers who can't internalize their success.

questions.q: BIRGing refers to:
options: Basking in reflected glory of a successful group
questions.explain: BIRGing = Basking In Reflected Glory — 'we won!' when your team wins, distance when it loses.

rounds.title: Trait & Humanistic Personality
rounds.desc: The Big Five, Maslow, Rogers, and the self — plus the biases that distort how we see ourselves.

title: Object Relations & Closing the Gaps
subject: Psychology 101
description: Klein, Winnicott, Mahler — and the exam details students most often miss.

questions.q: Object relations theory shifts focus from Freud's drives to:
questions.explain: Object relations theorists argued relationships — especially with early caregivers — shape personality.

questions.q: Melanie Klein is known for developing:
options: Play therapy with children and object relations ideas
questions.explain: Klein pioneered play therapy and argued infants form internal 'objects' from early experiences.

questions.q: Winnicott's term for a blanket or toy that comforts a child separating from a caregiver is:
questions.explain: A transitional object (like a blanket) helps the child bridge dependence and independence.

questions.q: Winnicott's 'good enough mother' refers to a caregiver who:
options: Never lets the child feel frustration
Is adequately responsive without being perfect
questions.explain: 'Good enough' care is responsive but imperfect — small frustrations help the child develop.

questions.q: Margaret Mahler's theory centers on:
options: Separation-individuation in the first years of life
questions.explain: Mahler described how infants psychologically 'hatch' from symbiosis into separate selves.

questions.q: In Mahler's phases, the period where infant and mother are experienced as one unit is:
questions.explain: Symbiosis (roughly months 1–5): the infant experiences no boundary between self and mother.

questions.q: A toddler who ventures off to explore, then returns to the caregiver for emotional 'refueling,' is in Mahler's:
questions.explain: Rapprochement: toddlers oscillate between independence and needing the caregiver close.

questions.q: Anna Freud is best known in personality theory for:
questions.explain: Anna Freud's 'The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence' (1936) organized the defense mechanisms.

questions.q: Freud's genital stage begins at:
questions.explain: The genital stage starts at puberty, when sexual interests mature toward adult relationships.

questions.q: A patient unconsciously repeating childhood relationship patterns with the therapist is evidence of transference — the concept was central to which theorist's method?
questions.explain: Freud made transference a core tool of psychoanalytic treatment.

rounds.title: Object Relations & Closing the Gaps
rounds.desc: Klein, Winnicott, Mahler — and the exam details students most often miss.

title: Social Psychology Essentials
subject: Psychology 101
description: Attribution, conformity, obedience, and why groups change what we do.

questions.q: Overestimating personality and underestimating the situation when judging others is the:
questions.explain: The fundamental attribution error: we blame their character, excuse our own with circumstances.

questions.q: In Milgram's obedience studies, about what share of participants delivered the maximum shock?
questions.explain: Roughly 65% went to the maximum 450V when prompted by the experimenter.

questions.q: Asch's line studies demonstrated:
questions.explain: Asch showed people will give an obviously wrong answer to match a unanimous group.

questions.q: The presence of others making each person feel less responsible for helping is:
questions.explain: Diffusion of responsibility underlies the bystander effect — more witnesses, less help.

questions.q: When being watched improves performance on easy tasks but hurts on hard ones, that's:
questions.explain: Social facilitation: arousal from an audience boosts dominant (well-learned) responses.

questions.q: A group that suppresses dissent to preserve harmony, making a flawed decision, shows:
questions.explain: Groupthink: cohesion and pressure for unanimity override realistic appraisal.

questions.q: Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort from:
options: Holding two conflicting attitudes or acting against your beliefs
questions.explain: Festinger: inconsistency between attitudes and behavior creates pressure to change one of them.

questions.q: The foot-in-the-door technique works by:
options: Getting a small yes first, then asking for more
questions.explain: A small initial agreement makes a larger related request more likely to succeed.

questions.q: Prejudice is best defined as a(n):
options: Unjustified negative attitude toward a group
questions.explain: Prejudice = attitude; stereotype = belief; discrimination = behavior.

questions.q: Thinking your own good traits explain your success but your rival's success is luck is an example of:
questions.explain: Self-serving bias — the same pattern, applied to the comparison in the question.

The fundamental attribution error: we explain others' behavior with internal traits ("she's rude") while downplaying situational forces (she just got bad news) — yet we do the reverse for ourselves (the actor-observer bias).
options: Blaming situations for our own failures
Overemphasizing personality and underemphasizing situations when judging others
Assuming everyone thinks the way we do
questions.q: The fundamental attribution error is:

questions.explain: Asch's line-judgment studies: about 37% of responses conformed to a unanimous majority giving clearly wrong answers — showing normative social influence (the need to fit in) can override obvious perception.
options: Gave obviously wrong answers to match the group
questions.q: In Asch's conformity experiments, participants:

questions.explain: Milgram (1963): 65% of participants delivered the maximum 450-volt shock to a "learner" when an authority figure insisted — revealing how powerfully legitimate authority can override personal conscience.
options: Ordinary people would deliver dangerous shocks when ordered by an authority
questions.q: Milgram's obedience studies are most famous for showing:

questions.explain: Festinger's cognitive dissonance: inconsistency between beliefs, or between a belief and a behavior, creates tension we reduce by changing the attitude — e.g., smokers downplaying health risks, or justifying a boring task they were paid $1 to praise.
options: Discomfort from holding conflicting cognitions, resolved by changing attitudes
questions.q: Cognitive dissonance is:

questions.explain: Darley and Latané: the more bystanders present, the LESS likely any individual helps — due to diffusion of responsibility ("someone else will act") and pluralistic ignorance (reading others' inaction as "no emergency").
options: People are less likely to help when others are present
questions.q: The bystander effect states that:

questions.explain: Zajonc's mere exposure effect: repeated exposure to a neutral stimulus increases liking for it — explaining catchy songs, familiar faces, and why advertisements repeat endlessly.
options: Liking a song more after hearing it repeatedly
questions.q: Which best illustrates the mere exposure effect?

questions.explain: Social facilitation (Triplett, Zajonc): the presence of others boosts arousal, which ENHANCES well-practiced or easy tasks but IMPAIRS complex or new ones. "Reduced effort in groups" is social LOAFING instead.
options: Improved performance on well-learned tasks when others are present
questions.q: Social facilitation refers to:

questions.explain: Janis's groupthink: highly cohesive groups under pressure suppress dissent to preserve harmony — producing flawed decisions (the Bay of Pigs invasion, the Challenger launch). Prevention: devil's advocates, anonymous input, outside experts.
options: Groups are diverse and debate openly
A cohesive group prioritizes harmony over critical thinking
The decision at stake is unimportant
questions.q: Groupthink is most likely when:

questions.explain: Foot-in-the-door: agreeing to a small request shifts self-perception ("I'm a helpful person"), making the larger follow-up harder to refuse — consistency with one's own prior behavior. Large-then-small is door-in-the-face.
options: People comply with a small request, then agree to a larger one to stay consistent
Large requests seem smaller by comparison
questions.q: The foot-in-the-door technique works because:

questions.explain: The classic ABCs: prejudice is the AFFECTIVE component (a prejudged attitude), stereotypes are the COGNITIVE component (beliefs about a group), and discrimination is the BEHAVIORAL component (unfair actions).
options: Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is behavior
questions.q: Prejudice differs from discrimination in that:

title: Psychological Disorders & Therapy
subject: Psychology 101
description: DSM-5 categories, signature symptoms, and matching therapies to schools.

questions.q: Hallucinations and delusions are called ___ symptoms of schizophrenia.
questions.explain: Positive symptoms ADD experiences (hallucinations, delusions). Negative symptoms subtract (flat affect, avolition).

questions.q: Flat affect and loss of motivation in schizophrenia are ___ symptoms.
questions.explain: Negative symptoms are absences: flat affect, poverty of speech, avolition.

questions.q: OCD consists of obsessions, which are ___, and compulsions, which are ___.
questions.explain: Obsessions are intrusive thoughts; compulsions are rituals meant to neutralize them.

questions.q: A major depressive episode requires symptoms for at least:
questions.explain: Two weeks of depressed mood or anhedonia plus other symptoms marks a major depressive episode.

questions.q: Bipolar disorder involves depressive episodes alternating with:
questions.explain: Mania: elevated mood, racing thoughts, reduced need for sleep, risky behavior.

questions.q: Systematic desensitization — gradual exposure paired with relaxation — is a ___ therapy.
questions.explain: Wolpe's technique applies classical conditioning to unlearn fear.

questions.q: Unconditional positive regard is the signature condition of ___ therapy.
questions.explain: Rogers' client-centered therapy: unconditional positive regard, empathy, genuineness.

questions.q: Beck's cognitive therapy focuses on:
questions.explain: Cognitive therapy targets distorted thinking patterns that drive distress.

questions.q: A diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder requires the person to be at least:
questions.explain: ASPD requires age 18+ plus evidence of conduct disorder before age 15.

questions.q: The diathesis-stress model says disorders arise from:
questions.explain: Diathesis (predisposition) + stress = onset — the standard biopsychosocial explanation.

rounds.title: Psychological Disorders & Therapy
rounds.desc: DSM-5 categories, signature symptoms, and matching therapies to schools.

title: Cells & Energy
subject: Biology 101
description: Organelles, membranes, photosynthesis, and cellular respiration.

questions.q: Which organelle produces most of a cell's ATP?
questions.explain: Mitochondria run cellular respiration, producing most ATP.

questions.q: The cell membrane is mainly built from a bilayer of:
questions.explain: The phospholipid bilayer forms the membrane's basic structure.

questions.q: Photosynthesis takes place in the:
questions.explain: Chloroplasts capture light energy to build sugars.

questions.q: Which molecule is the cell's main energy currency?
questions.explain: ATP stores and releases energy for cellular work.

questions.q: Movement of water across a membrane from low to high solute concentration is:
questions.explain: Osmosis is water's diffusion across a selectively permeable membrane.

questions.q: Which structure makes proteins?
questions.explain: Ribosomes translate mRNA into proteins.

questions.q: Plant cells differ from animal cells because plant cells have:
questions.explain: Cell walls and chloroplasts are found in plant cells, not animal cells.

questions.q: The overall equation for cellular respiration produces:
questions.explain: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP energy.

questions.q: Enzymes speed up reactions by:
questions.explain: Enzymes lower the activation energy needed for a reaction.

questions.q: A solution with more solute than a cell, causing the cell to shrink, is:
questions.explain: Hypertonic solutions draw water out of the cell.

rounds.title: Cells & Energy
rounds.desc: Organelles, membranes, photosynthesis, and cellular respiration.

title: Cell Division: Mitosis & Meiosis
subject: Biology 101
description: Interphase and the cell cycle, how mitosis copies a cell, how meiosis halves the chromosome number and creates variation, and what happens when division goes wrong.

questions.q: Mitosis in a human body cell produces:
options: One diploid and one haploid cell
questions.explain: Mitosis copies one diploid cell into two diploid cells with the same DNA, for growth and repair.

questions.q: During metaphase of mitosis, the chromosomes:
options: Line up along the middle of the cell
questions.explain: Chromosomes align on the metaphase plate so each new cell can receive one copy of each.

questions.q: Crossing over, which swaps segments between homologous chromosomes, occurs during:
questions.explain: Crossing over in prophase I shuffles alleles between homologs, creating new combinations passed to gametes.

questions.q: Meiosis in an animal produces:
questions.explain: Two rounds of division after one DNA replication cut the chromosome number in half and produce four varied gametes.

questions.q: A cell copies its DNA during which part of the cell cycle?
questions.explain: DNA synthesis happens in the S phase, between the G1 and G2 growth phases of interphase.

questions.q: In anaphase of mitosis, the structures that separate and move to opposite poles are:
questions.explain: Sister chromatids split at their centromeres and are pulled to opposite ends of the cell.

questions.q: Cytokinesis is the division of the:
questions.explain: After the nucleus divides, cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm, in animal cells by a pinching cleavage furrow.

questions.q: Besides crossing over, meiosis increases genetic variation through:
questions.explain: How each homologous pair lines up in metaphase I is random, so gametes get different mixes of maternal and paternal chromosomes.

questions.q: Cancer develops when cells:
options: Divide uncontrollably and ignore growth signals
questions.explain: Mutations in genes that control the cell cycle remove the brakes on division, forming tumors.

questions.q: A human gamete (sperm or egg) is haploid, meaning it contains:
questions.explain: Meiosis halves the usual 46 chromosomes to 23, so fertilization restores the full set.

rounds.title: Cell Division: Mitosis & Meiosis
rounds.desc: Interphase and the cell cycle, how mitosis copies a cell, how meiosis halves the chromosome number and creates variation, and what happens when division goes wrong.

title: Genetics & Heredity
subject: Biology 101
description: DNA, Punnett squares, inheritance patterns, and mutations.

questions.q: The shape of DNA is a:
questions.explain: Watson and Crick's model: DNA is a double helix.

questions.q: In DNA, adenine (A) pairs with:
questions.explain: Base pairing: A–T and C–G in DNA.

questions.q: A genotype of two different alleles, like Bb, is called:
questions.explain: Heterozygous means two different alleles for a gene.

questions.q: Crossing Bb × Bb, roughly what fraction of offspring show the recessive trait?
questions.explain: Bb × Bb gives 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb — 25% show the recessive phenotype.

questions.q: The process of copying DNA into RNA is:
questions.explain: Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template; translation builds protein.

questions.q: Which RNA carries amino acids to the ribosome?
questions.explain: Transfer RNA (tRNA) brings amino acids matched to codons.

questions.q: A change in a DNA sequence is called a:
questions.explain: Mutations are any changes to the DNA sequence.

questions.q: Humans normally have how many chromosomes in a body cell?
questions.explain: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) in a typical human somatic cell.

questions.q: An allele that masks another allele is:
questions.explain: Dominant alleles are expressed even with one copy.

questions.q: When both alleles show up fully in the phenotype (like AB blood), it's:
questions.explain: Codominance: both traits appear, e.g., AB blood type.

rounds.title: Genetics & Heredity
rounds.desc: DNA, Punnett squares, inheritance patterns, and mutations.

description: Mendelian crosses, dominance patterns, sex-linked traits, and how meiosis shuffles genes.

questions.explain: The genotype ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, but AA and Aa both show the dominant phenotype, so the visible ratio is 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
questions.q: In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa), what is the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring?

questions.explain: The phenotype is what you can observe (tall, blue eyes). The genotype is the underlying set of alleles, which may include hidden recessives.
questions.q: What is the term for the observable physical characteristics of an organism?

questions.explain: Males are XY and females are XX. The Y chromosome carries genes that trigger male development; YY is not viable.
questions.q: In humans, which sex chromosome combination produces a male?

questions.explain: A son gets his single X chromosome from his mother. A carrier passes the affected X to half her sons on average, and with no second X to mask it, he will express the trait.
questions.q: A woman who is a carrier for an X-linked recessive disorder (like hemophilia) has a son. What is the probability the son inherits the disorder?

questions.explain: Incomplete dominance blends the two alleles, so red plus white gives pink. AB blood is codominance, where both alleles show fully.
options: A red flower crossed with a white flower producing pink offspring
A person with AB blood type
A tall pea plant from a Tt cross
A black Labrador puppy from two yellow Lab parents
questions.q: Which cross is a classic example of incomplete dominance?

questions.explain: Crossing over in prophase I swaps segments between homologous chromosomes, building recombinant chromosomes. Independent assortment shuffles whole chromosomes, not segments.
questions.q: During meiosis, which process creates brand-new allele combinations on a single chromosome?

questions.explain: Crossing a dominant-showing individual with a homozygous recessive (aa) reveals whether it is AA or Aa: any recessive offspring proves it was Aa.
options: Whether a trait is dominant or recessive
The genotype of an individual showing the dominant phenotype
The mutation rate of a gene
questions.q: A test cross is performed to determine what?

questions.explain: Squares stand for males and circles for females; shading means the person expresses the trait. A half-shaded shape usually means a known carrier.
questions.q: In a pedigree chart, a filled-in (shaded) square represents what?

questions.explain: Messenger RNA is transcribed from DNA in the nucleus, then travels to the ribosome where its code is translated into protein.
questions.q: Which molecule carries genetic information from the nucleus to the ribosome?

questions.explain: Linked genes are physically joined, so they are inherited as a unit unless crossing over happens to split them, which is rare when they are close.
options: Be separated by crossing over frequently
questions.q: Two genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to do what?

subject: Biology 101
title: Genetics & Inheritance
Evolution & Natural Selection
subject: Biology 101
description: Darwin, adaptation, speciation, and evidence for evolution.

questions.q: Natural selection acts on which level?
questions.explain: Selection acts on phenotypes; evolution is the change in allele frequencies that follows.

questions.q: Structures with the same origin but different functions (bat wing, human arm) are:
questions.explain: Homologous structures share ancestry; analogous ones share function only.

questions.q: A trait that improves survival and reproduction is an:
questions.explain: Adaptations are heritable traits shaped by selection that aid fitness.

questions.q: When two populations can no longer interbreed, they are separate:
questions.explain: Reproductive isolation defines separate species under the biological species concept.

questions.q: Genetic drift has the biggest effect in:
questions.explain: Random changes matter most when the population is small.

questions.q: The raw material that natural selection works on comes from:
questions.explain: Without heritable variation, selection has nothing to act on.

questions.q: Darwin developed his theory partly from observing finches on the:
questions.explain: Galápagos finches' beaks varied by island and food source.

questions.q: A structure with no current function, like the human appendix, is called:
questions.explain: Vestigial structures are reduced remnants of ancestral features.
Selection favors individuals whose traits (phenotypes) help them survive and reproduce. Evolution - the shift in allele frequencies - is measured in populations, not individuals.
options: The phenotype of an individual organism
The genotype of an individual organism
questions.q: Natural selection acts directly on which of the following?

questions.explain: Analogous structures serve the same function but evolved independently from different origins - a sign of convergent evolution, not shared ancestry.
questions.q: The wings of a bat and the wings of a butterfly are an example of what?

questions.explain: Hardy-Weinberg describes a non-evolving population: no selection, no mutation, no gene flow, random mating, and a very large population.
questions.q: Which condition is required for a population to stay in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

questions.explain: Random changes hit hardest when few individuals carry the genes - a few deaths or migrations can swing allele frequencies dramatically.
questions.q: Genetic drift has the greatest effect on allele frequencies in which kind of population?

questions.explain: One ancestral finch diversified into many species with specialized beaks, each filling a different ecological niche - evolution's signature pattern of one lineage splitting many ways.
questions.q: Darwin's finches of the Galapagos Islands are a classic example of what?

questions.explain: Vestigial structures are reduced leftovers from a functional structure in an ancestor - evidence of descent with modification.
questions.q: A body part with no current function, like the human appendix, is called what?

questions.explain: Disruptive selection pushes a population toward both extremes, which can split one population into two - a first step toward speciation.
questions.q: Which type of natural selection favors both extreme phenotypes over the intermediate?

questions.explain: Allopatric speciation starts when a physical barrier blocks gene flow, letting the separated groups diverge genetically.
questions.q: Two groups of the same species stop interbreeding because a river divides them. This reproductive isolation is called what?

questions.explain: Homologous structures - same blueprint, different jobs - point to descent from a common ancestor with modifications over time.
questions.q: Humans, dogs, and whales all have forelimbs built on the same bone pattern. This is evidence of what?

questions.explain: Resistance already exists in a few cells; antibiotics kill the rest, and the survivors pass resistance on. Selection works on pre-existing variation - it does not create it.
options: Antibiotics mutate bacterial DNA on contact
Bacteria learn to resist after repeated exposure
Resistant bacteria survive treatment and pass their resistance genes to offspring
questions.q: Antibiotic resistance spreads so quickly through bacterial populations mainly because...?

rounds.title: Evolution & Natural Selection
rounds.desc: Darwin, adaptation, speciation, and evidence for evolution.

title: Ecology Basics
subject: Biology 101
description: Food webs, cycles, populations, and how organisms interact.

questions.q: Organisms that make their own food are called:
questions.explain: Producers (autotrophs) capture energy, usually by photosynthesis.

questions.q: Roughly how much energy transfers from one trophic level to the next?
questions.explain: The 10% rule: most energy is lost as heat at each level.

questions.q: A relationship where both species benefit is:
questions.explain: Mutualism benefits both partners.

questions.q: The maximum population an environment can support long-term is its:
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is set by resources like food, water, and space.

questions.q: Bacteria that break down dead matter and return nutrients to soil are:
questions.explain: Decomposers recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem.

questions.q: Which cycle relies heavily on bacteria to fix an atmospheric gas into usable form?
questions.explain: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N₂ into ammonia plants can use.

questions.q: When a predator and prey compete over the same limited resource, that's:
questions.explain: Competition between different species is interspecific.

questions.q: The first species to colonize bare rock after a disturbance are:
questions.explain: Pioneer species start ecological succession on bare surfaces.
Producers like plants and algae form the base of every food chain; every other level ultimately eats them or something that ate them.
questions.q: In a food chain, the organisms that convert sunlight into food energy are called what?

questions.explain: The 10% rule: most energy is lost as heat and metabolic work. This is why food chains are short - there is not enough energy left for many top predators.
questions.q: Roughly how much energy is passed from one trophic level to the next?

questions.explain: Commensalism is a one-sided win, like barnacles hitching a ride on a whale. Mutualism helps both; parasitism helps one and harms the other.
questions.q: A relationship where one species benefits and the other is unaffected is called what?

questions.explain: The warm, wet, stable climate near the equator supports more species per area than any other biome - possibly half of all known species.
questions.q: Which biome has the highest biodiversity on Earth?

questions.explain: Carrying capacity (K) is set by available resources like food, water, and space; growth slows as a population approaches it.
questions.q: The maximum population size an environment can support long-term is called its what?

questions.explain: Bacteria and fungi break down dead matter and recycle its nutrients back to producers, closing the nutrient loop.
options: Produce most of the oxygen we breathe
questions.q: Decomposers are essential to ecosystems because they do what?

questions.explain: Exponential growth makes a J-shaped curve - growth keeps accelerating. Logistic growth adds carrying capacity and levels off into an S-curve.
questions.q: A population growing with unlimited resources shows which growth pattern?

questions.explain: Photosynthesis fixes CO2 into sugars; respiration, burning, and decay all release CO2 back into the air.
questions.q: In the carbon cycle, plants pull carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere through what process?

questions.explain: Remove a keystone species like sea otters and the whole food web shifts. Abundance is not what matters - ecological impact is.
options: Is the most abundant species in its habitat
Has an outsized effect on its ecosystem relative to its numbers
Always sits at the top of the food chain
Was the first species to colonize an area
questions.q: A keystone species is one that does what?

questions.explain: Primary succession starts where no soil exists and builds from scratch; secondary succession follows a disturbance where soil is already present.
options: On bare rock or new volcanic land with no soil
questions.q: Primary succession takes place in what kind of location?

rounds.title: Ecology Basics
rounds.desc: Food webs, cycles, populations, and how organisms interact.

title: Plant Structure & Function
subject: Biology 101
description: Roots, stems, and leaves; xylem and phloem transport; stomata and transpiration; flowers, pollination, and seed dispersal.

questions.q: The vascular tissue that carries water and dissolved minerals upward from roots to leaves is the:
questions.explain: Xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes; evaporation from the leaves pulls the water column upward.

questions.q: Phloem tissue mainly transports:
options: Sugars made in the leaves to the rest of the plant
questions.explain: Phloem moves the products of photosynthesis from sources like leaves to sinks like roots, fruits, and growing tips.

questions.q: The small pores in a leaf's surface that open and close to allow gas exchange are called:
questions.explain: Guard cells change shape to open stomata for carbon dioxide intake, at the cost of losing water vapor.

questions.q: Most photosynthesis in a typical leaf takes place in:
questions.explain: Palisade mesophyll cells contain the most chloroplasts and sit where sunlight is strongest, just under the upper epidermis.

questions.q: Transpiration is best defined as:
options: The uptake of minerals by roots
The loss of water vapor from a plant's leaves
The movement of sugar through phloem
questions.explain: Transpiration drives the flow of water through the plant and also cools the leaves, much like sweating.

questions.q: Root hairs increase a root's ability to absorb water and minerals because they:
options: Greatly increase the root's surface area
questions.explain: Thousands of thin root hairs put far more absorbing surface in contact with the soil.

questions.q: In a flower, pollen is produced in the:
questions.explain: The anther sits on top of the stamen, the male reproductive structure, and releases pollen grains.

questions.q: Producing seeds that are carried far from the parent plant is an advantage mainly because it:
options: Reduces competition between offspring and the parent
Guarantees the seeds land in water
questions.explain: Dispersal by wind, water, or animals spreads offspring into new territory with less competition for light and nutrients.

questions.q: A plant bending and growing toward a light source is an example of:
questions.explain: Growth toward light is positive phototropism, driven by the hormone auxin accumulating on the shaded side.

questions.q: The region of rapidly dividing cells at the tips of roots and shoots, responsible for growth in length, is the:
questions.explain: Apical meristems at the tips produce new cells that elongate, pushing roots deeper and shoots higher.

rounds.title: Plant Structure & Function
rounds.desc: Roots, stems, and leaves; xylem and phloem transport; stomata and transpiration; flowers, pollination, and seed dispersal.

title: Human Body Systems
subject: Biology 101
description: Circulation, respiration, immunity, and homeostasis.

questions.q: Blood returning from the body enters the heart at the:
questions.explain: Body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body.

questions.q: Gas exchange in the lungs happens in the:
questions.explain: Alveoli are tiny air sacs wrapped in capillaries where O₂ and CO₂ diffuse.

questions.q: The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen is:
questions.explain: Hemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues.

questions.q: Vaccines work by:
options: Training memory cells before real infection
questions.explain: Vaccines present a harmless antigen so memory B/T cells are ready for the real pathogen.

questions.q: Homeostasis is maintained mainly through ___ feedback.
questions.explain: Negative feedback reverses a change (temperature, blood sugar). Positive feedback amplifies and is rare.

questions.q: Which organ filters blood and produces urine?
questions.explain: Kidneys filter blood, balance fluids, and form urine.

questions.q: Antibodies are produced by:
questions.explain: B cells mature into plasma cells that secrete antibodies against specific antigens.

questions.q: The diaphragm contracting causes you to:
questions.explain: The diaphragm flattens, expanding the chest, and air rushes in.

rounds.title: Human Body Systems
rounds.desc: Circulation, respiration, immunity, and homeostasis.

title: Microbes & Disease
subject: Biology 101
description: Bacteria vs viruses, transmission, and how we fight infection.

questions.q: Viruses differ from bacteria because viruses:
options: Are not alive and must hijack a host cell
questions.explain: Viruses are non-living particles of DNA/RNA in a protein coat — they need host cells to replicate.

questions.q: Antibiotics are effective against:
questions.explain: Antibiotics attack bacterial structures. They do nothing against viruses.

questions.q: Malaria is transmitted by a mosquito, making the mosquito a:
questions.explain: Vectors are organisms that carry pathogens between hosts.

questions.q: Binary fission is how ___ reproduce.
questions.explain: Bacteria copy their DNA and split into two — fast asexual reproduction.

questions.q: Quarantine applies to people who are ___; isolation applies to people who are ___.
questions.explain: Quarantine separates the exposed; isolation separates the ill.

questions.q: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?
questions.explain: Influenza is viral; strep, TB, and cholera are bacterial.

questions.q: Antibiotic resistance develops mainly because:
questions.explain: Stopping early leaves the hardiest bacteria alive to multiply — selection in action.

questions.q: Pasteurization protects food by:
questions.explain: Pasteurization uses controlled heat to cut pathogen counts in milk and juices.

rounds.title: Microbes & Disease
rounds.desc: Bacteria vs viruses, transmission, and how we fight infection.

title: Biotechnology & Genetic Engineering
subject: Biology 101
description: PCR, gel electrophoresis, restriction enzymes, recombinant DNA, CRISPR, DNA profiling, cloning, and gene therapy, with their real-world uses.

questions.q: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a laboratory technique used to:
options: Make millions of copies of a specific DNA segment
Read the exact order of bases in DNA
questions.explain: PCR cycles of heating and cooling let enzymes copy a targeted DNA region exponentially, starting from a tiny sample.

questions.q: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments mainly by their:
options: Size, with smaller fragments traveling farther
questions.explain: An electric field pulls negatively charged DNA through a gel; shorter fragments move faster and farther.

questions.q: Restriction enzymes are proteins that:
options: Cut DNA at specific recognition sequences
Unzip the double helix during replication
questions.explain: Bacteria use restriction enzymes against invading viruses, and researchers use them as precise molecular scissors.

questions.q: CRISPR-Cas9 technology allows scientists to:
options: Clone a whole organism in one step
Edit a chosen gene at a targeted location in the genome
questions.explain: A guide RNA steers the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA sequence, where it cuts so the cell's repair machinery changes the gene.

questions.q: Recombinant DNA is DNA that:
options: Combines genetic material from two different sources
questions.explain: A human insulin gene inserted into a bacterial plasmid is recombinant DNA, joining DNA from two species in one molecule.

questions.q: In genetic engineering, bacterial plasmids are commonly used as:
options: Vectors that carry a foreign gene into a cell
Markers that glow in the dark
questions.explain: A plasmid vector ferries the gene of interest into bacteria, which then copy it every time they divide.

questions.q: Human insulin used by many people with diabetes is produced by:
options: Bacteria engineered to carry the human insulin gene
Synthetic chemical reactions with no living cells
questions.explain: Engineered bacteria grow in large vats and secrete human insulin, which is purified for medical use.

questions.q: Forensic DNA profiling identifies individuals by comparing:
options: The exact sequence of every gene
Highly variable repeated regions of DNA called STRs
questions.explain: Short tandem repeats vary greatly between people, so matching STR patterns from a sample and a suspect is powerful evidence.

questions.q: A clone produced by somatic cell nuclear transfer is:
options: A mixture of two parents' genes
Genetically identical to the donor of the nucleus
questions.explain: The nucleus of a body cell is placed into an emptied egg, so the offspring's nuclear DNA matches the nucleus donor, like Dolly the sheep.

questions.q: Gene therapy aims to treat an inherited disorder by:
options: Delivering a working copy of a faulty gene to the patient's cells
questions.explain: A corrected gene, often carried by a modified virus, lets the patient's own cells make the missing or broken protein.
