rounds.desc: PCR, gel electrophoresis, restriction enzymes, recombinant DNA, CRISPR, DNA profiling, cloning, and gene therapy, with their real-world uses.

title: Matter & Measurement
subject: Chemistry 101
description: States of matter, physical vs chemical change, density, and sig figs.

questions.q: Dry ice turning directly into gas is:
questions.explain: Sublimation: solid → gas without becoming liquid.

questions.q: Melting ice is a ___ change.
questions.explain: Phase changes are physical — the substance (H₂O) is unchanged.

questions.q: Density is calculated as:
questions.explain: Density = mass/volume. Water's density is 1 g/mL.

questions.q: An object with density 0.6 g/mL placed in water will:
questions.explain: Less dense than water (1 g/mL) → it floats.

questions.q: How many significant figures are in 0.00450?
questions.explain: Leading zeros don't count; the trailing zero after 5 does: 4, 5, 0 = 3 sig figs.

questions.q: The metric prefix 'milli-' means:
questions.explain: Milli- = one thousandth (millimeter, milliliter).

questions.q: During a phase change, added heat:
options: Does not raise temperature until the change completes
questions.explain: The energy goes into breaking intermolecular attractions — temperature plateaus.

questions.q: A homogeneous mixture is also called a:
questions.explain: Solutions are homogeneous mixtures — uniform throughout.

rounds.title: Matter & Measurement
rounds.desc: States of matter, physical vs chemical change, density, and sig figs.

description: Protons, neutrons, electrons, isotopes, and electron configuration.

questions.explain: The atomic number (Z) defines the element: every carbon atom has 6 protons, every oxygen has 8. Protons plus neutrons gives the mass number instead.
options: The number of protons in its nucleus
The number of neutrons in its nucleus
The total of protons and neutrons
The number of electron shells it has
questions.q: The atomic number of an element is equal to what?

questions.explain: Isotopes share the same proton count but differ in neutrons, which is why carbon-12 and carbon-14 behave the same chemically but have different masses.
options: Number of electrons in a neutral atom
questions.q: Isotopes of the same element differ in what?

questions.explain: Electrons carry a negative (-) charge; protons are positive (+) and neutrons are neutral (0).
questions.q: Which subatomic particle carries a negative electric charge?

questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number (14) minus atomic number (6 protons) = 8 neutrons.
questions.q: Carbon-14 has 6 protons. How many neutrons does it have?

questions.explain: The 2n^2 rule gives shell capacities of 2, 8, 18, and 32 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4.
questions.q: How many electrons can the first electron shell (n = 1) hold at most?

questions.explain: Protons and neutrons in the tiny nucleus carry nearly all of the atom's mass; electrons contribute almost nothing.
questions.q: Nearly all of an atom's mass is concentrated where?

questions.explain: An anion has extra electrons (negative charge); a cation forms when an atom LOSES electrons (positive charge).
questions.q: An atom that gains an extra electron becomes what?

questions.explain: In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons, so sodium (atomic number 11) has 11 electrons.
questions.q: How many electrons does a neutral sodium atom (atomic number 11) have?

questions.explain: Count the superscripts: 2 + 2 + 6 + 1 = 11 electrons, which matches sodium's atomic number.
questions.q: Which element has the electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1?

questions.explain: Valence electrons sit in the outermost shell and are the ones gained, lost, or shared - they decide how an element bonds and reacts.
options: They determine the atom's total mass
They determine an element's chemical reactivity
questions.q: Valence electrons matter most in chemistry because they do what?

subject: Chemistry 101
title: Atomic Structure
Atoms & the Periodic Table
subject: Chemistry 101
description: Subatomic particles, atomic numbers, groups, and periods.

questions.q: The atomic number of an element equals its number of:
options: Electrons in the outer shell only
questions.explain: Atomic number = proton count, which defines the element.

questions.q: Which particle has a negative charge?
questions.explain: Electrons carry a −1 charge; protons +1; neutrons 0.

questions.q: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are:
questions.explain: Isotopes differ in neutrons, so they differ in mass.

questions.q: Elements in the same column of the periodic table share:
questions.explain: Groups (columns) share valence-electron patterns and similar behavior.

questions.q: How many electrons can the first shell hold?
questions.explain: The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons.

questions.q: Sodium (Na) has atomic number 11. A neutral sodium atom has how many electrons?
questions.explain: Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons: 11.

questions.q: Which group contains the highly reactive alkali metals?
questions.explain: Group 1 (except hydrogen) are the alkali metals.

questions.q: The noble gases are known for being:
questions.explain: Full outer shells make noble gases very unreactive.

questions.q: An atom that gains or loses electrons becomes a(n):
questions.explain: Ions are charged atoms (or groups of atoms).

questions.q: The mass number equals protons plus:
questions.explain: Mass number = protons + neutrons.

rounds.title: Atoms & the Periodic Table
rounds.desc: Subatomic particles, atomic numbers, groups, and periods.

title: Bonding & Reactions
subject: Chemistry 101
description: Ionic vs covalent bonds, balancing equations, and reaction types.

questions.q: An ionic bond forms by:
questions.explain: Ionic bonds: electrons transfer, typically from a metal to a nonmetal.

questions.q: A covalent bond involves:
questions.explain: Covalent bonds share electron pairs between atoms.

questions.q: The chemical formula H₂O tells you each molecule has:
questions.explain: Subscripts count atoms: H₂O = two H, one O.

questions.q: In a balanced equation, atoms must be:
options: Equal in number on both sides
questions.explain: Conservation of mass: same atoms in, same atoms out.

questions.q: A reaction that releases heat is:
questions.explain: Exothermic reactions give off energy, usually as heat.

questions.q: The pH scale measures:
questions.explain: pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic.

questions.q: Which is a sign a chemical reaction occurred?
questions.explain: Color change, gas, precipitate, or temperature change signal a reaction.

questions.q: A catalyst speeds a reaction by:
questions.explain: Catalysts lower activation energy and are not consumed.

questions.q: Table salt (NaCl) is held together by which bond type?
questions.explain: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine: a classic ionic compound.

questions.q: Water molecules stick to each other mainly through:
questions.explain: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules give water its cohesion.

rounds.title: Bonding & Reactions
rounds.desc: Ionic vs covalent bonds, balancing equations, and reaction types.

description: Ionic, covalent, hydrogen, and metallic bonds - and why atoms stick together.

questions.explain: In ionic bonding (typical of a metal plus a nonmetal), the transfer creates ions whose opposite charges attract and hold the compound together.
options: Electrons are transferred from one atom to another
Electrons are shared equally between atoms
Atoms float in a shared sea of electrons
A hydrogen atom bridges two larger atoms
questions.q: An ionic bond forms when what happens?

questions.explain: Covalent bonds are shared electron pairs, letting both atoms complete their outer shells - the standard bond between nonmetals.
questions.q: In a covalent bond, atoms are held together by what?

questions.explain: Sodium donates its valence electron to chlorine, forming Na+ and Cl- ions that attract - a classic ionic compound.
questions.q: Table salt (sodium chloride, NaCl) is held together mainly by what kind of bond?

questions.explain: Each covalent bond is one shared pair (2 electrons). A double bond has two pairs, so 4 shared electrons total.
questions.q: A double covalent bond shares a total of how many electrons?

questions.explain: Oxygen is more electronegative, so it holds the shared electrons closer, gaining a partial negative charge; water's bent shape keeps the positive and negative ends apart.
options: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does
It is held together by ionic bonds
Hydrogen has more protons than oxygen
Its molecules are shaped in a straight line
questions.q: Water is a polar molecule because of what?

questions.explain: Hydrogen bonds are individually weak but add up: they zip DNA's strands together and make water cohesive with a high boiling point.
options: They are the strongest type of chemical bond
They hold DNA's two strands together and give water its special properties
They form the covalent backbone of proteins
questions.q: Hydrogen bonds are important in biology because they do what?

questions.explain: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, so they share electrons. NaCl, MgO, and KBr pair metals with nonmetals - ionic compounds.
questions.q: Which compound is held together only by covalent bonds?

questions.explain: Metallic bonding's mobile sea of electrons carries current and lets metal atoms slide past each other without breaking - conductivity and malleability.
options: Delocalized electrons that move freely through the metal
Ionic charges locked in a rigid lattice
questions.q: Metals conduct electricity well because of what?

questions.explain: Mg donates its 2 valence electrons, one to each of two chlorine atoms (7 valence electrons each), satisfying everyone: MgCl2.
questions.q: Magnesium (2 valence electrons) bonds with chlorine (7 valence electrons). What is the formula of the compound?

questions.explain: A full outer shell of 8 electrons (2 for hydrogen and helium) is especially stable, and most bonding can be understood as atoms chasing that state.
options: Equal numbers of protons and electrons
questions.q: The octet rule says atoms tend to bond in ways that give them what?

subject: Chemistry 101
title: Chemical Bonds
Stoichiometry & the Mole
subject: Chemistry 101
description: Avogadro's number, molar mass, mole ratios from balanced equations, limiting reactants, percent yield, and empirical formulas.

questions.q: One mole of any substance contains how many particles (Avogadro's number)?
questions.explain: One mole always contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles, whether atoms, molecules, or ions.

questions.q: The molar mass of water, H2O, is approximately:
questions.explain: Two hydrogens (2 x 1) plus one oxygen (16) give 2 + 16 = 18 g/mol.

questions.q: From the equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, how many moles of water form from 4 moles of H2?
questions.explain: The ratio of H2 to H2O is 2:2, or 1:1, so 4 moles of H2 make 4 moles of water.

questions.q: In a chemical reaction, the limiting reactant is the reactant that:
options: Runs out first and limits how much product can form
Is present in the greatest amount
questions.explain: Once the limiting reactant is used up, the reaction stops, even if other reactants remain.

questions.q: How many moles are in 44 grams of carbon dioxide, CO2, if its molar mass is 44 g/mol?
questions.explain: Moles = mass / molar mass = 44 g / 44 g/mol = 1 mol.

questions.q: Percent yield compares:
options: The actual yield to the theoretical yield
questions.explain: Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100, and it shows how efficient a real reaction was.

questions.q: In the balanced equation CH4 + __O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, the coefficient in front of O2 is:
questions.explain: Balancing the oxygens: the right side has 2 + 2 = 4 oxygen atoms, so 2 O2 molecules are needed on the left.

questions.q: An empirical formula shows:
options: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound
The exact number of atoms in one molecule
questions.explain: Glucose has the molecular formula C6H12O6 but the empirical formula CH2O, the simplest 1:2:1 ratio.

questions.q: From N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, how many moles of ammonia (NH3) form from 3 moles of H2 and excess N2?
questions.explain: The ratio of H2 to NH3 is 3:2, so 3 moles of H2 produce 2 moles of NH3.

questions.q: At standard temperature and pressure (STP), one mole of an ideal gas occupies about:
questions.explain: The molar volume at STP (0 degrees C and 1 atm) is 22.4 liters for any ideal gas.

rounds.title: Stoichiometry & the Mole
rounds.desc: Avogadro's number, molar mass, mole ratios from balanced equations, limiting reactants, percent yield, and empirical formulas.

title: Acids, Bases & Solutions
subject: Chemistry 101
description: pH in daily life, neutralization, concentration, and mixtures.

questions.q: Pure water has a pH of:
questions.explain: pH 7 is neutral — pure water is neither acidic nor basic.

questions.q: Lemon juice, with a pH around 2, is:
questions.explain: pH below 7 means acidic.

questions.q: Mixing an acid and a base produces water and a salt in a ___ reaction.
questions.explain: Neutralization: acid + base → salt + water.

questions.q: The substance dissolved in a solution is the:
questions.explain: Solute dissolves in the solvent (the larger amount).

questions.q: In salt water, water is the:
questions.explain: Water does the dissolving, so it is the solvent.

questions.q: A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature is:
questions.explain: Saturated = holding the maximum dissolved solute at equilibrium.

questions.q: Which would increase how fast a solid dissolves in water?
questions.explain: Stirring and more surface area speed dissolving.

questions.q: Baking soda is commonly used as a mild:
questions.explain: Sodium bicarbonate is a weak base — it neutralizes acids.

rounds.title: Acids, Bases & Solutions
rounds.desc: pH in daily life, neutralization, concentration, and mixtures.

description: The pH scale, neutralization, buffers, and strong versus weak acids.

questions.explain: The pH scale runs 0-14: below 7 is acidic (lower = stronger), 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic.
questions.q: A solution with a pH of 3 is best described as what?

questions.explain: Arrhenius acids increase H+ (which forms hydronium in water); Arrhenius bases increase OH- (hydroxide) instead.
questions.q: An Arrhenius acid is a substance that releases which ion in water?

questions.explain: Neutralization: H+ from the acid joins OH- from the base to make water, and the leftover ions form a salt.
questions.q: When an acid and a base neutralize each other, the products are what?

questions.explain: The pH scale is logarithmic: 7 minus 2 = 5 pH units, so 10^5 = 100,000 times more acidic.
questions.q: Lemon juice (pH about 2) is how many times more acidic than pure water (pH 7)?

questions.explain: Ammonia solution is basic (around pH 11) and is a common glass-cleaner ingredient. Vinegar, citric acid, and carbonic acid are all acids.
questions.q: Which of these is a common base found in household products?

questions.explain: Buffers mop up added H+ or OH- so pH stays stable - blood buffers hold human blood near pH 7.4 despite everything we eat and do.
options: Instantly neutralizes any amount of acid
questions.q: A buffer solution is valuable because it does what?

questions.explain: Litmus rules: blue litmus turns red in acid, and red litmus turns blue in base. Phenolphthalein, by contrast, turns pink in bases, not acids.
questions.q: Which indicator change signals an acidic solution?

questions.explain: Blood is slightly basic, held near 7.4 by buffers. Deviations of even a few tenths can be dangerous.
questions.q: Normal human blood has a pH of about what?

questions.explain: Strength is about ionization: HCl is strong because it dissociates fully; acetic acid is weak because most molecules stay intact. Strength is not the same as concentration.
options: It has a higher pH than weak acids
It ionizes (dissociates) almost completely in water
It tastes more sour than a weak acid
It cannot be neutralized by a base
questions.q: A strong acid differs from a weak acid because a strong acid does what?

questions.explain: Antacids contain mild bases like calcium carbonate that react with and neutralize excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
options: Coat the stomach so acid cannot touch it
Slow down acid production for a full day
questions.q: Antacid tablets relieve heartburn mainly by doing what?

subject: Chemistry 101
title: Acids & Bases
Gas Laws & Kinetic Theory
subject: Chemistry 101
description: Boyle's, Charles's, and Gay-Lussac's laws, the ideal gas law, Kelvin temperatures, and how particle motion explains pressure, diffusion, and real-gas behavior.

questions.q: Boyle's law states that at constant temperature, the pressure of a gas and its volume are:
options: Inversely related: as volume decreases, pressure increases
questions.explain: Squeezing a gas into half the volume doubles its pressure, because the particles hit the walls twice as often.

questions.q: Charles's law says that at constant pressure, the volume of a gas increases when:
questions.explain: Heating a gas makes its particles move faster and push outward, expanding the volume in direct proportion to Kelvin temperature.

questions.q: Temperatures used in gas law calculations must always be expressed in:
options: Any unit, it does not matter
questions.explain: Kelvin starts at absolute zero, so ratios of temperatures only work in Kelvin. Convert by adding 273 to the Celsius value.

questions.q: The ideal gas law is written as:
questions.explain: The ideal gas law combines the individual gas laws and uses R, the gas constant, with n equal to the number of moles.

questions.q: Standard temperature for gas calculations (STP) is:
questions.explain: STP is defined as 273 K and 1 atm of pressure.

questions.q: According to kinetic molecular theory, gas pressure is caused by:
options: Gas particles colliding with the walls of the container
The weight of the gas alone
questions.explain: Each collision exerts a tiny force; billions of collisions per second add up to the measured pressure.

questions.q: If the Kelvin temperature of a gas in a rigid container doubles, its pressure will:
questions.explain: Gay-Lussac's law: at constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature.

questions.q: Graham's law of diffusion predicts that, at the same temperature:
options: All gases diffuse at the same rate
Diffusion does not depend on the gas
Lighter gas particles diffuse faster than heavier ones
questions.explain: Lighter particles move faster at the same temperature, so helium escapes through a balloon's pores faster than heavier gases.

questions.q: Real gases behave least like an ideal gas at:
questions.explain: At high pressure and low temperature, particle volume and attractions between particles can no longer be ignored.

questions.q: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain:
options: Equal numbers of atoms in every case
questions.explain: This is why one mole of any ideal gas takes up the same 22.4 liters at STP, no matter which gas it is.

rounds.title: Gas Laws & Kinetic Theory
rounds.desc: Boyle's, Charles's, and Gay-Lussac's laws, the ideal gas law, Kelvin temperatures, and how particle motion explains pressure, diffusion, and real-gas behavior.

title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
subject: Chemistry 101
description: Carbon compounds: alkanes, alkenes, and aromatic rings; functional groups including alcohols and carboxylic acids; isomers, polymers, and why carbon forms so many compounds.

questions.q: Organic chemistry is defined as the study of compounds that contain:
questions.explain: Nearly all compounds built around carbon, especially with hydrogen, are classed as organic, from methane to DNA.

questions.q: The simplest organic compound, with one carbon atom and four hydrogens, is:
questions.explain: Methane is the main component of natural gas and the first member of the alkane family.

questions.q: Alkanes are hydrocarbons whose carbon atoms are connected only by:
questions.explain: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n+2, such as ethane and propane.

questions.q: A compound containing the -OH group attached to a carbon chain belongs to which family?
questions.explain: The hydroxyl group defines alcohols like ethanol; the -OH here is bonded to carbon, not free hydroxide in a base.

questions.q: Ethene (ethylene), C2H4, is an alkene because its carbon atoms are joined by a:
questions.explain: Alkenes contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond, which makes them more reactive than alkanes.

questions.q: Isomers are compounds that:
options: Have the same molecular formula but different structures
questions.explain: Butane and isobutane are both C4H10, yet their different shapes give them different boiling points.

questions.q: Benzene, C6H6, is the best-known example of:
options: An aromatic compound with a ring structure
questions.explain: Benzene's six-carbon ring with delocalized electrons makes aromatic compounds unusually stable.

questions.q: Polymerization is the process in which:
options: A polymer breaks down into monomers
Many small monomer molecules join into one very large molecule
A gas turns directly into a solid
questions.explain: Plastics like polyethylene form when thousands of ethene monomers link into long chains.

questions.q: Acetic acid, the acid in vinegar, belongs to the carboxylic acid family because it contains the group:
questions.explain: The carboxyl group, -COOH, releases a hydrogen ion in water, which is what makes carboxylic acids acidic.

questions.q: A neutral carbon atom in organic compounds typically forms how many covalent bonds?
questions.explain: Carbon has four valence electrons and completes its octet by forming four bonds, which is why it can build chains, branches, and rings.

rounds.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
rounds.desc: Carbon compounds: alkanes, alkenes, and aromatic rings; functional groups including alcohols and carboxylic acids; isomers, polymers, and why carbon forms so many compounds.

title: Colonial Era & Revolution
subject: AP US History
description: Colonies, taxation, independence, and the Constitution.

questions.q: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in:
questions.explain: Adopted July 4, 1776, primarily authored by Thomas Jefferson.

questions.q: The British tax on printed materials that angered colonists was the:
questions.explain: The Stamp Act (1765) taxed printed goods and sparked 'no taxation without representation.'

questions.q: The first battles of the Revolutionary War were at:
questions.explain: Lexington and Concord, April 1775 — 'the shot heard round the world.'

questions.q: The Constitution was written in which year?
questions.explain: The Constitutional Convention met in Philadelphia in 1787.

questions.q: The Bill of Rights consists of the first ___ amendments.
questions.explain: The first ten amendments, ratified in 1791, protect individual liberties.

questions.q: The system that prevents any one branch from dominating is:
questions.explain: Checks and balances let each branch limit the others.

questions.q: The turning-point battle that convinced France to ally with America was:
questions.explain: Saratoga (1777) proved the Americans could win, bringing French support.

questions.q: The war effectively ended with the British surrender at:
questions.explain: Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown in 1781.

rounds.title: Colonial Era & Revolution
rounds.desc: Colonies, taxation, independence, and the Constitution.

title: Foundations of American Government
subject: AP US History
description: Articles of Confederation, the Constitutional Convention, federalism, and how the new republic was designed to work.

questions.q: The Articles of Confederation created a national government that was weak mainly because it:
options: Lacked the power to tax and regulate trade
Had a president who served for life
Gave states no representation in Congress
Created a large standing national army
questions.explain: Without taxing power, Congress had to beg states for money and could not regulate commerce, which is why the Articles were replaced.

questions.q: The Virginia Plan at the Constitutional Convention favored large states by basing representation in Congress on:
questions.explain: The Virginia Plan proposed proportional representation, while the small-state New Jersey Plan wanted equality; the Connecticut Compromise combined both.

questions.q: The Supreme Court case Marbury v. Madison (1803) is most important because it established:
options: The right to a trial by jury in civil cases
The legality of the national bank
The president's power to remove judges
questions.explain: Chief Justice John Marshall claimed the power for courts to strike down laws that violate the Constitution, making the judiciary a co-equal branch.

questions.q: The Tenth Amendment to the Constitution states that powers not given to the federal government are:
options: Shared equally by Congress and the president
Reserved to the states or the people
questions.explain: The Tenth Amendment is the constitutional basis for reserved state powers in the federal system.

questions.q: The Federalist Papers were written mainly to:
options: Persuade New York to ratify the Constitution
Draft the Bill of Rights word for word
questions.explain: Hamilton, Madison, and Jay published the essays as Publius to build support for ratification in New York.

questions.q: A presidential veto that Congress can override with a two-thirds vote best illustrates:
questions.explain: Checks and balances let each branch limit the others, so no branch can act entirely alone.

questions.q: Under the Constitution, the president of the United States is formally chosen by:
options: The House of Representatives in every election
questions.explain: Voters choose electors, and the Electoral College formally elects the president; the House decides only if no candidate wins an electoral majority.

questions.q: Anti-Federalists opposed the new Constitution mainly because they feared:
options: A strong central government would threaten individual liberties
The president would be too weak to lead
questions.explain: Anti-Federalists demanded a bill of rights as protection against a distant, powerful national government.

questions.q: Amending the Constitution requires:
options: A simple majority of Congress and the president's signature
Proposal by two-thirds of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states
Approval by all thirteen original states
A unanimous vote of the Supreme Court
questions.explain: Article V makes amendments deliberately difficult: supermajorities are needed to propose and to ratify.

questions.q: The necessary and proper clause, often called the elastic clause, gives Congress the power to:
options: Declare war on any nation without debate
Make laws needed to carry out its listed powers
questions.explain: The elastic clause stretches congressional power beyond the enumerated list, and it was central to the ruling in McCulloch v. Maryland.

rounds.title: Foundations of American Government
rounds.desc: Articles of Confederation, the Constitutional Convention, federalism, and how the new republic was designed to work.

title: Westward Expansion & Manifest Destiny
subject: AP US History
description: Louisiana Purchase, the Monroe Doctrine, Texas and the Mexican-American War, trails west, and the cost paid by Native peoples.

questions.q: The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 doubled the size of the United States with land bought from:
questions.explain: Napoleon's France sold the Louisiana Territory for about 15 million dollars, giving the US control of the Mississippi River and New Orleans.

questions.q: President Thomas Jefferson sent the Lewis and Clark expedition west mainly to:
options: Explore the new territory and find a route to the Pacific
questions.explain: The Corps of Discovery (1804-1806) mapped the West, recorded its resources, and built relationships with Native nations.

questions.q: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, and it banned slavery in the Louisiana Territory north of:
questions.explain: The compromise kept the Senate balance at 12 free and 12 slave states while drawing a line for slavery's future expansion.

questions.q: The idea of Manifest Destiny held that the United States was destined to expand:
options: Only within its original thirteen states
Across North America to the Pacific Ocean
Back across the Atlantic into Europe
questions.explain: Supporters framed continental expansion as inevitable and justified, ignoring the Native peoples and nations already living on the land.

questions.q: The Mexican-American War (1846-1848) ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which gave the United States:
options: California and much of the present-day Southwest
Only the city of New Orleans
questions.explain: Mexico ceded about half its territory, including California, and the Rio Grande became the Texas border in exchange for 15 million dollars.

questions.q: Most families who traveled the Oregon Trail in the 1840s were heading west to:
options: Claim fertile farmland in the Oregon Country
questions.explain: Emigrants sought free or cheap farmland in the Willamette Valley, enduring a roughly 2,000-mile, months-long journey.

questions.q: The California Gold Rush began in 1848 after gold was discovered at:
questions.explain: John Marshall's discovery at Sutter's Mill drew roughly 300,000 people to California and sped its admission as a free state in 1850.

questions.q: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 led to the forced relocation of the Cherokee and other southeastern nations on a journey remembered as:
questions.explain: About 4,000 Cherokee died from disease, exposure, and starvation during the forced removal to Indian Territory in present-day Oklahoma.

questions.q: Northern opposition delayed the annexation of Texas for nearly a decade mainly because annexing Texas would:
options: Expand slavery and upset the balance in Congress
Make the US responsible for French debts
Force a war with Britain over Canada
questions.explain: Texas entered the Union as a slave state in 1845, and many northerners feared it might be split into several more slave states.

questions.q: The Monroe Doctrine of 1823 warned European powers that:
options: New colonization in the Western Hemisphere would be seen as a threat to the US
The US would colonize parts of Africa
All European trade with the Americas must end immediately
The US would guarantee the independence of every European colony
questions.explain: Monroe declared the Americas closed to new European colonization while pledging the US would not interfere in European affairs.

rounds.title: Westward Expansion & Manifest Destiny
rounds.desc: Louisiana Purchase, the Monroe Doctrine, Texas and the Mexican-American War, trails west, and the cost paid by Native peoples.

title: Civil War & Reconstruction
subject: AP US History
description: Slavery, secession, emancipation, and rebuilding the Union.

questions.q: The Civil War began in:
questions.explain: Fighting began at Fort Sumter in April 1861.

questions.q: The Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people in:
questions.explain: Lincoln's 1863 proclamation applied to Confederate states in rebellion.

questions.q: Which amendment abolished slavery nationwide?
questions.explain: The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery.

questions.q: The amendment granting citizenship and equal protection is the:
questions.explain: The 14th Amendment (1868) defines citizenship and equal protection.

questions.q: The bloodiest single day of the war was at:
questions.explain: Antietam (1862) remains the bloodiest single day in US military history.

questions.q: The Union general who accepted Lee's surrender was:
questions.explain: Ulysses S. Grant accepted the surrender at Appomattox in 1865.

questions.q: The 15th Amendment addressed:
questions.explain: Ratified 1870, it barred denying the vote based on race (for men).

questions.q: President Lincoln was assassinated in:
questions.explain: Lincoln was shot by John Wilkes Booth in April 1865, days after the war ended.

rounds.title: Civil War & Reconstruction
rounds.desc: Slavery, secession, emancipation, and rebuilding the Union.

title: Gilded Age & Progressives
subject: AP US History
description: Big business, labor, immigration, and the reform movements.

questions.q: Carnegie's steel empire used ___ integration — controlling every step from mines to mills.
questions.explain: Vertical integration controls the whole supply chain; Rockefeller's horizontal integration bought competitors.

questions.q: The Populist Party most strongly demanded:
questions.explain: Populists backed bimetallism ('free silver'), railroad regulation, and a graduated income tax.

questions.q: Upton Sinclair's 'The Jungle' led directly to:
options: Meat Inspection and Pure Food & Drug Acts (1906)
questions.explain: Sinclair exposed meatpacking horrors; Congress passed food-safety laws in 1906.

questions.q: The 17th Amendment established:
questions.explain: A Progressive reform — senators elected directly by voters, not state legislatures.

questions.q: The Spanish-American War (1898) resulted in the US gaining:
options: Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines
questions.explain: The Treaty of Paris gave the US Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines — an overseas empire.

questions.q: Jane Addams is associated with:
questions.explain: Hull House in Chicago provided services and reform energy in immigrant neighborhoods.

questions.q: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) was the first US law to:
options: Ban immigration by a specific nationality
questions.explain: It barred Chinese labor immigration — the first nationality-based exclusion.

questions.q: The Federal Reserve was created in 1913 under which president?
questions.explain: Wilson's New Freedom program created the Federal Reserve System.

rounds.title: Gilded Age & Progressives
rounds.desc: Big business, labor, immigration, and the reform movements.

title: World War I & the Roaring Twenties
subject: AP US History
description: America enters the Great War, the fight over the peace treaty, Prohibition, the Harlem Renaissance, and a booming consumer culture.

questions.q: The United States declared war on Germany in 1917 largely after Germany:
options: Resumed unrestricted submarine warfare against shipping
questions.explain: German U-boats sank American merchant ships, and the Zimmermann Telegram pushed public opinion toward war.

questions.q: The Zimmermann Telegram proposed a military alliance between Germany and:
questions.explain: Germany promised Mexico could recover Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona, and British publication of the telegram outraged Americans.

questions.q: President Woodrow Wilson's plan for a fair peace after World War I was called the:
questions.explain: Wilson's points called for open diplomacy, free trade, self-determination, and a League of Nations to prevent future wars.

questions.q: The US Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles mainly because many senators feared the League of Nations would:
options: Limit US freedom to decide on war for itself
Force the US to free its colonies
questions.explain: Led by Henry Cabot Lodge, reservationists wanted changes to Article X, and Wilson's refusal to compromise helped kill the treaty in the Senate.

questions.q: The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, granted:
questions.explain: After a decades-long suffrage movement, the amendment prohibited denying the vote on account of sex.

questions.q: The Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s was best described as:
options: A political party based in New York
A plan to rebuild housing in Harlem
A flowering of African American art, music, and literature
questions.explain: Writers like Langston Hughes and musicians like Duke Ellington celebrated Black culture and challenged racist stereotypes.

questions.q: Prohibition, which banned the manufacture and sale of alcohol nationwide, was established by the:
questions.explain: Prohibition lasted from 1920 until the Twenty-first Amendment repealed it in 1933, the only amendment ever repealed.

questions.q: The Scopes Trial of 1925 became a national symbol of the clash between:
options: Teaching evolution and traditional religious beliefs
Urban voters and rural voters over taxes
questions.explain: John Scopes was convicted of teaching evolution in a Tennessee public school, dramatizing the tension between modern science and fundamentalism.

questions.q: Flappers of the 1920s became a symbol of:
options: New independence and changing social roles for young women
A campaign to lower the voting age
questions.explain: With shorter dresses, bobbed hair, and public dancing and smoking, flappers visibly broke with Victorian expectations for women.

questions.q: Assembly-line mass production made cars affordable for millions of Americans and was most associated with:
options: Thomas Edison and the light bulb
Henry Ford and the Model T
questions.explain: Ford's moving assembly line cut the price of a Model T from about 850 dollars to under 300, transforming American transportation and consumer culture.

rounds.tag: World War I & the Roaring Twenties
rounds.title: World War I & the Roaring Twenties
rounds.desc: America enters the Great War, the fight over the peace treaty, Prohibition, the Harlem Renaissance, and a booming consumer culture.

title: Great Depression & WWII
subject: AP US History
description: The crash, the New Deal, and America's path through World War II.

questions.q: The stock market crash that began the Great Depression occurred in:
questions.explain: Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929.

questions.q: Franklin D. Roosevelt's program to fight the Depression was the:
questions.explain: The New Deal brought relief, recovery, and reform programs.

questions.q: The attack that brought the US into WWII was on:
questions.explain: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941.

questions.q: D-Day, the Allied invasion of Normandy, was in:
questions.explain: June 6, 1944 — the largest seaborne invasion in history.

questions.q: The Social Security Act was part of which program?
questions.explain: Passed in 1935 under the New Deal, it created old-age pensions.

questions.q: WWII in Europe ended in:
questions.explain: V-E Day was May 8, 1945.

questions.q: The US dropped atomic bombs on which two Japanese cities?
questions.explain: Hiroshima (Aug 6) and Nagasaki (Aug 9), 1945.

questions.q: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) ruled that:
questions.explain: The Court overturned 'separate but equal' in public education.

questions.q: The closest the US and USSR came to nuclear war was the:

questions.q: Medicare and Medicaid were created as part of:

questions.q: The Voting Rights Act of 1965:

title: Civil Rights Movement & Social Change
subject: AP US History
description: Boycotts, sit-ins, and freedom rides; Black Power, the women's movement, and Stonewall: how postwar movements expanded American rights.

questions.q: The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-1956 began after the arrest of:
questions.explain: Parks's refusal to give up her seat sparked a 381-day boycott that ended with a Supreme Court ruling desegregating Montgomery's buses.

questions.q: In 1957, nine Black students needed federal troops to protect them as they integrated Central High School in:
questions.explain: Governor Orval Faubus used the state National Guard to block the Little Rock Nine, so President Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne to enforce the court order.

questions.q: The Freedom Rides of 1961 challenged segregation in:
options: Interstate bus travel and bus terminals
questions.explain: Integrated groups of riders tested Supreme Court rulings against segregated interstate travel and met violent resistance across the South.

questions.q: At the March on Washington in August 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. delivered a speech famous for the repeated phrase:
questions.explain: Speaking before roughly 250,000 people at the Lincoln Memorial, King demanded jobs, freedom, and an end to racial injustice.

questions.q: Student sit-ins, beginning in Greensboro in 1960, were a nonviolent tactic aimed at desegregating:
questions.explain: Students politely occupied whites-only lunch counter seats, and the tactic spread to more than 100 cities within months.

questions.q: The Birmingham campaign of 1963 shifted national opinion largely because television showed:
options: Police using dogs and fire hoses against peaceful protesters, including children
questions.explain: Images from Birmingham embarrassed the nation, and President Kennedy soon called for a strong civil rights bill.

questions.q: The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), founded in 1960, focused mainly on:
options: Supporting only legal challenges in court
Coordinating student-led protests and voter registration drives
Organizing labor unions in the North
questions.explain: SNCC field workers organized sit-ins, freedom rides, and the Mississippi Freedom Summer voter registration campaign of 1964.

questions.q: The Black Panther Party, founded in Oakland in 1966, became widely known for:
options: Community survival programs such as free breakfasts for children, alongside armed patrols monitoring police
Opposing all forms of community organizing
Working only through the Democratic Party
questions.explain: The Panthers combined self-defense and Black empowerment with practical programs like free breakfasts and health clinics.

questions.q: Betty Friedan's 1963 book The Feminine Mystique helped launch the modern women's movement by arguing that:
options: Women should avoid all paid work
Many suburban women felt trapped and unfulfilled by a life limited to home and family
Voting rights for women should be repealed
questions.explain: Friedan named 'the problem that has no name' and helped inspire the founding of the National Organization for Women in 1966.

questions.q: The Stonewall uprising of 1969 in New York City is a landmark in the movement for:
questions.explain: After a police raid on the Stonewall Inn, days of protest galvanized a national movement for gay and lesbian equality.

title: America Since 1980: Globalization & Change
subject: AP US History
description: Reaganomics, the end of the Cold War, NAFTA, September 11, the Great Recession, and the digital transformation of American life.

questions.q: President Ronald Reagan's economic program, called Reaganomics, emphasized:
options: Tax cuts, deregulation, and reduced domestic spending
Higher taxes and expanded welfare programs
A return to the gold standard
questions.explain: Reagan argued supply-side tax cuts would spur investment and growth, while critics said the policy widened income inequality.

questions.q: The Cold War ended most directly with:
options: The signing of the Camp David Accords
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991
The end of the Vietnam War in 1975
questions.explain: Communist governments fell across Eastern Europe in 1989, and the USSR dissolved in December 1991, leaving the US as the sole superpower.

questions.q: The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA, 1994) sharply reduced trade barriers among the United States, Canada, and:
questions.explain: Supporters credited NAFTA with cheaper goods and export growth; critics blamed it for manufacturing job losses to Mexico.

questions.q: In response to the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, the United States first invaded:
questions.explain: The US and its allies toppled the Taliban government of Afghanistan, which had sheltered al-Qaeda, in late 2001.

questions.q: The Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 prohibited discrimination based on:
options: Disability in employment and public accommodations
questions.explain: The ADA required reasonable accommodations at work and accessible public spaces such as ramps, elevators, and transit.

questions.q: The dot-com boom of the late 1990s was driven mainly by rapid growth in:
questions.explain: New web companies attracted huge investment before the bubble burst in 2000, even as the internet permanently changed business and daily life.

questions.q: The Affordable Care Act of 2010 was designed mainly to:
options: Replace all private insurance with one government plan
Expand health insurance coverage and regulate insurance practices
Require states to run all hospitals
questions.explain: The law expanded Medicaid, created insurance marketplaces, and barred insurers from denying coverage for pre-existing conditions.

questions.q: The presidential election of 2008 was historic because Americans elected:
options: The first president born outside the US
The first African American president, Barack Obama
questions.explain: Obama defeated John McCain amid a financial crisis, becoming the first Black president in US history.

questions.q: The Great Recession of 2007-2009 was triggered most directly by a crisis in:
options: The housing and subprime mortgage market
questions.explain: Risky subprime loans, housing price collapse, and bank failures spread through the global financial system.

questions.q: One major effect of smartphones and social media on American politics since the 2000s has been:
options: Faster spread of both news and misinformation, with campaigns organized online
A steady decline in voter interest in national news
questions.explain: Platforms let candidates speak directly to voters and movements organize quickly, but they also accelerate rumors and false claims.

title: Vital Signs & Patient Safety
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Normal ranges, fall prevention, and the safety checks that matter.

questions.q: A normal adult oral temperature is about:

questions.q: Blood pressure of 120/80 — the 120 represents:

questions.q: Normal adult respiratory rate is:

questions.q: Before giving any medication, the nurse first verifies:
questions.explain: Two identifiers (e.g., name + DOB) are required before medication administration.

options: Keep the bed in high position
Keep the call light within reach and answer promptly

questions.q: SpO₂ measures:
questions.explain: Pulse oximetry measures the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen.

questions.q: A temperature of 101.5°F in an adult is considered:
questions.explain: Above 100.4°F is generally classified as a fever.

questions.q: When should hand hygiene be performed?

questions.q: Bradycardia is a heart rate below:

title: Vital Signs & Assessment
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Measuring and interpreting temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and pain.

questions.q: According to current guidelines, a normal blood pressure for an adult is:
questions.explain: The AHA defines normal as below 120/80. Readings of 120-129/<80 are 'elevated,' and 130/80 or higher is hypertension — these thresholds guide when treatment begins.

questions.q: Which temperature site is considered the most accurate reflection of core body temperature?
questions.explain: Rectal readings most closely reflect core temperature, though they are invasive. Axillary runs about a degree lower and is the least accurate; oral and temporal are practical compromises.

questions.q: Tachycardia in an adult is defined as a heart rate above:
questions.explain: Above 100 bpm at rest is tachycardia; below 60 is bradycardia. Context matters — fever, pain, anxiety, and exercise all raise the rate, so trend the numbers, not just one reading.

questions.q: When assessing respirations, the best nursing practice is to:
options: Announce you are counting breaths and count for 15 seconds
Count for 30 seconds right after telling the patient
Count during conversation for one minute
Count for a full minute after taking the pulse, without the patient knowing
questions.explain: People unconsciously change their breathing when they know it's being watched. Counting for a full minute after the pulse keeps the patient unaware and catches irregular patterns a 15-second count would miss.

questions.q: A normal pulse oximetry (SpO2) reading for a healthy adult is:
questions.explain: 95-100% is normal; below 90% generally requires intervention. Remember that oximetry measures saturation, not ventilation — a patient can have a normal SpO2 and still be in trouble, so assess breathing, not just the number.

questions.q: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a systolic drop of at least ___ within 3 minutes of standing:
questions.explain: A drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic (with symptoms like dizziness) within 3 minutes of standing defines orthostatic hypotension. It signals fall risk — sit the patient back down and notify the provider.

questions.q: Using a blood pressure cuff that is too small for the patient's arm will produce a reading that is:
questions.explain: A cuff that's too narrow needs extra pressure to compress the artery, inflating the reading. The bladder should encircle about 80% of the arm — when in doubt, use the larger cuff.

questions.q: Pain is frequently referred to as the:
questions.explain: Pain is called the fifth vital sign because it must be assessed with every set of vitals. It's the one subjective sign — measured by the patient's report, often on a 0-10 scale.

questions.q: The apical pulse is best auscultated at which location?
options: 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line
questions.explain: The apex of the heart sits at the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line (point of maximal impulse). This is the true ventricular rate — always use it for irregular rhythms and before digoxin.

questions.q: A temperature above ___ is generally considered a fever (pyrexia) in adults:
questions.explain: 100.4 F (38 C) or higher is the standard fever threshold. Report fevers promptly — they can signal infection, transfusion reactions, or other complications, especially in postoperative or immunocompromised patients.

title: Infection Control
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Chain of infection, precautions, and PPE essentials.

questions.q: The single most effective way to break the chain of infection is:
questions.explain: Hand hygiene is the #1 infection-prevention measure.

questions.q: Droplet precautions are used for infections spread by:
questions.explain: Droplets (flu, pertussis) travel short distances — mask and distance matter.

questions.q: Airborne precautions require which special mask?
questions.explain: Airborne diseases like TB require a fit-tested N95 and a negative-pressure room.

questions.q: Standard precautions apply to:
questions.explain: Standard precautions treat all blood/body fluids as potentially infectious, for every patient.

questions.q: The correct order for removing (doffing) PPE starts with:
questions.explain: Gloves are the most contaminated — remove them first, then goggles, gown, mask.

questions.q: Alcohol-based hand rub is NOT effective against:
questions.explain: C. diff spores require soap-and-water washing.

questions.q: Sharps containers should be replaced when they are:
questions.explain: Replace sharps containers at the fill line, about three-quarters full.

questions.q: Contact precautions require:
questions.explain: Contact precautions (e.g., MRSA, C. diff): gown + gloves when entering.

questions.q: The single most important measure for preventing the spread of infection is:
questions.explain: Hand hygiene outperforms every other intervention — more infections are transmitted by hands than by any other route. Gloves supplement it but never replace washing.

questions.q: Standard precautions are applied to:
questions.explain: Standard precautions treat ALL blood, body fluids (except sweat), secretions, and excretions as potentially infectious — because infection status is often unknown at the time of care.

questions.q: A patient is on contact precautions for MRSA. The nurse must wear:
questions.explain: Contact precautions target organisms spread by touch: gown and gloves on entry, dedicated equipment, and a private room when available. Masks aren't required unless splash risk exists.

questions.q: Airborne precautions — including an N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room — are required for:
questions.explain: TB, measles, and varicella travel on tiny particles that stay suspended in air, so they need N95 respirators and negative-pressure rooms. Flu and most colds spread by larger droplets, not airborne particles.

questions.q: When donning PPE, the correct order is:
options: Gown, then mask or respirator, then goggles or face shield, then gloves
Gloves, then gown, then mask, then goggles
Mask, then gown, then gloves, then goggles
Goggles, then gloves, then gown, then mask
questions.explain: Donning goes from dirtiest to cleanest contact: gown, mask, eye protection, then gloves (which go over the gown cuffs). Removing reverses it — gloves first, mask last — to avoid contaminating your face.

questions.q: For a patient with Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), the nurse should perform hand hygiene with:
questions.explain: C. diff forms spores that alcohol cannot kill — only soap-and-water washing removes them. This is the classic exam exception to the 'alcohol rub is fine' rule.

questions.q: An N95 respirator is required for which category of transmission-based precautions?
questions.explain: N95s filter 95% of airborne particles and are reserved for airborne diseases. Droplet precautions (influenza, pertussis) use a regular surgical mask worn within about 3 feet of the patient.

questions.q: Droplet precautions — surgical mask within 3 feet of the patient — are used for:
questions.explain: Droplets are larger particles that fall within about 3 feet, so a surgical mask and eye protection suffice — no negative-pressure room needed. Influenza, pertussis, and mumps are classic droplet diseases.

questions.q: Hand hygiene most directly breaks which link in the chain of infection?
questions.explain: The mode of transmission — how germs travel from person to person — is the link most easily interrupted. Hand hygiene stops organisms from hitching a ride on your hands to the next patient.

questions.q: While working at a sterile field, which action would contaminate it?
options: Opening the drape away from the body
questions.explain: Anything crossing over a sterile field — hands, sleeves, equipment — contaminates it, because particles shed downward. Sterile items stay above the waist, below the shoulders, and in front of the body.

rounds.title: Infection Control
rounds.desc: Chain of infection, precautions, and PPE essentials.

title: Patient Safety
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Fall prevention, restraints, sentinel events, and keeping patients safe.

questions.q: Immediately after a patient falls, the nurse's first action should be to:
options: Help the patient back to bed
questions.explain: Assessment always comes first — a fall can cause fractures, head injury, or bleeding that must be found before anything else. The provider call and incident report follow, and the fall gets documented in the chart.

questions.q: Before applying physical restraints, the nurse is required to first:
options: Document the need in the chart
questions.explain: Restraints are a last resort: federal rules and nursing ethics require trying alternatives first (reorientation, family presence, toileting, pain control). Restraints need a provider order, time limits, and frequent monitoring.

questions.q: Which patient is at the highest risk for a fall?
options: A 30-year-old on postoperative day 3, walking with help
A 45-year-old with a peripheral IV, resting in bed
A 78-year-old on a sedative and a diuretic
questions.explain: Fall risk multiplies with age, altered mentation, and medications — sedatives impair balance and diuretics cause urgency and orthostatic drops. Screen every patient with a fall-risk tool and act on the score.

questions.q: The surgical 'time out' immediately before an incision verifies the:
options: Correct patient, correct site, and correct procedure
questions.explain: The whole team pauses to confirm identity, site (with marking), and procedure aloud. It was created specifically to eliminate wrong-patient, wrong-site, wrong-procedure surgery — a classic sentinel event.

questions.q: Keeping the bed in its lowest position with the call light in reach is an example of:
questions.explain: Low bed, locked brakes, call light within reach, and hourly rounding are the core fall-prevention bundle. They're simple, evidence-based, and required by most hospital policies.

questions.q: A medication error is caught before reaching the patient (a near miss). The nurse should:
options: Ignore it since no harm occurred
Document it only in the patient's chart
Tell the patient what almost happened
questions.explain: Near misses are reported through the incident system so the process flaw can be fixed before someone is harmed. Incident reports are quality-improvement tools — they do not go in the patient's chart and are not for punishment.

questions.q: Using the RACE fire-response sequence, the nurse's first action is to:
questions.explain: RACE = Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish. People come first — move anyone in immediate danger, then pull the alarm, close doors to contain smoke and fire, and only then attempt to extinguish if trained.

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as a sentinel event?
questions.explain: A sentinel event is an unexpected occurrence involving death or serious harm — wrong-site surgery is the textbook example. Sentinel events trigger root-cause analysis and must be reported to The Joint Commission.

questions.q: Raising all four side rails on a patient's bed may be considered:
questions.explain: Four raised rails can trap a patient in bed and are treated as a restraint under many facility policies — requiring assessment, orders, and monitoring. Two or fewer rails for positioning is generally not a restraint.

questions.q: The primary purpose of filing an incident report is:
options: To document the event in the patient's medical record
To inform the patient of the error
questions.explain: Incident reports identify system problems so they can be fixed — they exist for quality improvement, not blame. They are internal risk-management documents and are never filed in the patient's chart.

title: Medication Administration
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: The rights of med administration, routes, and dosage safety.

questions.q: The traditional 'Five Rights' of medication administration include right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, and right:
questions.explain: The fifth right is the right time.

questions.q: The abbreviation 'PO' means a medication is given:
questions.explain: PO = per os, by mouth.

questions.q: 'IM' indicates an injection into the:
questions.explain: IM = intramuscular.

questions.q: A medication ordered 'STAT' should be given:
questions.explain: STAT means immediately, as soon as possible.

questions.q: Before administering a drug, the nurse should check for:
questions.explain: Allergy checking is a critical safety step for every medication.

questions.q: Sublingual medications are placed:
questions.explain: Sublingual = under the tongue for rapid absorption.

questions.q: If a patient refuses a medication, the nurse should:
options: Hide it in food without telling them
Document the refusal and notify the provider
questions.explain: Patients have the right to refuse; document it and inform the provider.

questions.q: The 'right documentation' means charting:
questions.explain: Document right after giving the medication — never before.

questions.q: Insulin is typically given by which route?
questions.explain: Insulin is given subcutaneously (into fatty tissue).

questions.q: A nurse finds a medication error was made. The priority action is:
options: Assess the patient and report per policy
questions.explain: Patient safety first: assess, then report and complete an incident report.

rounds.title: Medication Administration
rounds.desc: The rights of med administration, routes, and dosage safety.

title: Pharmacology Basics
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: ADME, drug-class suffixes, and the antidotes every nurse knows.

questions.q: The 'M' in ADME (pharmacokinetics) stands for metabolism, which happens mainly in the:
questions.explain: The liver metabolizes most drugs; the kidneys excrete most.

questions.q: A drug's half-life is the time it takes for:
options: Half the drug to be eliminated
The drug to reach the brain
questions.explain: About 4–5 half-lives reach steady state or clear the drug.

questions.q: Drugs ending in '-lol' (metoprolol) are usually:
questions.explain: -lol = beta blocker: slows heart rate, lowers BP.

questions.q: Drugs ending in '-pril' (lisinopril) are:
questions.explain: -pril = ACE inhibitor; a dry cough is its classic side effect.

questions.q: The antidote for opioid overdose is:
questions.explain: Naloxone (Narcan) reverses opioids. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

questions.q: Vitamin K is the antidote for:
questions.explain: Warfarin reversal = vitamin K. Heparin's antidote is protamine; acetaminophen's is N-acetylcysteine.

questions.q: IV medications have 100% bioavailability because they:
questions.explain: IV drugs go straight into circulation — nothing is lost to absorption or liver first pass.

questions.q: Digoxin toxicity is made worse by low levels of:
questions.explain: Hypokalemia increases digoxin binding and toxicity risk — vision changes and arrhythmias result.

rounds.title: Pharmacology Basics
rounds.desc: ADME, drug-class suffixes, and the antidotes every nurse knows.

title: Pharmacology Basics
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Medication rights, routes, safety checks, and common drug facts every nurse must know.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the traditional five rights of medication administration?
questions.explain: The five rights are right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, and right time. The diagnosis guides prescribing but is not one of the administration rights — right documentation is often added as the sixth right.

questions.q: A nurse sees an order for Tylenol. What is the generic name the pharmacy will dispense?
questions.explain: Tylenol is the brand name for acetaminophen. Nurses should know generics because orders, labels, and references often list them — and mixing up names (e.g., aspirin vs. acetaminophen) causes real errors.

questions.q: Which medication route provides the fastest onset of action?
questions.explain: IV drugs enter the bloodstream immediately, so onset is nearly instant. Sublingual is fast but slower than IV; oral is the slowest because the drug must survive digestion and first-pass metabolism in the liver.

questions.q: A patient shows signs of anaphylaxis after a new medication. The nurse's first-line treatment is:
questions.explain: Epinephrine IM into the lateral thigh is the first-line treatment — it reverses airway swelling and restores blood pressure in minutes. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, never substitutes.

questions.q: Before administering digoxin, the nurse must assess the:
options: Apical pulse for one full minute
questions.explain: Digoxin slows the heart; the apical pulse must be counted for a full minute and the dose held (and the provider notified) if the rate is below 60 bpm in adults. A wrist pulse is not accurate enough.

questions.q: Which abbreviation is on the official 'Do Not Use' list because it is easily misread?
questions.explain: 'QD' has been misread as 'QID' (four times daily), causing overdoses. It must be written as 'daily.' Trailing zeros (1.0 mg), 'U' for units, and MSO4/MgSO4 are also banned.

questions.q: Peak and trough drug levels are routinely monitored for which medication?
questions.explain: Vancomycin (and aminoglycosides like gentamicin) have a narrow therapeutic window — too little fails to kill bacteria, too much damages kidneys and hearing. Troughs are drawn just before the next dose.

questions.q: A patient on warfarin is bleeding. The specific antidote the nurse should anticipate is:
questions.explain: Vitamin K reverses warfarin's anticoagulant effect; in life-threatening bleeding, fresh frozen plasma or PCC is also given. Protamine sulfate reverses heparin, and naloxone reverses opioids — know the pairing for each drug class.

questions.q: Which drug is an opioid antagonist used to reverse opioid overdose?
questions.explain: Naloxone displaces opioids from receptors and can restore breathing within minutes. Because its effect is shorter than most opioids, patients must still be monitored for re-sedation.

questions.q: A patient asks to crush their enteric-coated tablet because it is hard to swallow. The nurse should:
options: Crush it and mix with applesauce
Tell the patient to swallow it whole and contact the provider for an alternative
questions.explain: Enteric coating protects the stomach from the drug (or the drug from stomach acid); crushing destroys that protection and can cause harm. Never crush enteric-coated, extended-release, or sublingual medications — request an alternative formulation instead.

title: Dosage Calculations
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Worked medication math: desired over have, IV flow rates, drip rates, weight-based dosing, and safe rounding.

questions.q: Order: 500 mg. On hand: 250 mg tablets. How many tablets do you give?
questions.explain: Desired over have: 500 divided by 250 equals 2 tablets.

questions.q: Order: 0.5 g by mouth. Pharmacy sends 500 mg tablets. How many tablets equal the dose? Note 1 g equals 1000 mg.
questions.explain: Convert first: 0.5 g equals 500 mg. Then 500 divided by 500 equals 1 tablet.

questions.q: IV order: 1000 mL over 8 hours. What is the flow rate in mL per hour?
questions.explain: 1000 mL divided by 8 hours equals 125 mL per hour.

questions.q: IV: 500 mL over 4 hours with tubing that delivers 15 drops per mL. What is the drip rate in drops per minute?
questions.explain: Volume times drop factor divided by minutes: 500 times 15 divided by 240 minutes equals 31.25, about 31 drops per minute.

questions.q: Weight-based order: 5 mg per kg for a child who weighs 20 kg. What is the total dose?
questions.explain: Multiply dose by weight: 5 mg per kg times 20 kg equals 100 mg.

questions.q: Order: 750 mg. Stock: 250 mg per 5 mL suspension. How many mL do you give?
questions.explain: 750 divided by 250 equals 3, and 3 times 5 mL equals 15 mL.

questions.q: A safe range is 10 to 20 mg per kg per day in 2 divided doses. Child weighs 30 kg. What is the maximum single dose?
questions.explain: Maximum daily: 20 times 30 equals 600 mg per day. Divided by 2 doses equals 300 mg per dose.

questions.q: Order: heparin 800 units per hour. Bag: 25000 units in 500 mL. At what mL per hour should the pump run?
questions.explain: Concentration is 25000 divided by 500 equals 50 units per mL. 800 divided by 50 equals 16 mL per hour.

questions.q: Calculated dose is 1.74 mL. To what should you round for measuring in a standard oral syringe marked in tenths?
questions.explain: Round to the nearest tenth you can measure accurately: 1.74 rounds to 1.7 mL. Always follow facility policy for rounding.

questions.q: Order: 0.25 mg. Stock: 1 mg per mL. The calculated volume is 0.25 mL. What is the safest check before giving it?
options: Give 2.5 mL because decimals are unsafe
Verify the math and dose with the order and, per policy, an independent double-check for high-alert drugs
questions.explain: Small decimal volumes are high risk for tenfold errors. Recheck the conversion and calculation, and use an independent double-check where policy requires it.

rounds.title: Dosage Calculations
rounds.desc: Worked medication math: desired over have, IV flow rates, drip rates, weight-based dosing, and safe rounding.

title: Fluids & Electrolytes
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Fluid balance, key electrolytes, IV fluids, and the assessments that catch imbalance early.

questions.q: A patient has dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, and concentrated urine. These signs most suggest:
questions.explain: Dry membranes, poor turgor, and concentrated urine are classic signs the body is conserving water in a fluid deficit.

questions.q: Normal serum potassium range is about 3.5 to 5.0 mEq per L. A result of 6.1 mEq per L is:
questions.explain: 6.1 is above the normal range. High potassium risks dangerous cardiac rhythm changes, so report it promptly.

questions.q: Which assessment best tracks day-to-day fluid balance changes?
options: Daily weights at the same time on the same scale
questions.explain: Daily weights are the most sensitive bedside indicator: a change of 1 kg roughly equals 1 liter of fluid.

questions.q: A patient on IV fluids develops crackles in the lungs, shortness of breath, and a bounding pulse. The nurse suspects:
questions.explain: Crackles, dyspnea, and a bounding pulse during IV therapy suggest fluid overload. Slow or stop per orders/protocol and assess and notify promptly.

questions.q: Hyponatremia (low sodium) most characteristically affects which system first?
questions.explain: Low sodium shifts water into brain cells, so early signs are neurologic: headache, confusion, and in severe cases seizures.

questions.q: Which food instruction fits a patient who must limit potassium?
options: Drink orange juice with each meal
questions.explain: Oranges, bananas, potatoes, and many salt substitutes are high in potassium and should be limited on a low-potassium diet.

questions.q: 0.9 percent sodium chloride (normal saline) is classified as:
questions.explain: Normal saline has about the same tonicity as body fluids, so it is isotonic and expands intravascular volume.

questions.q: A patient with vomiting and diarrhea for 3 days is at greatest risk for which acid-base problem?
options: Metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss plus volume depletion - assess and report
questions.explain: Prolonged diarrhea loses bicarbonate-rich fluid and vomiting/diarrhea together cause volume depletion; assess perfusion and electrolytes. Note vomiting alone tends toward metabolic alkalosis - the combined picture needs lab confirmation.

questions.q: Strict intake and output shows intake 2400 mL and output 900 mL in 24 hours, with new leg swelling. Best action?
options: Assess for fluid overload and notify the provider
Ignore it - intake always exceeds output
Restrict all oral intake on your own without orders
questions.explain: A large positive balance with new edema suggests fluid retention or overload: assess lungs, weight, and vitals, then notify the provider.

questions.q: Calcium is most closely tied to which bedside assessment when it is low?
options: Muscle excitability - cramps, tingling, positive Chvostek/Trousseau signs
questions.explain: Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability: perioral tingling, cramps, and positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs.

rounds.title: Fluids & Electrolytes
rounds.desc: Fluid balance, key electrolytes, IV fluids, and the assessments that catch imbalance early.

title: Wound Care & Skin Integrity
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Pressure injury staging, wound assessment, drainage, healing, and prevention for skin breakdown.

questions.q: A pressure injury with full-thickness skin loss where fat is visible but bone and muscle are not is stage:
questions.explain: Stage 3 is full-thickness loss with adipose (fat) visible. Stage 4 extends to muscle, tendon, or bone.

questions.q: Intact skin with non-blanchable redness over a bony area is a pressure injury at stage:
questions.explain: Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable erythema. Blanching that returns to normal color is not stage 1.

questions.q: The best way to prevent pressure injuries in an immobile patient is to:
options: Keep the head of the bed at 90 degrees all day
Reposition at least every 2 hours and keep skin clean and dry
questions.explain: Regular repositioning, skin care, moisture control, and nutrition are the core prevention bundle. Avoid donut cushions and vigorous massage over bony prominences.

questions.q: Purulent drainage from a wound is best described as:
options: Thick, cloudy, yellow-green drainage that suggests infection
questions.explain: Purulent drainage is thick and cloudy and often signals infection. Serous is clear, sanguineous is bloody, serosanguineous is pink and watery.

questions.q: A wound that is healing by primary intention has:
options: Edges well approximated, as with a sutured surgical incision
A large open area filling with granulation
questions.explain: Primary intention: edges are closed and approximated, healing quickly with minimal scar.

questions.q: When assessing a wound, the nurse notes redness spreading beyond the edges, warmth, and increased pain. Best interpretation?
options: Possible wound infection - assess, document, and notify the provider
A sign to remove all dressings permanently
questions.explain: Spreading erythema, warmth, increasing pain, and purulent drainage are signs of infection requiring prompt reporting.

questions.q: Which patient is at HIGHEST risk for skin breakdown?
options: A young ambulatory patient eating well
An immobile older adult with incontinence and poor nutrition
A patient with intact sensation who repositions often
questions.explain: Immobility plus moisture from incontinence plus poor nutrition is the highest-risk combination for pressure injury.

questions.q: Granulation tissue in a healing wound should look:
questions.explain: Healthy granulation is beefy red and moist. Black suggests eschar/necrosis; yellow stringy tissue suggests slough.

questions.q: Before a dressing change, the nurse's priority steps include:
options: Skipping hand hygiene if gloves are worn
Hand hygiene, pain assessment/premedication if ordered, and sterile or clean technique as ordered
Opening supplies after touching the wound
questions.explain: Hand hygiene is required even with gloves; assessing and treating pain before the procedure improves tolerance and assessment.

questions.q: A wound covered by black eschar so the depth cannot be seen is classified as:
questions.explain: When slough or eschar covers the wound bed, depth cannot be determined, so it is unstageable until debrided.

rounds.title: Wound Care & Skin Integrity
rounds.desc: Pressure injury staging, wound assessment, drainage, healing, and prevention for skin breakdown.

title: Prioritization & Delegation
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: ABCs, Maslow, stable versus unstable, and what the RN can and cannot delegate to assistive personnel.

questions.q: Using ABCs, which patient should the nurse assess FIRST?
options: A patient with stridor and difficulty breathing
A stable patient due for a routine bath
questions.explain: Airway comes first. Stridor signals a threatened airway and outranks comfort, teaching, and hygiene needs.

questions.q: Which task can the RN appropriately delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
options: Measuring vital signs on a stable patient and reporting results
questions.explain: UAP may collect data such as vital signs on stable patients. Assessment, teaching, and evaluation remain RN responsibilities.

questions.q: Four patients call. Who is the priority?
options: A patient asking when lunch arrives
A patient requesting a TV channel change
A post-op patient reporting sudden chest pain and shortness of breath
questions.explain: Sudden chest pain with dyspnea post-op could signal a pulmonary embolism or cardiac event - assess immediately.

questions.q: Which patient is appropriate to assign to a float RN with limited unit experience?
options: A stable patient on day 3 with predictable needs
A patient requiring frequent titration of IV drips
questions.explain: Assign the most stable, predictable patient to the least experienced nurse; unstable and titrating patients need experienced staff.

questions.q: A UAP reports a blood pressure of 88/52 on a patient who was 118/74 an hour ago. The RN should:
options: Ask the UAP to recheck it in 4 hours
Go assess the patient personally and intervene as indicated
Delegate the assessment to the UAP
questions.explain: Delegation never transfers accountability. A significant change requires the RN to assess the patient directly.

questions.q: Which statement reflects correct delegation of ambulation?
options: Decide if Mrs. Lee is ready to ambulate and walk her
Teach Mrs. Lee how to use her walker for the first time
Walk Mrs. Lee, who is stable post-op day 2, to the nurses station and back, and report any dizziness to me at once
Evaluate whether Mrs. Lee tolerated ambulation yesterday
questions.explain: The RN delegates the task with clear limits and reporting instructions. Deciding readiness, first-time teaching, and evaluation stay with the RN.

questions.q: Prioritization by Maslow: which need is met FIRST?
options: Physiologic needs like oxygen and circulation
questions.explain: Maslow puts physiologic needs first; higher needs are addressed after survival needs are stable.

questions.q: A nurse has 4 tasks. Which should be done FIRST?
options: Check a patient whose oxygen saturation just dropped to 88 percent
questions.explain: A falling oxygen saturation is an acute physiologic threat and outranks documentation, restocking, and callbacks.

questions.q: Which task must NOT be delegated to UAP?
options: Helping a stable patient to the bathroom
questions.explain: Medication administration cannot be delegated to UAP. Vital signs, toileting help, and intake/output measurement on stable patients can be.

questions.q: Two patients need the nurse: one is anxious before a procedure, one is a diabetic whose glucose is 52 mg per dL and who is shaky and sweaty. Priority?
options: The hypoglycemic patient - treat low glucose per protocol first
The anxious patient - anxiety always outranks glucose
Both can wait until after lunch
Delegate the hypoglycemia treatment to UAP
questions.explain: Symptomatic hypoglycemia (52 mg per dL, shaky, sweaty) is an immediate physiologic threat. Treat per protocol (fast-acting carbohydrate if safe to swallow) before addressing anxiety.
