title: Essentials & Greetings
subject: Spanish Basics
description: Hello, goodbye, please, thank you — the survival phrases.

questions.q: 'Thank you' in Spanish is:
questions.explain: Gracias = thank you.

questions.q: How do you say 'Good morning'?
questions.explain: Buenos días is used until around midday.

questions.q: 'Por favor' means:
questions.explain: Por favor = please.

questions.q: 'De nada' is the response to 'gracias' and means:
questions.explain: De nada = you're welcome (literally 'of nothing').

questions.q: '¿Cómo estás?' asks:
questions.explain: ¿Cómo estás? = How are you? (informal).

questions.q: 'Hasta luego' means:
questions.explain: Hasta luego = see you later.

questions.q: The number 'seven' in Spanish is:
questions.explain: Uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete...

questions.q: 'Lo siento' means:
questions.explain: Lo siento = I'm sorry.

questions.q: 'Buenas noches' is used:
questions.explain: Buenas noches = good evening / good night.

questions.q: 'Me llamo...' means:
questions.explain: Me llamo = my name is (literally 'I call myself').

rounds.title: Essentials & Greetings
rounds.desc: Hello, goodbye, please, thank you — the survival phrases.

description: Count to 100, name the days and months, and tell time in Spanish.

questions.explain: "Quince" = 15. Don't confuse it with "cincuenta" (50) or "cinco" (5). The -ce pattern marks the teens: once (11), doce (12), trece (13), catorce (14), quince (15).
questions.q: What number is "quince"?

questions.explain: 21 is "veintiuno" — a single word. After 30 the pattern switches to separate words: "treinta y uno" (31), "cuarenta y dos" (42).
questions.q: How do you say "twenty-one" in Spanish?

questions.explain: "Miércoles" = Wednesday. Spanish days are masculine and NOT capitalized: el lunes (Mon), el martes (Tue), el miércoles (Wed), el jueves (Thu), el viernes (Fri), el sábado (Sat), el domingo (Sun).
questions.q: What day is "miércoles"?

questions.explain: "Agosto" = August. Like days, Spanish months are written lowercase: enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto...
questions.q: Which month is "agosto"?

questions.explain: "¿Qué hora es?" = "What time is it?" The verb "es" is singular because "la hora" is singular — but watch out: for 2:00 and later, answers switch to plural "Son las dos," "Son las tres"...
questions.q: What does "¿Qué hora es?" mean?

questions.explain: Half past = "y media." And it's "SON las tres" (plural) because 3 is more than 1 — "es" is only used for 1:00, "Es la una."
questions.q: How do you say "It's 3:30" in Spanish?

questions.explain: "Cien" = 100 (used before nouns: "cien años"). "Ciento" appears in compounds like "ciento uno" (101). "Mil" = 1,000 — note there's no "un" before it.
questions.q: What number is "cien"?

questions.explain: "Jueves" = Thursday, so the next day is "viernes" (Friday). The week runs: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo.
questions.q: Which day comes right after "jueves"?

questions.explain: "Hoy" = today (the h is silent). "Ayer" = yesterday, "mañana" = tomorrow (or morning, depending on context), "ahora" = now.
questions.q: How do you say "today" in Spanish?

questions.explain: "El fin de semana" literally means "the end of the week" = the weekend. Related: "entre semana" means "during the week" (weekdays).
questions.q: What does "el fin de semana" mean?

subject: Spanish Basics

Food & Daily Life
subject: Spanish Basics
description: Ordering food, household words, and everyday nouns.

questions.q: 'La manzana' is:
questions.explain: Manzana = apple.

questions.q: How do you say 'water'?
questions.explain: Agua = water.

questions.q: 'El desayuno' refers to:
questions.explain: Desayuno = breakfast; almuerzo = lunch; cena = dinner.

questions.q: 'La casa' means:
questions.explain: Casa = house/home.

questions.q: 'El perro' is:
questions.explain: Perro = dog; gato = cat.

questions.q: To ask for the check at a restaurant: 'La ___, por favor.'
questions.explain: La cuenta = the check/bill.

questions.q: 'El pan' is:
questions.explain: Pan = bread.

questions.q: 'La leche' means:
questions.explain: Leche = milk.

questions.q: 'Hoy' means:
questions.explain: Hoy = today; mañana = tomorrow; ayer = yesterday.

questions.q: 'La escuela' is:
questions.explain: Escuela = school.

title: Core Verbs

description: Ser, estar, tener, ir — the verbs everything else builds on.

questions.q: 'Yo soy' means:
questions.explain: Soy is from ser — used for identity, origin, traits.

questions.q: 'Estoy cansado' means:
questions.explain: Estar covers temporary states: estoy cansado = I am tired.

questions.q: 'Tener' means:
questions.explain: Tener = to have (also used for age and hunger expressions).

questions.q: 'Voy' comes from the verb 'ir,' meaning:
questions.explain: Ir = to go; yo voy = I go / I'm going.

questions.q: 'Quiero' means:
questions.explain: Querer = to want; yo quiero = I want.

questions.q: 'Hablar' means:
questions.explain: Hablar = to speak/talk.

questions.q: Which verb would you use for location: 'La tienda ___ aquí'?
questions.explain: Locations use estar: está aquí = it is (located) here.

questions.q: 'Comer' means:
questions.explain: Comer = to eat.

questions.q: 'Puedo' (from poder) means:
questions.explain: Poder = to be able to; yo puedo = I can.

questions.q: 'Vivir' means:
questions.explain: Vivir = to live.

title: Travel, Directions & Family

questions.q: 'A la derecha' means:
questions.explain: Derecha = right; izquierda = left; derecho/recto = straight.

questions.q: '¿Dónde está la estación?' asks:
questions.explain: Dónde está…? = Where is…? — the essential travel question.

questions.q: 'Cerca' means ___ and 'lejos' means ___.
questions.explain: Cerca = near, lejos = far.

questions.q: 'La hermana' is:
questions.explain: Hermano = brother, hermana = sister.

questions.q: 'Mis abuelos' means:
questions.explain: Abuelo/a = grandparent; abuelos = grandparents (or grandfathers).

questions.q: Which is correct for 'our house' (casa is feminine)?
questions.explain: Possessives agree with the thing owned: casa is feminine → nuestra.

questions.q: 'Simpático' in Spanish means:
questions.explain: A classic false friend — simpático means nice, pleasant, friendly.

questions.q: 'Voy a estudiar mañana' means:
questions.explain: Ir a + infinitive = the near future: 'going to' do something.

questions.q: 'El esposo' is:
questions.explain: Esposo/a = husband/wife (spouse).

questions.q: 'Son las tres y media' means:
questions.explain: Y media = :30 — son las tres y media = 3:30.

description: Essential everyday phrases: greetings, thanks, excuses, and questions you'll actually use.

questions.explain: "Muchas gracias" literally means "many thanks" and is the standard way to say "thank you very much." "Por favor" = please, "de nada" = you're welcome, "buenas noches" = good evening.
questions.q: How do you say "Thank you very much" in Spanish?

questions.explain: "¿Cómo estás?" is the informal way to ask "How are you?" — use it with friends and family. "¿Cómo está usted?" is the formal version for strangers and elders.
questions.q: What does "¿Cómo estás?" mean?

questions.explain: "Perdón" works for both "excuse me" (getting attention or bumping into someone) and a light "sorry." "Lo siento" is deeper — a sincere apology. "Salud" = bless you / cheers.
questions.q: Which phrase means "Excuse me"?

questions.explain: "Hasta luego" = "until later" → "see you later." Watch out: "hasta mañana" specifically means "see you tomorrow."
questions.q: How do you say "See you later" in Spanish?

questions.explain: "¡Salud!" (literally "health!") is what Spanish speakers say after a sneeze — the equivalent of "bless you." It also means "cheers!" when toasting.
questions.q: Your friend just sneezed. What do you say?

questions.explain: "De nada" literally means "of nothing" — it's the standard reply to "gracias," just as "you're welcome" answers "thank you."
questions.q: What does "De nada" mean?

questions.explain: "¿Dónde está el baño?" = "Where is the bathroom?" "Dónde" asks about location, and "está" is the form of "to be" used for where things are. An essential travel phrase.
questions.q: How do you ask "Where is the bathroom?"?

questions.explain: Said to someone about to eat (or already eating), "¡Buen provecho!" = "Enjoy your meal!" — the Spanish equivalent of "bon appétit."
questions.q: What does "¡Buen provecho!" mean?

questions.explain: "¿Cómo te llamas?" literally asks "How do you call yourself?" — the standard informal "What's your name?" In formal situations, use "¿Cómo se llama usted?"
questions.q: How do you ask "What is your name?" to a new classmate?

questions.explain: "¡Felicidades!" = "Congratulations!" — said for birthdays, graduations, promotions, and any achievement worth celebrating.
questions.q: Your friend says "¡Felicidades!" What are they doing?

subject: Spanish Basics
description: Asking detailed questions with que, quien, cuanto, por que, and more.

questions.q: 'Que' in a question most often means:
questions.explain: Que is used to ask what something is or means.

questions.q: How do you ask 'Who is that?' in Spanish?
questions.explain: Quien means who, so 'Quien es?' asks who someone is.

questions.q: 'Cuanto cuesta?' means:
questions.explain: Cuanto asks about amount; cuesta is from costar, to cost.

questions.q: 'Por que' is used to ask:
questions.explain: Por que asks for a reason; porque (one word) means because.

questions.q: How do you ask 'When is the party?' in Spanish?
questions.explain: Cuando means when.

questions.q: 'Cual' is usually the best choice when you are:
options: Selecting from a group of options
questions.explain: Cual is used to choose among known options, like 'which one.'

questions.q: How do you ask 'How many students are there?' in Spanish?
questions.explain: Cuantos means how many for masculine plural nouns.

questions.q: 'Como se dice...?' is a useful question that means:
questions.explain: Como se dice is the standard way to ask how to say a word in Spanish.

questions.q: To ask about place, the question word you need is:
questions.explain: Donde means where and asks about location.

questions.q: Which question asks about the way something is done?
questions.explain: Como can mean how, asking about manner or method.

title: Past Tense Basics
subject: Spanish Basics
description: Talking about yesterday: regular preterite forms of -ar, -er, and -ir verbs.

questions.q: Yesterday, 'yo hable' (from hablar) means:
questions.explain: Hable with yo in past context is the preterite: I spoke.

questions.q: The preterite ending for 'tu' with -ar verbs (hablar -> tu ...) is:
questions.explain: For -ar preterite, tu takes -aste: tu hablaste, you spoke.

questions.q: 'Comimos' means:
questions.explain: Comimos is the nosotros preterite of comer: we ate.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly says 'She studied last night' in Spanish?
questions.explain: Estudio is the ella preterite of estudiar, and anoche means last night.

questions.q: The verb 'fui' can be the past tense of both ser and:
questions.explain: Fui means I was and also I went; context tells which verb is meant.

questions.q: 'Ayer' means:
questions.explain: Ayer is the key time word for talking about the past day.

questions.q: How do you say 'They watched the movie' in Spanish?
questions.explain: Miraron is the ellos preterite of mirar: they watched.

questions.q: The preterite of 'vivir' for 'yo' is:
questions.explain: For -ir preterite, yo takes -i: yo vivi, I lived.

questions.q: Which phrase signals the preterite (a completed past action)?
questions.explain: La semana pasada (last week) points to a completed past time.

questions.q: 'Tuve' is the preterite of tener and means:
questions.explain: Tener has an irregular preterite stem tuv-: yo tuve, I had.

questions.q: Someone asks 'Te gusta la musica?' A good positive answer is:
questions.explain: Me gusta mucho means I like it a lot, answering a gusta question.

questions.q: How do you say 'I think that...' to give an opinion in Spanish?
questions.explain: Creo que (I think that) introduces an opinion.

questions.q: Your friend says 'Estoy enfermo.' A caring response is:
questions.explain: Que te mejores pronto means I hope you get well soon.

questions.q: How do you ask a friend 'What are you doing this weekend?' in Spanish?
options: Que haces este fin de semana?
questions.explain: Que haces asks what are you doing; este fin de semana is this weekend.

questions.q: 'Yo tambien' is the right reply when someone says 'Me gusta el futbol' and you:
questions.explain: Tambien means also or too, showing agreement.

questions.q: To politely disagree, you can begin with:
questions.explain: No estoy de acuerdo means I do not agree.

questions.q: How do you say 'See you tomorrow' in Spanish?
questions.explain: Hasta manana literally means until tomorrow.

questions.q: Someone says 'Gracias por tu ayuda.' You reply:
questions.explain: Fue un placer (it was a pleasure) is a warm reply to thanks for help.

questions.q: 'Vamos a ...' at the start of a sentence usually proposes:
options: Let us go to / we are going to ...
questions.explain: Vamos a suggests a plan or proposal: let us go / we are going to.

questions.q: How do you ask 'Can you repeat that, please?' in Spanish?
questions.explain: Puedes repetir means can you repeat, a key conversation rescue phrase.

title: Reading Short Passages
subject: Spanish Basics
description: Reading short Spanish passages and answering questions about the details.

questions.q: Passage: 'Maria vive en una casa pequena con su familia. Tiene un perro que se llama Max.' Where does Maria live?
questions.explain: Casa pequena means small house.

questions.q: Passage: 'Hoy es lunes. Pablo tiene clase de matematicas a las nueve y clase de arte a las once.' What is Pablo's first class today?
questions.explain: The passage lists matematicas at nine, before arte at eleven.

questions.q: Passage: 'El restaurante abre a las doce y cierra a las diez de la noche. Sirve comida italiana.' When does the restaurant close?
questions.explain: Cierra a las diez de la noche means it closes at 10 p.m.

questions.q: Passage: 'Luis compro pan, huevos y fruta en el mercado. Pago con dinero en efectivo.' How did Luis pay?
questions.explain: Dinero en efectivo means cash.

questions.q: Passage: 'Ana esta triste porque su amiga se muda a otra ciudad la semana que viene.' Why is Ana sad?
options: Her friend is moving to another city
questions.explain: Se muda a otra ciudad means is moving to another city.

questions.q: Passage: 'El tren sale a las seis de la manana. Llega a Madrid a las nueve.' How long is the train trip?
questions.explain: From six in the morning to nine is three hours.

questions.q: Passage: 'Carlos quiere ser doctor. Estudia medicina en la universidad y trabaja en una biblioteca los fines de semana.' Where does Carlos work on weekends?
questions.explain: Trabaja en una biblioteca means he works in a library.

questions.q: Passage: 'La clase de espanol es interesante, pero un poco dificil. La profesora es muy paciente.' How does the writer describe the teacher?
questions.explain: La profesora es muy paciente: the teacher is very patient.

questions.q: Passage: 'En verano, vamos a la playa cada sabado. Nadamos y jugamos en la arena.' What do they do at the beach?
options: Swim and play in the sand
questions.explain: Nadamos (we swim) y jugamos en la arena (we play in the sand).

questions.q: Passage: 'Mi hermano menor tiene ocho anos. Le gusta dibujar y leer cuentos antes de dormir.' What does the younger brother like to do before sleeping?
questions.explain: Leer cuentos antes de dormir means read stories before sleeping.

description: Universal numbering, tooth types, surfaces, cusps, roots, and enamel — the map every dental exam starts with.

questions.explain: Numbering starts at the maxillary (upper) right third molar as #1, runs across the upper arch to #16, drops to the lower left third molar (#17), and ends at the lower right third molar (#32).
questions.q: In the Universal Numbering System, tooth #1 is the:

questions.explain: Counting from #1 (upper right wisdom tooth), #8 is the maxillary right central incisor — the front tooth just right of the midline.
questions.q: Tooth #8 in the Universal system is the:

questions.explain: #30 is the mandibular right first molar — one of the most commonly restored teeth, and often the first permanent tooth to erupt around age six.
questions.q: Tooth #30 is the:

questions.explain: Primary teeth use capital letters A through T (20 teeth total), starting at the upper right second molar (A) and following the same path as permanent numbering.
questions.q: How are primary (deciduous) teeth identified in the Universal system?

questions.explain: Adults have 32 permanent teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, and 12 molars including the third molars (wisdom teeth). Primary dentition has 20 — no premolars and no third molars.
questions.q: A full permanent dentition contains how many teeth?

questions.explain: Mesial faces the midline; distal faces away from it. Every tooth has exactly one mesial and one distal surface.
questions.q: The tooth surface facing toward the midline of the arch is the:

questions.explain: Posterior teeth meet on their occlusal surfaces; anterior teeth (incisors, canines) have an incisal edge instead — there is no occlusal surface in front.
questions.q: The chewing surface of a premolar or molar is called the:

questions.explain: Maxillary first molars typically have three roots — two buccal and one large palatal root — while mandibular molars usually have two (mesial and distal).
questions.q: A maxillary first molar normally has how many roots?

questions.explain: The maxillary canine has the longest root of any tooth, which is why canines are often called the cornerstones of the arch.
questions.q: Which tooth usually has the longest root in the mouth?

questions.explain: Enamel covers the crown and is about 96% mineral — harder than bone — but it contains no living cells, so once lost it cannot regenerate.
questions.q: The hardest substance in the human body is:

subject: Dental Fundamentals
title: Tooth Anatomy & Numbering

description: All 32 permanent teeth by Universal number — sort every tooth into its type. Built for Sort Sprint.

questions.explain: #1 is the upper right third molar (wisdom tooth) — numbering starts here, and it's the tooth most often impacted or missing.
questions.q: #1 · Upper Right 3rd Molar (Wisdom)

questions.explain: The second molar sits just in front of the wisdom tooth and usually erupts around age 12.
questions.q: #2 · Upper Right 2nd Molar

questions.explain: #3, the upper right first molar, typically has three roots and is a cornerstone of chewing.
questions.q: #3 · Upper Right 1st Molar

questions.explain: Premolars sit between the canines and molars; the second premolar usually has a single root.
questions.q: #4 · Upper Right 2nd Premolar

questions.explain: The upper first premolar often has two roots (buccal and palatal) — unlike most other premolars.
questions.q: #5 · Upper Right 1st Premolar

questions.explain: The canine is the pointed cornerstone tooth, and the upper canine has the longest root in the mouth.
questions.q: #6 · Upper Right Canine

questions.explain: Lateral incisors sit beside the centrals; upper laterals are the teeth most often congenitally missing after wisdom teeth.
questions.q: #7 · Upper Right Lateral Incisor

questions.explain: #8 is the upper right central incisor — the most visible tooth in the smile and the most commonly injured in falls.
questions.q: #8 · Upper Right Central Incisor

questions.explain: #9 mirrors #8 across the midline — the count crosses to the left side at the upper centrals.
questions.q: #9 · Upper Left Central Incisor

questions.explain: The upper left lateral incisor is #10, continuing the count outward from the midline.
questions.q: #10 · Upper Left Lateral Incisor

questions.explain: #11 is the upper left canine — upper canines are sometimes called eyeteeth.
questions.q: #11 · Upper Left Canine

questions.explain: The first premolar replaces the primary first molar — primary teeth have no premolars at all.
questions.q: #12 · Upper Left 1st Premolar

questions.explain: #13 is the upper left second premolar, a two-cusped tooth built for crushing.
questions.q: #13 · Upper Left 2nd Premolar

questions.explain: #14, the upper left first molar, erupts around age six behind the baby teeth — no baby tooth is lost for it.
questions.q: #14 · Upper Left 1st Molar

questions.explain: Second molars erupt around age 12, which is why they're nicknamed the 12-year molars.
questions.q: #15 · Upper Left 2nd Molar

questions.explain: #16 finishes the upper arch — the count then drops down to #17 on the lower left.
questions.q: #16 · Upper Left 3rd Molar (Wisdom)

questions.explain: #17 is the lower left wisdom tooth; lower third molars are the most commonly impacted teeth.
questions.q: #17 · Lower Left 3rd Molar (Wisdom)

questions.explain: Lower molars usually have two roots (mesial and distal) — unlike the three-rooted upper molars.
questions.q: #18 · Lower Left 2nd Molar

questions.explain: #19, the lower left first molar, is often the most heavily restored tooth because it erupts earliest and does the most chewing.
questions.q: #19 · Lower Left 1st Molar

questions.explain: #20 is the lower left second premolar, counting forward from the molars toward the midline.
questions.q: #20 · Lower Left 2nd Premolar

questions.explain: Lower premolars look more canine-like than upper premolars do, with one dominant buccal cusp.
questions.q: #21 · Lower Left 1st Premolar

questions.explain: #22 is the lower left canine — canines guide the bite during side-to-side jaw movement.
questions.q: #22 · Lower Left Canine

questions.explain: Lower incisors are the smallest teeth in the mouth, and #23 is the lower left lateral.
questions.q: #23 · Lower Left Lateral Incisor

questions.explain: #24 is the lower left central incisor, just left of the lower midline.
questions.q: #24 · Lower Left Central Incisor

questions.explain: #25 crosses the midline to the lower right central incisor.
questions.q: #25 · Lower Right Central Incisor

questions.explain: #26 is the lower right lateral incisor, slightly wider than the central beside it.
questions.q: #26 · Lower Right Lateral Incisor

questions.explain: #27 is the lower right canine — all four canines mark the corners of the dental arches.
questions.q: #27 · Lower Right Canine

questions.explain: #28 is the lower right first premolar; premolars are also called bicuspids for their two cusps.
questions.q: #28 · Lower Right 1st Premolar

questions.explain: #29 is the lower right second premolar, the last tooth before the molars on this side.
questions.q: #29 · Lower Right 2nd Premolar

questions.explain: #30, the lower right first molar, is a favorite exam answer — one of the most commonly crowned and root-canaled teeth.
questions.q: #30 · Lower Right 1st Molar

questions.explain: #31 is the lower right second molar, sitting just in front of the wisdom tooth.
questions.q: #31 · Lower Right 2nd Molar

questions.explain: #32 is the last tooth in the system — the lower right third molar completes the count of 32.
questions.q: #32 · Lower Right 3rd Molar (Wisdom)

description: Sterilization, PPE, sharps safety, and the rules that keep patients and staff safe.

questions.explain: Sterilization destroys all microbial life including bacterial spores. Disinfection only reduces microbes to safer levels and does not reliably kill spores.
options: Kill all microorganisms, including bacterial spores
Reduce the number of microbes to a safe level
Remove all visible debris from instruments
Kill viruses but leave bacteria unharmed
questions.q: The primary goal of sterilization is to do what?

questions.explain: Autoclaves use steam under pressure to kill microbes quickly and reliably, making them the workhorse sterilizer in most dental offices.
questions.q: What is the most common method dental offices use to sterilize instruments?

questions.explain: Standard order: hand hygiene, gown, mask, protective eyewear, then gloves last so they stay cleanest. Doffing reverses it - gloves come off first.
questions.q: Which piece of PPE is put on LAST before beginning patient care?

questions.explain: The CDC calls hand hygiene the single most important measure for preventing infection, before and after gloves and patient contact.
questions.q: What is considered the single most important step in preventing cross-contamination?

questions.explain: OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard requires employers to offer the HBV vaccine series free of charge, usually within 10 working days of assignment.
questions.q: Which hepatitis virus has an effective vaccine that OSHA requires employers to offer dental healthcare workers?

questions.explain: Sharps containers must be puncture-resistant, leakproof, biohazard-labeled, and placed close to the point of use. Never recap used needles by hand.
options: Regular trash, wrapped carefully in paper
questions.q: Where must contaminated needles and other sharps be disposed of?

questions.explain: Items saturated with blood or saliva that could release it if squeezed - like blood-soaked gauze - are regulated medical waste and go in the red biohazard bag.
questions.q: Which of these is classified as regulated medical waste requiring special disposal?

questions.explain: Spaulding's classification: critical items penetrate tissue or bone (sterilize them); semicritical items touch mucous membranes (sterilize or high-level disinfect); noncritical items touch skin only.
questions.q: Which category of patient-care items must be sterilized between every patient because they penetrate soft tissue or bone?

questions.explain: Biological monitors contain heat-resistant Geobacillus spores. If the spores die, the cycle worked; growth means the sterilizer failed - the only true test of sterilization.
options: To check the temperature gauge reading
To verify the sterilizer is actually killing resistant spores
questions.q: Why are weekly biological monitors (spore tests) run on sterilizers?

questions.explain: Unprotected clinical contact surfaces must be cleaned and then disinfected between patients with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant, with full contact time observed.
options: Left until the end of the day
Cleaned and then disinfected with an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant
questions.q: After each patient, clinical contact surfaces that were not barrier-protected should be handled how?

description: Bitewing vs periapical vs panoramic, ALARA, shielding, digital imaging, and reading radiolucent vs radiopaque.

questions.explain: Bitewings show the crowns of upper and lower teeth together with the alveolar crest — ideal geometry for spotting decay between teeth and early bone loss.
options: Interproximal (between-the-teeth) caries and crestal bone levels
questions.q: Bitewing radiographs are the best choice for detecting:

questions.explain: The PA is the diagnostic image for the whole tooth — apex included — which is why it's used for abscesses, root fractures, and endodontic working lengths.
options: The entire tooth from crown tip to root apex plus surrounding bone
questions.q: A periapical (PA) radiograph shows:

questions.explain: Panoramic images trade fine detail for coverage: both jaws in one shot for wisdom teeth, large lesions, fractures, and growth assessment — but never for fine caries diagnosis.
options: A broad overview — impacted third molars, jaw lesions, trauma, and development
questions.q: A panoramic image is most useful for:

questions.explain: ALARA means every exposure must be justified and optimized — take only images that change care, and use fast receptors, collimation, and correct technique to keep dose minimal.
questions.q: ALARA, the guiding principle of dental radiography, stands for:

questions.explain: Lead shielding absorbs scatter; the thyroid collar matters because the thyroid is radiation-sensitive — especially in children — and sits close to the beam path.
options: Shield the patient's torso and thyroid from scatter radiation
questions.q: During radiography, the lead apron and thyroid collar serve to:

questions.explain: Digital sensors are more sensitive than film, cutting dose significantly, and images appear immediately, can be enhanced, and are stored electronically — no darkroom chemistry.
options: Uses less radiation and produces images instantly without chemicals
questions.q: Compared with traditional film, digital radiography generally:

questions.explain: Radiolucent = X-rays pass through easily, exposing the receptor more → dark. Soft tissue, pulp, decay, and abscesses are radiolucent; dense structures block rays and appear light.
questions.q: On a radiograph, a radiolucent structure appears:

questions.explain: Radiopacity tracks density: enamel is the most mineralized tissue in the body and metals block nearly all radiation, so both image bright white against darker dentin and bone.
options: Enamel and metallic restorations like amalgam
questions.q: Which of these appears most radiopaque (bright white) on a radiograph?

questions.explain: When receptor and tooth are parallel and the beam is aimed at right angles to both, the image is dimensionally accurate — critical for endodontic measurements.
options: Produces the least distortion by keeping the receptor parallel to the tooth and the beam perpendicular
Uses half the radiation of any other method
questions.q: The paralleling technique is preferred for periapical images because it:

questions.explain: Routine images are deferred, but a needed diagnostic image (with apron/collar and modern low-dose technique) delivers negligible fetal exposure and should not be withheld in an emergency.
options: Take a full series at every visit
Postpone elective images; take only diagnostically necessary ones with shielding
Never take any image under any circumstance, even emergencies
questions.q: For a pregnant patient, the standard approach to dental radiographs is to:

description: Fluoride, sealants, home-care coaching, medical-history red flags, and recall intervals that keep disease from starting.

questions.explain: Fluoride in plaque fluid drives calcium and phosphate back into early lesions (remineralization) and forms fluorapatite, which withstands acid better than the original enamel — plus it mildly inhibits bacterial enzymes.
options: Coating teeth so bacteria slide off
Promoting remineralization and making enamel more acid-resistant
questions.q: Fluoride protects teeth mainly by:

questions.explain: Varnish's sticky resin holds high-concentration fluoride (about 22,600 ppm) against the enamel for hours, and little is swallowed, so it's safe even for young children — applied 2–4 times a year for high-risk patients.
options: Deliver high-concentration fluoride that sticks to teeth for hours, for high-caries-risk patients
questions.q: Professional fluoride varnish is applied in the office primarily to:

questions.explain: Molar grooves are too narrow for bristles but perfect for bacteria; sealants physically barricade them — most effective on newly erupted first and second permanent molars.
options: Flowing resin into the deep grooves of molars so plaque and food can't lodge there
questions.q: Pit-and-fissure sealants work by:

questions.explain: The 'six-year molars' erupt behind the baby teeth (no tooth is lost for them), and their deep fissures decay quickly — sealing soon after eruption gives the most protection.
questions.q: First permanent molars erupt around age ___ and should be sealed soon after eruption.

questions.explain: Twice-daily two-minute brushing with fluoride toothpaste plus daily floss or interdental brushes is the evidence-based baseline; technique (gentle, angled at the gumline — e.g., Bass) matters more than force.
options: Once a day, hard, for 30 seconds
Twice daily for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, plus daily interdental cleaning
With a hard brush and no toothpaste
questions.q: Effective home care coaching recommends brushing:

questions.explain: Bisphosphonates suppress bone turnover; after invasive procedures the jawbone may fail to heal, exposing necrotic bone (MRONJ) — so dental clearance and conservative planning before starting therapy matter.
options: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) after extractions or surgery
questions.q: A patient taking bisphosphonates is a red flag mainly because of the risk of:

questions.explain: Warfarin thins clotting; INR confirms anticoagulation intensity. Many minor procedures proceed without stopping warfarin if the INR is acceptable — stopping it risks dangerous clots, so the physician guides any changes.
options: Bleeding risk; verify the INR is in a safe range (often in coordination with the physician)
questions.q: Before extracting a tooth in a patient on warfarin, the key concern and check is:

questions.explain: Saliva is the mouth's defense system — buffering acid, washing debris, and delivering repair minerals. Losing it (medications, radiation, Sjögren's syndrome) is why dry-mouth patients get rapid, atypical decay.
options: Buffers acids, clears food, and supplies calcium/phosphate for remineralization
questions.q: Dry mouth (xerostomia) sharply raises caries risk because saliva normally:

questions.explain: Each sugar exposure restarts a roughly 20–40 minute acid attack (the Stephan curve); frequent sipping and snacking keep pH low and demineralizing — frequency, not just amount, is the counseling target.
options: Total sugar eaten at one meal
How often sugar is consumed through the day
questions.q: For caries prevention, dietary counseling should emphasize that decay risk rises most with:

questions.explain: Six-month recalls remain the common default for low-risk patients (exam, cleaning, cancer screening), while high-risk patients — active perio, high caries rate, xerostomia — are seen every 3–4 months.
questions.q: A standard recall interval for a healthy, low-risk adult is every:

description: Probing depths, attachment loss, Stage I–IV periodontitis, scaling and root planing, and maintenance intervals.

questions.explain: Probing depths of 1–3 mm with no bleeding indicate health; deeper readings suggest a periodontal pocket has formed as attachment migrates down the root.
questions.q: A healthy gingival sulcus typically probes at:

questions.explain: CAL uses the fixed CEJ landmark: probing depth plus gingival recession (when the margin sits below the CEJ). It measures total support lost, which pocket depth alone can hide.
options: The gumline to the base of the pocket
The cementoenamel junction (CEJ) to the base of the pocket
The crown tip to the root tip
The bone crest to the apex
questions.q: Clinical attachment loss (CAL) is measured from:

questions.explain: Inflamed pocket epithelium is thin and ulcerated, so gentle probing provokes bleeding; absence of bleeding is a strong sign of periodontal stability.
questions.q: Bleeding on probing at a site indicates:

questions.explain: Staging runs by worst-site attachment loss: Stage I = 1–2 mm, Stage II = 3–4 mm, Stage III/IV = 5 mm or more, with increasing tooth-loss risk and treatment complexity.
questions.q: Under the current staging system, Stage I periodontitis shows interdental CAL of about:

questions.explain: Stage II is moderate periodontitis — 3–4 mm of attachment loss and radiographic bone loss into the coronal third of the root (roughly 15–33%).
questions.q: Stage II periodontitis corresponds to interdental CAL of:

questions.explain: SRP is the cornerstone nonsurgical therapy for periodontitis: thorough subgingival debridement so the gum can heal against a clean, smooth root and pocket depths shrink.
options: A cosmetic polish above the gumline
Nonsurgical deep cleaning that removes calculus and smooths root surfaces below the gumline
questions.q: Scaling and root planing (SRP) is best described as:

questions.explain: Periodontal pathogens recolonize pockets within weeks; the classic 3–4 month maintenance interval keeps bacterial loads below the threshold that restarts attachment loss.
questions.q: After active periodontal therapy, supportive maintenance visits are typically scheduled every:

questions.explain: Smoking impairs blood flow and immune defense in the gums and blunts healing — smokers lose more attachment and respond worse to treatment; it also masks bleeding, hiding disease.
questions.q: The strongest modifiable risk factor for periodontitis is:

questions.explain: Poorly controlled diabetes accelerates periodontal destruction, and periodontal inflammation in turn worsens insulin resistance and glycemic control — treating one helps the other.
questions.q: The relationship between diabetes and periodontitis is:

questions.explain: When attachment loss reaches the fork between molar roots, cleaning becomes difficult and prognosis drops — furcation involvement is a key finding on molars.
options: Bone loss has entered the area where a multirooted tooth's roots divide
questions.q: Furcation involvement means:

description: Reversible vs irreversible pulpitis, necrosis, periapical diagnosis, apex locators, and obturation with gutta-percha.

questions.explain: A brief, sharp response that fades = reversible pulpitis (the pulp can recover). Lingering or spontaneous pain means the inflamed pulp cannot recover — irreversible pulpitis, treated with root canal therapy or extraction.
questions.q: Pain that lingers for 30+ seconds after a cold stimulus is removed suggests:

questions.explain: If the pulp can recover, conservative care — removing caries or leaky restorations and sealing the tooth — lets inflammation resolve; no endodontic treatment is needed.
options: Removing the irritant (e.g., replacing the leaking filling) and monitoring
questions.q: Reversible pulpitis is typically treated by:

questions.explain: A dead pulp can't respond: necrosis is the usual finding, though multirooted teeth can have mixed status and recently traumatized teeth can give false negatives, so results are confirmed with other tests.
questions.q: A tooth that gives NO response to cold testing or electric pulp testing most likely has:

questions.explain: Percussion tenderness localizes inflammation to the periodontal ligament around the root apex — a hallmark of apical periodontitis, often from a dying pulp or a high bite.
questions.q: Pain on biting or percussion of a tooth points to inflammation in the:

questions.explain: Apex locators sense when a file reaches the apical constriction/foramen, letting the clinician set working length accurately (confirmed with a radiograph) and avoid over-instrumenting.
options: Determine the working length by locating the apical constriction
questions.q: An electronic apex locator is used during root canal therapy to:

questions.explain: Sodium hypochlorite dissolves organic tissue and kills bacteria inside the canal system — functions no file can accomplish in fins and lateral canals.
questions.q: The primary irrigant used to clean root canals is:

questions.explain: Gutta-percha — a rubbery, biocompatible material — is compacted with sealer to three-dimensionally fill and seal the cleaned canal space against re-infection.
questions.q: Canals are obturated (filled) primarily with:

questions.explain: The dam prevents saliva (and its bacteria) from contaminating the canal and stops small files or caustic irrigant from being swallowed or aspirated — a clinical and legal standard of care.
options: It isolates the tooth, keeping the canal aseptic and protecting the airway from instruments/irrigants
It is only for patient comfort
questions.q: Why is a rubber dam mandatory for root canal treatment?

questions.explain: RCT follows a fixed logic: enter the pulp chamber, measure each canal, disinfect and shape, seal with gutta-percha, then protect the tooth — usually with a crown on back teeth.
options: Access opening → determine working length → clean & shape → obturate → restore the crown
Fill the crown → drill the root
questions.q: In sequence, the major steps of root canal therapy are:

questions.explain: Chronic apical periodontitis destroys bone at the apex, producing the classic periapical radiolucency; treating the canal source usually allows the bone to heal.
options: A periapical lesion (bone lost to inflammation from the necrotic pulp)
questions.q: A dark (radiolucent) circle at the tip of a root on a radiograph, in a non-vital tooth, most likely represents:

description: Amalgam vs composite, glass ionomer, luting cements, and impression materials — picking the right material for the job.

questions.explain: Amalgam forms when liquid mercury is mixed (triturated) with a silver–tin–copper alloy powder; the set material is strong and durable, especially under heavy back-tooth chewing loads.
questions.q: Dental amalgam is an alloy of mercury combined mainly with:

questions.explain: Composite bonds to etched enamel and dentin, so the dentist removes less healthy tooth than amalgam's mechanical-retention shapes require — and it's tooth-colored.
options: Bonds adhesively to tooth structure, allowing more conservative preparations
Sets without any light or mixing
questions.q: A key advantage of composite resin over amalgam is that it:

questions.explain: Glass ionomer chemically bonds to tooth and slowly releases fluoride, making it a favorite for root-surface lesions, pediatric fillings, and high-caries-risk patients — though it's weaker than composite.
options: Releases fluoride and bonds chemically to tooth structure
questions.q: Glass ionomer cement is especially valued in dentistry because it:

questions.explain: Eugenol is a free-radical scavenger, so residual ZOE under a composite restoration can prevent the resin from curing properly — a classic materials-compatibility exam point.
options: Inhibits the polymerization (setting) of composite resin
questions.q: Zinc oxide–eugenol (ZOE) is known for its soothing effect on the pulp, but its eugenol:

questions.explain: Zinc phosphate holds crowns by mechanical interlocking into microscopic irregularities; it is strong in compression but has zero chemical adhesion and is acidic when freshly mixed.
options: Retains crowns mechanically and has no true adhesion to tooth
questions.q: Zinc phosphate cement, one of the oldest luting cements:

questions.explain: Its polyacrylic acid chains bond to calcium in the tooth, and it's notably kind to the pulp — a gentler, adhesive alternative to zinc phosphate.
questions.q: Polycarboxylate cement was historically important because it was the first cement to:

questions.explain: Alginate (irreversible hydrocolloid) is cheap and easy but dimensionally unstable — it gains and loses water fast, so casts must be poured within minutes for accuracy.
options: Study models — and it must be poured promptly
questions.q: Alginate impression material is best used for:

questions.explain: PVS captures fine detail and stays dimensionally stable for days, unlike alginate — which is why it's the standard for definitive restorative impressions.
questions.q: For a final crown-and-bridge impression, the most accurate, stable choice is:

questions.explain: Calcium hydroxide's high pH mildly irritates the pulp in a controlled way, prompting odontoblasts to lay down a reparative dentin bridge over a near-exposure.
options: Stimulates the pulp to form reparative (secondary) dentin
questions.q: Calcium hydroxide liner (e.g., Dycal) is placed in deep preparations because it:

questions.explain: Acid etching dissolves enamel rod ends, creating a frosted, high-energy surface full of micro-undercuts; resin tags lock into these, giving composite its bond strength.
options: Create microscopic pores that resin flows into for micromechanical retention
Kill all bacteria in the dentin
questions.q: Enamel is etched with phosphoric acid (about 37%) before bonding in order to:

description: Caries progression, gum disease, abscesses, and the oral-cancer warning signs that demand a biopsy or referral.

questions.explain: A white spot lesion is subsurface enamel demineralization — chalky white and still reversible with fluoride and plaque control before a cavity (cavitation) forms.
questions.q: The earliest visible stage of tooth decay is a:

questions.explain: Streptococcus mutans ferments dietary sugars into acid; sustained acid drops plaque pH and dissolves enamel mineral — the core of the caries process.
questions.q: The bacterium most strongly linked to starting dental caries is:

questions.explain: Gingivitis is reversible inflammation with no permanent damage. Periodontitis adds irreversible clinical attachment loss and bone loss — the finding that changes the diagnosis.
options: Loss of attachment and alveolar bone
questions.q: What separates periodontitis from gingivitis?

questions.explain: When pulp tissue dies — usually from deep caries or trauma — bacteria exit the root apex and form a periapical abscess, seen as a radiolucency at the root tip.
questions.q: A periapical abscess most often develops from:

questions.explain: Leukoplakia is a clinical description, not a diagnosis: a white plaque that won't rub off and can't be attributed to another condition. Because some are precancerous, persistent lesions are biopsied.
options: Cannot be scraped off or diagnosed as another disease
questions.q: Leukoplakia is best defined as a white patch that:

questions.explain: Pseudomembranous candidiasis forms soft white plaques that wipe away to an erythematous (red) base — the wipe test is the quickest way to separate it from leukoplakia. It's common with dentures, recent antibiotics, and immune suppression.
options: Wipe off, leaving a red, raw surface
questions.q: Oral candidiasis (thrush) plaques typically:

questions.explain: Over 90% of oral cancers are squamous cell carcinomas arising from the surface epithelium; tobacco and alcohol are the dominant risk factors, with HPV driving many throat (oropharyngeal) cancers.
questions.q: The most common type of oral cancer is:

questions.explain: Any ulcer, lump, or red/white patch persisting beyond two weeks must be evaluated for malignancy — early oral cancers are often painless, so 'it doesn't hurt' is not reassuring.
options: A canker sore that heals in 10 days
An ulcer that has not healed after two weeks
A small traumatic bite mark from yesterday
questions.q: Which finding most urgently needs referral/biopsy?

questions.explain: Red lesions are rarer but far more dangerous: a large share of erythroplakias already show severe dysplasia or carcinoma at biopsy. High-risk sites include the lateral tongue and floor of the mouth.
options: Is always a burn from hot food
Has a higher rate of severe dysplasia/cancer than leukoplakia
questions.q: Erythroplakia (a red patch) is concerning because it:

questions.explain: Aphthae form inside the mouth on non-keratinized mucosa (inner cheeks, lips, tongue underside) and are not infectious; cold sores are herpes simplex, contagious, and typically crust on the lip border.
options: Are caused by herpes simplex virus
Occur on movable inner-mouth mucosa and are not contagious
questions.q: Recurrent aphthous ulcers (canker sores) differ from cold sores because they:

title: Oral Pathology

description: Lidocaine and articaine, infection antibiotics, endocarditis prophylaxis, and pain control — plus who needs caution.

questions.explain: 2% lidocaine with epinephrine is the workhorse: reliable onset, moderate duration, and the vasoconstrictor extends working time. Benzocaine is topical only — it numbs surface tissue before the injection.
questions.q: The most commonly used local anesthetic in dentistry is:

questions.explain: Epinephrine is a vasoconstrictor: less blood flow at the site means the anesthetic washes out more slowly (longer duration), with less bleeding and lower peak blood levels of the drug.
options: It constricts local blood vessels, prolonging anesthesia and reducing bleeding
It speeds up the onset to seconds
questions.q: Why is epinephrine added to local anesthetic solutions?

questions.explain: Pulling back the plunger checks for blood return — a positive aspiration means the needle tip is intravascular, and injecting there could cause rapid systemic effects like a racing heart from epinephrine.
options: Confirm the needle is not inside a blood vessel
questions.q: Before depositing anesthetic, the clinician aspirates mainly to:

questions.explain: Cardiac patients tolerate small, carefully aspirated doses, but epinephrine can raise heart rate and blood pressure — so the total dose is limited, or a plain anesthetic like 3% mepivacaine is chosen for short procedures.
options: Use unlimited amounts — it's only local
Limit the dose and consider a plain (no-epi) anesthetic
Use epinephrine only in the front teeth
questions.q: For a patient with significant cardiovascular disease, the safest approach to epinephrine is to:

questions.explain: Articaine's chemical structure gives it superior bone penetration, so a simple infiltration can sometimes numb lower molars where lidocaine usually needs a nerve block.
options: Diffuses through bone better than other amides
Is the only anesthetic safe in pregnancy
questions.q: Articaine 4% is often chosen for mandibular teeth because it:

questions.explain: Amoxicillin covers the mixed oral flora of a dental abscess well and is first-line. Antibiotics support — never replace — draining the infection and treating the tooth itself.
questions.q: The first-line antibiotic for a typical odontogenic (tooth) infection in a non-allergic adult is:

questions.explain: Clindamycin is the classic alternative for penicillin-allergic patients because it covers oral anaerobes and streptococci without the penicillin ring.
questions.q: A patient with a true penicillin allergy who needs an antibiotic for a dental infection is typically prescribed:

questions.explain: Per AHA guidance, high-risk cardiac patients take a single 2 g amoxicillin dose shortly before the appointment so blood levels peak during the procedure's brief bacteremia. Clindamycin 600 mg is the classic alternative for penicillin allergy.
options: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for a week
Amoxicillin 2 g by mouth, single dose 30–60 minutes before the procedure
An antibiotic started the day after treatment
questions.q: Standard antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis before invasive dental work (for high-risk patients) is:

questions.explain: Ibuprofen (an NSAID) blocks prostaglandin production, attacking the inflammation causing the pain; acetaminophen relieves pain centrally but has almost no anti-inflammatory effect — the two are often combined for stronger relief.
options: It is anti-inflammatory, and most dental pain is driven by inflammation
questions.q: Why is ibuprofen usually preferred over acetaminophen for post-extraction pain?

questions.explain: NSAIDs reduce the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining and support kidney blood flow, so ulcer history, chronic kidney disease, and anticoagulant use are the classic cautions.
options: A history of stomach ulcers or kidney disease
questions.q: NSAIDs like ibuprofen should be used cautiously or avoided in patients with:

description: Four-handed dentistry, instrument transfer, suctioning, and moisture control.

questions.explain: Four-handed dentistry frees the operator to stay focused: the assistant keeps the field visible and dry with suction and retraction while passing instruments on cue.
options: Keep the field visible and dry, transfer instruments, and retract tissue
Take the final impression without help
Adjust the chair and leave the room
questions.q: In four-handed dentistry, the dental assistant's main role is to do what?

questions.explain: The HVE tip belongs at the operative site with its bevel parallel to the tooth surface, placed before the handpiece starts, to capture spray and debris at the source.
options: Close to the tooth being treated, with the bevel parallel to the tooth surface
Only in the back of the mouth
questions.q: Where should the high-volume evacuator (HVE) tip be positioned?

questions.explain: For a right-handed operator: the operator's zone is 7 to 12 o'clock, the assistant's zone is 2 to 4, the transfer zone is 4 to 7, and the static zone is 12 to 2.
questions.q: For a right-handed dentist, the operator's working zone is which area?

questions.explain: Deliver the instrument handle-first with its working end already oriented for the arch being treated, so the dentist can use it immediately without repositioning.
options: Handle first, with the working end pointing anywhere
With the working end pointing toward the assistant
Only when the dentist looks up from the patient
With the working end positioned for use on the correct arch
questions.q: When transferring an instrument, the assistant should deliver it how?

questions.explain: The saliva ejector is low-volume - fine for saliva control but unable to keep up with handpiece spray. The HVE is the tool for moisture control during active treatment.
options: To remove small amounts of saliva and fluids for patient comfort (low-volume suction)
To replace the HVE during restorative work
To dry a tooth for bonding
questions.q: What is the purpose of the saliva ejector?

questions.explain: Trays are laid out in the sequence the instruments will be needed, so transfer is automatic and the operator never waits.
options: In the order of use, from left to right
Randomly, as long as everything is present
questions.q: Instruments on a preset tray should be arranged in what order?

questions.explain: The dental dam gives the best isolation, retracts the cheeks and tongue, and protects the airway; cotton rolls and dry angles are quicker but less complete alternatives.
questions.q: Which moisture-control method uses a thin sheet to isolate a single tooth or quadrant?

questions.explain: The transfer zone is over the patient's chest in the 4 to 7 o'clock area. Never pass instruments over the patient's face.
options: Over the patient's chest, below the chin area (4 to 7 o'clock)
Above the head of the chair
questions.q: The instrument transfer zone is located where?

questions.explain: Maxillary (upper) work gets the working end pointed up; mandibular (lower) work gets it pointed down - matched to the arch so no adjustment is needed.
options: Down, toward the mandibular arch in use
questions.q: When the dentist is working on a mandibular (lower) tooth, instruments are delivered with the working end pointing which way?

questions.explain: The assistant sits slightly higher (eyes about 4-6 inches above the operator's eye level) to see into the mouth clearly and reach the oral cavity without leaning over the patient.
options: At exactly the same height as the dentist
Slightly higher than the dentist (eyes 4-6 inches above the operator's eye level)
questions.q: For proper four-handed dentistry, the chairside assistant sits how?

description: What endodontists, periodontists, orthodontists, and the other recognized specialists actually do.

questions.explain: Endodontics focuses on the tooth's interior: root canal therapy, retreatments, and apicoectomy surgery on the root tip.
questions.q: Which dental specialist focuses on root canal therapy?

questions.explain: Periodontics covers the gums and supporting bone: treating gum disease, scaling and root planing, bone grafts, and placing implants.
questions.q: A periodontist specializes in what?

questions.explain: Orthodontists diagnose and correct malocclusion - crooked teeth, bite problems, and jaw growth - using braces, aligners, and other appliances.
options: Correcting malocclusion and aligning the teeth and jaws
questions.q: An orthodontist's primary focus is what?

questions.explain: Pediatric dentists (pedodontists) treat infants through adolescents, combining dentistry with behavior guidance and preventive care for young patients.
questions.q: Which specialist would most often treat a 4-year-old with extensive decay?

questions.explain: Prosthodontics is the restoration and replacement of teeth: crowns, bridges, veneers, implants, and full or partial dentures.
options: Replacing missing teeth with crowns, bridges, implants, and dentures
questions.q: A prosthodontist specializes in what?

questions.explain: Oral and maxillofacial surgeons handle extractions (including impacted wisdom teeth), corrective jaw surgery, trauma repair, and implant placement.
options: Surgical removal of impacted third molars (wisdom teeth)
questions.q: An oral and maxillofacial surgeon would perform which procedure?

questions.explain: Oral pathologists are the diagnosticians of dentistry: they examine biopsied tissue under a microscope to identify oral diseases and cancers.
options: Diagnose diseases of the oral cavity by examining biopsy tissue
questions.q: An oral pathologist's primary role is what?

questions.explain: Bone grafting, guided tissue regeneration, and treating advanced bone loss are periodontal surgical procedures.
questions.q: A patient with severe gum recession and bone loss needing a bone graft is referred to which specialist?

questions.explain: Oral and maxillofacial radiology is the specialty devoted to interpreting advanced imaging, from CBCT scans to complex diagnoses of jaw pathology.
questions.q: Which specialty centers on interpreting advanced dental imaging, such as CBCT scans for complex diagnoses?

questions.explain: Dental public health works at the population level: water fluoridation, school sealant and screening programs, access-to-care initiatives, and health education.
options: Community prevention programs like water fluoridation and school sealant programs
questions.q: Dental public health specialists focus on what kind of work?

questions.q: If f(x) = x^2 - 3x + 1, what is f(0)?

questions.explain: If a vertical line crossed twice, one x-value would have two y-values, so the graph would not be a function.
options: every vertical line crosses the graph at most once
every horizontal line crosses the graph at most once
the graph is a straight line
the graph passes through the origin
questions.q: A graph passes the vertical line test if...

questions.explain: Squaring a negative gives a positive: g(-3) = (-3)^2 = 9.

questions.explain: A horizontal line never rises, so rise / run = 0 over any run: the slope is 0.

subject: Algebra 1
title: Functions & Graphs
Systems of Linear Equations
subject: Algebra 1
description: Solve pairs of linear equations by graphing, substitution, and elimination, and tell whether a system has one solution, none, or infinitely many.

questions.q: Solve the system: y = 2x and x + y = 6. The solution is:
questions.explain: Substitute 2x for y: x + 2x = 6, so x = 2 and y = 4. The pair (2, 4) satisfies both equations.

questions.q: Solve the system: x + y = 10 and x - y = 2. The solution is:
questions.explain: Add the equations to eliminate y: 2x = 12, so x = 6. Then 6 + y = 10 gives y = 4.

questions.q: A system of two linear equations whose graphs are distinct parallel lines has:
questions.explain: Parallel lines never meet, so there is no point that satisfies both equations at once.

questions.q: The substitution method is usually the easiest choice when:
options: Both equations are in standard form
One variable is already solved for or has a coefficient of 1
questions.explain: If y is already isolated, you can substitute its expression directly into the other equation in one step.

questions.q: Solve the system: 2x + y = 7 and x = 2. Then y equals:
questions.explain: Substitute x = 2: 4 + y = 7, so y = 3.

questions.q: If two equations in a system describe the exact same line, the system has:
questions.explain: Every point on the line satisfies both equations, so there are infinitely many solutions.

questions.q: Using elimination on x + y = 5 and x - y = 1, adding the equations eliminates which variable?
questions.explain: The +y and -y cancel when the equations are added, leaving 2x = 6.

questions.q: Two numbers add to 12 and differ by 4. The larger number is:
questions.explain: Call the numbers a and b: a + b = 12 and a - b = 4. Adding gives 2a = 16, so a = 8.

questions.q: Solve the system: y = x + 1 and y = -x + 5. The solution is:
questions.explain: Set the expressions equal: x + 1 = -x + 5, so x = 2, and y = 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.q: Graphically, the solution of a system of two linear equations is:
options: The y-intercept of the first line
The point where the two lines intersect
The slope of the steeper line
questions.explain: A solution must satisfy both equations, which is exactly the point the two graphs share.

title: Exponents & Exponential Functions
subject: Algebra 1
description: Exponent rules, negative and zero exponents, scientific notation, and growth and decay models.

questions.q: Simplify: x^3 * x^4
questions.explain: When multiplying powers with the same base, add the exponents: 3 + 4 = 7.

questions.q: Evaluate: (2^3)^2
questions.explain: Raise a power to a power by multiplying exponents: 2^(3*2) = 2^6 = 64.

questions.q: Any nonzero number raised to the power 0 equals:
questions.explain: By the zero exponent rule, a^0 = 1 for any nonzero a, since a^n / a^n = 1.

questions.q: Simplify: 5^-2
questions.explain: A negative exponent means a reciprocal: 5^-2 = 1/5^2 = 1/25.

questions.q: A colony of 100 bacteria doubles every hour. How many bacteria are there after 3 hours?
questions.explain: Start with 100 and double three times: 100, 200, 400, 800.

questions.q: In the decay function y = 100(0.8)^t, the decay factor is:
questions.explain: The base of the exponential, 0.8, is the factor the quantity is multiplied by each time period.

questions.q: Simplify: x^6 / x^2
questions.explain: When dividing powers with the same base, subtract the exponents: 6 - 2 = 4.

questions.q: Write 45,000 in scientific notation:
questions.explain: Move the decimal 4 places left so the first factor is between 1 and 10: 4.5 x 10^4.

questions.q: You deposit 1,000 dollars in an account earning 5 percent per year. Your balance after 1 year is:
questions.explain: Five percent of 1,000 is 50, so the new balance is 1,000 + 50 = 1,050 dollars.

questions.q: Simplify: (3x^2)^2
questions.explain: Square both the coefficient and the power: 3^2 = 9 and (x^2)^2 = x^4.

questions.explain: Distribute 2x to both terms: 2x * 3x = 6x^2 and 2x * -4 = -8x.

Expand: (x + 3)(x + 5)

questions.explain: Find two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7: 3 and 4, so (x + 3)(x + 4).

questions.explain: The degree is the highest exponent of the variable, which is 3 in the term 5x^3.

questions.explain: The greatest common factor is 3x. Dividing each term by 3x gives 3x(x + 2).

subject: Algebra 1
title: Polynomials & Factoring
Quadratic Equations & Functions
subject: Algebra 1
description: Graph parabolas, find vertices and discriminants, and solve quadratics by factoring, completing the square, and the quadratic formula.

questions.q: Solve: x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0
questions.explain: Factor as (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 3.

questions.q: The vertex of the parabola y = x^2 - 4x + 3 is:
questions.explain: The axis is x = 4/2 = 2, and y = 4 - 8 + 3 = -1, so the vertex is (2, -1).

questions.q: The discriminant of x^2 + 2x + 5 = 0 is negative. This means the equation has:
questions.explain: A negative discriminant (here 4 - 20 = -16) means the parabola never crosses the x-axis, so there are no real roots.

questions.q: The graph of y = -x^2 + 4 opens:
questions.explain: A negative leading coefficient flips the parabola so it opens downward and has a maximum point.

questions.q: Solve: x^2 - 9 = 0
questions.explain: This is a difference of squares: (x - 3)(x + 3) = 0, giving x = 3 or x = -3.

questions.q: The axis of symmetry of y = 2x^2 + 8x + 1 is:
Which expression is the quadratic formula for solving ax^2 + bx + c = 0?
options: x = (-b plus or minus sqrt(b^2 + 4ac)) / a
questions.explain: The quadratic formula is x = (-b plus or minus sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a), where the part under the root is the discriminant.

questions.q: What is the y-intercept of y = x^2 - 3x - 4?
questions.explain: Set x = 0: y = -4, which is also the constant term of the equation.

questions.q: To complete the square for x^2 + 6x, you should add:
questions.explain: Take half of 6, which is 3, and square it: 3^2 = 9. Then x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2.

questions.q: A ball's height is h = -16t^2 + 32t feet after t seconds. At what time does it reach its maximum height?
questions.explain: The vertex is at t = -b/(2a) = -32/(2 * -16) = 1 second.

title: Radicals & Rational Expressions
subject: Algebra 1
description: Simplify square roots, solve simple radical equations, and add, multiply, and simplify rational expressions while tracking excluded values.

questions.q: Simplify: sqrt(49)
questions.explain: Since 7 * 7 = 49, the square root of 49 is 7.

questions.q: Simplify: sqrt(50)
questions.explain: Factor out the largest perfect square: sqrt(50) = sqrt(25 * 2) = 5 sqrt(2).

questions.q: Solve: sqrt(x) = 6
questions.explain: Square both sides: x = 6^2 = 36.

questions.q: For x not equal to 2, (x^2 - 4) / (x - 2) simplifies to:
questions.explain: Factor the numerator as (x - 2)(x + 2) and cancel the common factor (x - 2), leaving x + 2.

questions.q: The excluded value of the expression 5 / (x - 3) is:
questions.explain: A denominator cannot be zero, so x - 3 = 0 gives the excluded value x = 3.
With a common denominator, add the numerators: (1 + 2)/4 = 3/4.

questions.q: Simplify: sqrt(12)
questions.explain: Factor out the perfect square 4: sqrt(12) = sqrt(4 * 3) = 2 sqrt(3).

questions.q: Multiply: (3/x) * (x/6), for x not equal to 0
questions.explain: Cancel the common factor x and simplify 3/6 to 1/2.

questions.q: Solve: sqrt(x + 1) = 4
questions.explain: Square both sides: x + 1 = 16, so x = 15. Check: sqrt(16) = 4, so it works.

questions.q: The distance formula between two points is a direct application of:
questions.explain: Distance is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical differences between the points.

title: Statistics & Data Analysis
subject: Algebra 1
description: Mean, median, mode, and range; scatterplots and correlation; probability basics and reading two-way tables and box plots.

questions.q: The mean of 2, 4, 6, and 8 is:
questions.explain: Add the values (20) and divide by how many there are (4): 20 / 4 = 5.

questions.q: The median of 3, 7, 9, 12, 15 is:
questions.explain: The data are already in order, so the median is the middle value, 9.

questions.q: The mode of 4, 4, 5, 7, 7, 7 is:
questions.explain: The value 7 appears three times, more than any other value.

questions.q: The range of the data set 5, 9, 14, 20 is:
questions.explain: Range = maximum - minimum = 20 - 5 = 15.

questions.q: What is the probability of rolling a 4 on one fair six-sided die?
questions.explain: One favorable outcome out of six equally likely outcomes gives a probability of 1/6.

questions.q: A scatterplot whose points generally rise from left to right shows:
questions.explain: When larger x-values tend to go with larger y-values, the association is positive.

questions.q: Which measure of center is changed the most by one extremely large outlier?
options: Range is a measure of center
questions.explain: The mean uses every value in its calculation, so one huge value pulls it upward; the median barely moves.

questions.q: In a box plot, the line drawn inside the box represents the:
questions.explain: The box shows the quartiles, and the line inside it marks the median of the data.

questions.q: In a survey of 100 students, 30 say soccer is their favorite sport. The relative frequency of soccer is:
questions.explain: Relative frequency = count / total = 30/100 = 0.30, or 30 percent.

questions.q: A study finds that towns with more ice cream sales also have more swimming pool visits. The best conclusion is:
options: Ice cream causes people to swim
Correlation does not by itself prove causation
questions.explain: Both variables likely rise because of a lurking variable, hot weather. Association alone never proves cause and effect.
