rounds.desc: The major glands and hormones: pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas, and how negative feedback keeps hormone levels in range.

title: Respiratory System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: Airways, lungs, and the mechanics of breathing and gas exchange.

questions.q: Gas exchange between air and blood takes place in the:
questions.explain: The alveoli are tiny thin-walled air sacs wrapped in capillaries; oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across this single-cell barrier. Their combined surface area is roughly the size of a tennis court.

questions.q: When the diaphragm contracts and flattens, what phase of breathing occurs?
options: Neither — it only contracts at rest
questions.explain: Diaphragm contraction increases chest volume, dropping air pressure inside the lungs so air flows in. Quiet exhalation is mostly passive — the diaphragm relaxes and the lungs recoil.

questions.q: Which flap of tissue keeps food and liquid out of the airway when you swallow?
questions.explain: The epiglottis folds down over the larynx during swallowing. If it mistimes, material 'goes down the wrong pipe' and triggers the cough reflex.

questions.q: The normal respiratory rate for a resting adult is:
questions.explain: 12-20 breaths per minute is the normal adult range. It's the vital sign most sensitive to early deterioration — rising rates often signal trouble before other signs change.

questions.q: Oxygen is transported through the bloodstream primarily by binding to:
questions.explain: Each hemoglobin molecule carries four oxygen molecules, picking them up in the lungs and releasing them in the tissues. Very little oxygen travels dissolved in plasma.

questions.q: The pleura is best described as:
options: A ring of cartilage in the trachea
questions.explain: The double-layered pleura wraps each lung and lines the chest cavity, with fluid between the layers for frictionless movement. Inflammation of it (pleurisy) makes breathing painful.

questions.q: Which lung has three lobes?
questions.explain: The right lung is wider and has upper, middle, and lower lobes. The left lung has only two lobes plus the cardiac notch — space that makes room for the heart.

questions.q: Pulmonary surfactant functions mainly to:
options: Reduce surface tension so alveoli don't collapse
questions.explain: Surfactant coats alveoli and lowers surface tension, keeping them open between breaths. Premature infants who can't yet make it develop respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.q: The muscles primarily responsible for forced exhalation (like coughing or exercise) are:
questions.explain: Forced expiration is active: the abdominals compress the abdomen and internal intercostals pull the ribs down, squeezing air out. The diaphragm relaxes during exhalation.

questions.q: Most carbon dioxide is carried in the blood in the form of:
questions.explain: About 70% of CO2 rides as bicarbonate, formed in red blood cells by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. This doubles as the blood's main pH buffer system.

title: Digestive System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: The GI tract, accessory organs, and how food becomes fuel.

questions.q: Most nutrient absorption takes place in the:
questions.explain: The small intestine's villi and microvilli give it an enormous absorptive surface. The stomach mostly churns and begins protein digestion; the large intestine mainly reclaims water.

questions.q: Bile is produced by which organ?
questions.explain: The liver makes bile continuously; the gallbladder merely stores and concentrates it. People who lose their gallbladder still digest fat — bile just drips into the intestine steadily.

questions.q: Chemical digestion of carbohydrates begins in the mouth through the action of:
questions.explain: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) starts breaking starches into sugars right in the mouth — that's why starchy food tastes sweeter the longer you chew it.

questions.q: The highly acidic environment of the stomach has a pH of roughly:
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid drops gastric pH to about 1.5-2, which kills most ingested microbes and activates pepsin. A mucus barrier keeps the stomach from digesting itself.

questions.q: Peristalsis refers to:
options: Wave-like muscular contractions that move food through the GI tract
Absorption of water in the colon
questions.explain: Peristalsis is the rhythmic squeezing of smooth muscle behind a food bolus, propelling it from esophagus to rectum regardless of gravity — that's why you can swallow while upside down.

questions.q: Which structures most increase the surface area of the small intestine?
questions.explain: Circular folds, villi, and microvilli multiply the inner surface roughly 600-fold. Rugae are the stomach's folds, and haustra are pouches of the colon.

questions.q: Insulin is secreted by which cells?
questions.explain: Pancreatic beta cells in the islets of Langerhans release insulin when blood glucose rises; alpha cells release its opposite number, glucagon. In type 1 diabetes, the beta cells are destroyed.

questions.q: The first segment of the small intestine, where most digestion occurs, is the:
questions.explain: The duodenum receives chyme plus bile and pancreatic juices, making it the main site of chemical digestion. The jejunum and ileum follow, doing most of the absorption.

questions.q: Most water absorption from digested material takes place in the:
questions.explain: The large intestine reclaims about a liter of water per day. When it fails — as in severe diarrhea — dehydration can become dangerous quickly.

questions.q: The gastric enzyme pepsin primarily digests:
questions.explain: Pepsin begins protein digestion in the stomach; it's secreted as inactive pepsinogen and activated by hydrochloric acid so it doesn't attack the cells that made it.

title: Lymphatic & Immune System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: Lymph vessels and nodes, the spleen and thymus, innate versus adaptive defenses, antibodies, and how vaccines create memory.

questions.q: Lymph nodes are important because they:
options: Store most of the body's fat
Filter lymph and house white blood cells that attack trapped pathogens
questions.explain: As lymph passes through nodes, macrophages and lymphocytes inspect it and respond to bacteria and other invaders.

questions.q: The largest lymphatic organ in the body, which filters blood and removes old red blood cells, is the:
questions.explain: The spleen filters blood (not lymph), recycles iron from worn-out red cells, and stores platelets and white blood cells.

questions.q: Antibodies are produced and released by:
options: Plasma cells, which develop from activated B cells
questions.explain: When a B cell meets its matching antigen, it multiplies and its plasma cell offspring pour out antibodies against that antigen.

questions.q: The body's first line of defense against pathogens is:
options: Physical and chemical barriers such as skin and mucous membranes
questions.explain: Intact skin, mucus, stomach acid, and tears keep most microbes out before the immune system is ever activated.

questions.q: Cytotoxic T cells protect the body mainly by:
options: Directly killing virus-infected and cancerous body cells
questions.explain: Cytotoxic T cells recognize abnormal antigens on a cell's surface and destroy that cell before a virus can finish copying itself.

questions.q: The primary job of the lymphatic vessels is to:
options: Collect excess fluid from tissues and return it to the bloodstream
questions.explain: Lymphatic capillaries pick up fluid that leaks from blood capillaries and return it to veins near the heart, preventing swelling.

questions.q: A vaccine protects against future infection because it produces:
options: Active immunity, with memory cells ready to respond faster next time
A weakened live infection every time
questions.explain: Vaccines present a harmless antigen so the body builds memory B and T cells; a later real exposure triggers a fast, strong response.

questions.q: During inflammation, the chemical histamine is released mainly by:
options: Mast cells in the injured tissue
questions.explain: Histamine from mast cells dilates nearby blood vessels and makes them leaky, producing the redness, heat, and swelling of inflammation.

questions.q: T lymphocytes mature and are 'educated' to distinguish self from non-self in the:
questions.explain: T cells are born in bone marrow but mature in the thymus, which gives them their name.

questions.q: A newborn receiving antibodies through a mother's breast milk is an example of:
questions.explain: The antibodies are borrowed, not made by the baby, so passive protection fades within months.

rounds.title: Lymphatic & Immune System
rounds.desc: Lymph vessels and nodes, the spleen and thymus, innate versus adaptive defenses, antibodies, and how vaccines create memory.

title: Urinary System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: Kidneys and nephrons, filtration and reabsorption, the ureters, bladder, and urethra, and how the kidneys help regulate blood pressure and pH.

questions.q: The functional filtering unit of the kidney is the:
questions.explain: Each kidney holds about a million nephrons, and each nephron filters blood and adjusts the filtrate to form urine.

questions.q: Urine leaves each kidney and travels to the bladder through the:
questions.explain: Peristaltic waves in the ureters move urine to the bladder; the urethra later carries it out of the body.

questions.q: Blood filtration in the kidney begins in the:
options: Glomerulus, a ball of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule
questions.explain: High pressure in the glomerulus forces water and small solutes out of the blood while cells and most proteins stay behind.

questions.q: Erythropoietin, a hormone released by the kidneys when oxygen is low, stimulates:
options: Red blood cell production in bone marrow
questions.explain: Erythropoietin raises the red blood cell count, increasing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, for example at high altitude.

questions.q: Nearly all glucose and amino acids are reclaimed from the filtrate in the:
questions.explain: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about 65 percent of the filtrate, including virtually all of its glucose and amino acids.

questions.q: In a healthy person, urine normally contains little or no:
questions.explain: Glucose in the urine usually signals that blood glucose is too high for the tubules to reclaim, as in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.

questions.q: Urine exits the body through the:
questions.explain: The urethra drains the bladder to the outside; in males it also carries semen.

questions.q: When blood pressure falls, the kidneys release renin, which ultimately helps raise blood pressure by triggering production of:
questions.explain: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system constricts blood vessels and increases salt and water reabsorption, restoring pressure and volume.

questions.q: The main role of the loop of Henle is to:
options: Create a salt concentration gradient in the medulla so water can be reabsorbed
questions.explain: The loop builds the medullary gradient that lets ADH concentrate urine and conserve water.

questions.q: A patient on dialysis is using a machine to do which kidney job that their own kidneys can no longer do?
options: Filter wastes and excess fluid from the blood
questions.explain: Dialysis passes blood across a semipermeable membrane that removes urea, excess salts, and fluid the failed kidneys cannot clear.

rounds.title: Urinary System
rounds.desc: Kidneys and nephrons, filtration and reabsorption, the ureters, bladder, and urethra, and how the kidneys help regulate blood pressure and pH.

description: Convert between binary and decimal, understand bits and bytes, and evaluate AND, OR, and NOT logic.

questions.explain: Binary is base 2, so every digit (bit) is either 0 or 1.
questions.q: The binary number system uses which digits?

questions.explain: 5 = 4 + 1, so the 4s and 1s places are on: 101.
questions.q: What is the decimal number 5 written in binary?

questions.explain: Add the place values that are on: 8 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 10.
questions.q: What is the binary number 1010 in decimal?

questions.explain: A byte is made of 8 bits and can store values from 0 to 255.
questions.q: How many bits are in one byte?

questions.explain: AND requires both inputs to be true; if either one is false, the result is false.
options: at least one of them is true
both A and B are true
questions.q: In logic, A AND B is true when...

questions.explain: OR needs just one true input. It is false only when both inputs are false.
options: at least one input is true
questions.q: In logic, A OR B is true when...

questions.explain: NOT flips the value: NOT True = False and NOT False = True.
questions.q: If A is True, what is NOT A?

questions.explain: Add the place values: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.
questions.q: What is the binary number 111 in decimal?

questions.explain: 1111 has all four places on: 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15, the most a 4-bit number can hold.
questions.q: Which of these is the largest 4-bit binary number?

questions.explain: A kilobyte is about 1000 bytes (the older binary definition is exactly 1024). A megabyte is about a million bytes.
questions.q: Roughly how many bytes are in 1 kilobyte?

subject: Computer Science Basics
title: Binary & Logic

description: Python basics: print and input, comments, indentation, variables, and simple expressions.

questions.explain: print() outputs whatever is inside the parentheses to the screen.
options: It saves Hello to a file
It displays Hello on the screen
It creates a variable named Hello
questions.q: What does print("Hello") do in Python?

questions.explain: Everything after a # on a line is a comment and is ignored when the program runs.
questions.q: Which symbol starts a comment in Python?

questions.explain: input() pauses and waits for the user to type something, and gives back what they typed as a string.
options: It reads text the user types, returned as a string
It prints text to the screen
questions.q: What does the input() function do?

questions.explain: Python uses indentation (usually 4 spaces) to group lines into blocks, such as the body of an if statement or a loop.
options: It defines which lines belong to a block of code
It is only used inside comments
It makes the program run slower
questions.q: Why does indentation matter in Python?

questions.explain: Multiplication happens before addition: 3 * 2 = 6, then 2 + 6 = 8.
questions.q: What does this code print? print(2 + 3 * 2)

questions.explain: len() counts the characters in the string: c, a, t — that is 3 characters.
questions.q: What does len("cat") return?

questions.explain: Python does not need int, var, or declare keywords — you just write the name, an equals sign, and the value.
questions.q: Which line correctly creates a variable in Python?

questions.explain: x holds 5, so x + 1 is 6, and print shows 6.
questions.q: What does this code print? x = 5; print(x + 1)

questions.explain: Python source files end in .py, such as game.py.
questions.q: What is the file extension for a Python file?

questions.explain: import is a Python keyword used to load modules. function and var belong to JavaScript, and echo is a shell command.
questions.q: Which of these is a Python keyword?

subject: Computer Science Basics
title: Intro to Python

description: Learn the basic data types (int, float, string, bool), variables, constants, and type conversion.

questions.explain: Text inside quotes is a string. 42 is an integer, 3.14 is a float, and True is a boolean.
questions.q: Which of these is a string?

questions.explain: Numbers with a decimal point are floats (floating-point numbers).
questions.q: What data type is the value 3.14?

questions.explain: A single = is the assignment operator: it stores the value 5 in the variable x.
options: It assigns the value 5 to the variable x
questions.q: In most programming languages, what does the statement x = 5 do?

questions.explain: Names cannot start with a number or contain spaces or dashes. Underscores are allowed, so my_score works.
questions.q: Which is a valid variable name in Python?

questions.explain: A boolean (bool) has exactly two possible values: True or False.
questions.q: Boolean values can only be...

questions.explain: Both values are strings, so + joins (concatenates) them into the string "53" instead of adding.
questions.q: In Python, what is the result of "5" + "3"?

questions.explain: Whole numbers without a decimal point are integers, type int.
questions.q: A variable storing the whole number 7 has which type?

questions.explain: Square brackets make a list. Parentheses make a tuple, and braces with colons make a dictionary.
questions.q: Which literal creates a list in Python?

questions.explain: int() converts the string "42" into the integer 42 so it can be used in math.
questions.q: What does int("42") return in Python?

questions.explain: Constants hold fixed values (like PI = 3.14159) that the program should not change.
options: a value that does not change while the program runs
questions.q: In programming, a constant is...

subject: Computer Science Basics
title: Data Types & Variables

description: Control program flow with if/elif/else statements, while loops, for loops, break, and continue.

questions.explain: An if statement checks a condition and runs its block only when the condition is true.
options: It runs code only when a condition is true
It stores data in a variable
questions.q: What does an if statement do?

questions.explain: 7 > 5 is true, so the if branch runs and prints "big".
questions.q: What does this code print? x = 7; if x > 5: print("big") else: print("small")

questions.explain: Before each pass, a while loop checks its condition; it keeps looping while the condition is true.
options: as long as its condition stays true
until the user closes the program
questions.q: A while loop repeats...

questions.explain: range(3) produces 0, 1, 2 — three values, so the loop body runs 3 times.
questions.q: How many times does this loop run? for i in range(3): print(i)

questions.explain: range starts at the first number and stops before the second, so 1, 2, 3, 4.
questions.q: Which values does range(1, 5) produce?

questions.explain: elif (short for 'else if') adds another condition that is only checked if the earlier ones were false.
options: test another condition when the previous one is false
questions.q: In an if/elif/else chain, elif is used to...

questions.explain: If the condition stays true forever (often because a variable never changes), the loop never stops.
options: A loop that runs exactly once
A loop whose condition never becomes false, so it never ends
A loop with no code inside it
questions.q: What is an infinite loop?

questions.explain: count goes 0 to 1 to 2 to 3. When count reaches 3, the condition count < 3 is false and the loop stops.
questions.q: What is the value of count after this code? count = 0; while count < 3: count = count + 1

questions.explain: break jumps out of the loop entirely, and the program continues with the code after the loop.
options: It skips to the next iteration
It restarts the loop from the top
questions.q: What does the break statement do inside a loop?

questions.explain: continue skips whatever is left in the current pass and starts the next iteration. (pass, by contrast, does nothing at all.)
questions.q: Which keyword skips the rest of the current loop iteration and moves to the next one?

subject: Computer Science Basics
title: Conditionals & Loops

description: Define and call functions, use parameters and return values, and understand variable scope.

questions.explain: Functions package code under a name so you can run it again whenever you need it.
options: A reusable block of code that performs a specific task
questions.q: What is a function in programming?

questions.explain: def starts a function definition: def name(): followed by the function's code block.
questions.q: In Python, what does the keyword def do?

questions.explain: Variables listed in the definition are parameters — placeholders for the values the function will receive. The values passed in when calling are the arguments.
questions.q: In the definition def greet(name):, what is 'name'?

questions.explain: return hands a result back to the caller, which can store or use it. Displaying a value is done by print().
options: It prints a value to the screen
It sends a value back to whoever called the function
questions.q: What does the return statement do?

questions.explain: double(6) returns 6 * 2 = 12, which is stored in result.
questions.q: What is the result of this code? def double(n): return n * 2; result = double(6)

questions.explain: Python automatically returns the special value None when a function ends without a return statement.
questions.q: In Python, a function that has no return statement returns...

questions.explain: Write the code once and call it many times — this makes programs shorter and easier to fix.
options: To reuse code instead of copying it everywhere
questions.q: What is the main reason programmers use functions?

questions.explain: Calling (or invoking) a function runs its code, the way double(6) does.
options: To execute it so its code runs
To save it to a file
questions.q: What does it mean to 'call' a function?

questions.explain: Variables defined in a function have local scope — they exist only while that function runs.
options: local: it can only be used inside that function
global: it can be used everywhere
a constant: it can never change
questions.q: A variable created inside a function is usually...

questions.explain: add(3, 4) returns 3 + 4 = 7. (34 would be string joining, but these are numbers.)
questions.q: What does this return? def add(a, b): return a + b; add(3, 4)

subject: Computer Science Basics
title: Functions
Strings in Depth
subject: Computer Science Basics
description: Indexing, slicing, and everyday text methods for working with strings in Python.

questions.q: In Python, what is the index of the first character of a string?
options: It depends on the string length
questions.explain: Python indexing starts at 0, so the first character is always at index 0.

questions.q: What does the expression 'hello'[1] give you?
options: An error, strings have no indexes
questions.explain: Index 1 is the second character, and the second character of 'hello' is e.

questions.q: What does 'python'[0:3] return?
questions.explain: A slice takes characters from the start index up to, but not including, the end index, so [0:3] gives the first three letters.

questions.q: In Python, what does the index -1 refer to in a string?
options: An invalid position that always errors
The character before the string starts
questions.explain: Negative indexes count from the end, so -1 is the last character and -2 is the one before it.

questions.q: What does 'cat'.upper() return?
questions.explain: The upper method returns a new string with every letter converted to uppercase; the original string is unchanged.

questions.q: What is the result of 'ab' * 3 in Python?
options: An error, strings cannot be multiplied
questions.explain: Multiplying a string by a number repeats it that many times, so 'ab' repeated 3 times is 'ababab'.

questions.q: Strings in Python are immutable. This means:
options: You cannot change a character in place; you must build a new string
Strings can never be stored in variables
Strings only hold letters, never digits
A string can only be used once
questions.explain: Immutability means methods like upper return new strings instead of editing the original one.

questions.q: What does the strip method do to the string '  hi  '?
options: Deletes the letters h and i
Removes the spaces from both ends, giving 'hi'
Splits it into a list of words
questions.explain: strip removes leading and trailing whitespace, which is handy for cleaning up user input.

questions.q: An f-string in Python is used to:
options: Find a character in a string
Freeze a string so it cannot be printed
Convert a string to a float
Put variable values directly inside a string of text
questions.explain: An f-string starts with the letter f before the quote, and anything in curly braces is replaced by its value.

questions.q: What does 'banana'.count('a') return?
questions.explain: count tallies how many times the given piece appears; the letter a appears three times in banana.

rounds.title: Strings in Depth
rounds.desc: Indexing, slicing, and everyday text methods for working with strings in Python.

title: Lists & Dictionaries
subject: Computer Science Basics
description: Ordered lists you can change, key-value dictionaries, tuples, and simple list comprehensions.

questions.q: What does the append method do to a list?
options: Adds one item to the end of the list
Counts the items in the list
questions.explain: append grows a list by one item at the end, which is how you build up results inside a loop.

questions.q: A Python dictionary stores data as:
options: Key-value pairs, where each key maps to one value
questions.explain: Dictionaries look values up by name-like keys instead of by position, like looking up a word in a real dictionary.

questions.q: Given person = {'name': 'Ana', 'age': 9}, what does person['age'] return?
options: An error, dictionaries use numbers only
questions.explain: You read a dictionary value by giving its key in square brackets, and the key 'age' maps to 9.

questions.q: How is a tuple different from a list in Python?
options: A tuple can only hold strings
A tuple cannot be changed after it is created
questions.explain: Tuples are written with parentheses and are immutable, so they suit data that should stay fixed, like coordinates.

questions.q: What does the expression 4 in [1, 2, 3, 4] evaluate to?
questions.explain: The in operator tests membership and returns a Boolean: True when the value is in the list, False when it is not.

questions.q: After nums = [3, 1, 2] and then nums.sort(), what is nums?
options: An error, lists cannot be sorted
questions.explain: sort rearranges the list itself into ascending order.

questions.q: What does the pop method do when called with no argument?
options: Removes and returns the last item of the list
questions.explain: pop removes an item and hands it back to you; with no index it takes the last one, like taking the top card off a stack.

questions.q: Given grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], what does grid[1][0] return?
questions.explain: The first index picks the inner list [3, 4], and the second index picks its first item, which is 3.

questions.q: What does this list comprehension produce: [x * 2 for x in [1, 2, 3]]?
questions.explain: A comprehension builds a new list by applying an expression to every item of the original list.

questions.q: Why would a programmer choose a dictionary over a list for storing a student's grades by subject?
options: Each grade can be looked up directly by subject name instead of by position
questions.explain: Named keys make lookups clear and direct: grades['math'] says exactly what it means.

rounds.title: Lists & Dictionaries
rounds.desc: Ordered lists you can change, key-value dictionaries, tuples, and simple list comprehensions.

title: Files & Error Handling
subject: Computer Science Basics
description: Reading and writing files safely, the with statement, and using try and except so programs do not crash.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of opening a file with the with statement?
options: The file loads twice as fast
The file is closed automatically, even if an error happens
The file can never be deleted
questions.explain: with guarantees the file is closed when the block ends, so you do not leak open files or lose saved data.

questions.q: Opening a file in mode 'w' does what if the file already exists?
options: Adds new text to the very end
Erases its contents and starts fresh
questions.explain: Mode 'w' means write and truncate; use mode 'a' when you want to append to what is already there.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a try and except block?
options: To run code twice for safety
To hide code from other programmers
To catch errors and handle them gracefully instead of crashing
questions.explain: Code that might fail goes in try, and the except block decides what to do when that specific failure occurs.

questions.q: What happens by default if a program opens a file that does not exist, with no error handling?
options: It silently skips the whole program
It prints an empty line and continues forever
questions.explain: Python raises an exception; without a try block the program halts and shows the error and traceback.

questions.q: After opening a text file as f, what does f.read() return?
options: The whole contents of the file as one string
questions.explain: read pulls the entire file into a single string; readlines instead gives a list with one string per line.

questions.q: Code inside a finally block runs:
options: Only when there is an error
Only when there is no error
Always, whether the try block succeeded or raised an error
Never, it is just a comment
questions.explain: finally is for cleanup that must happen either way, such as closing a connection or a file.

questions.q: Which line writes the text 'hello' into an open file object named f?
questions.explain: Writing uses the file object's write method with the string you want stored.

questions.q: Why is closing a written file important even if you forget the with statement?
options: Unsaved data sitting in a buffer may never reach the disk
Python deletes open files at midnight
It is not important at all
questions.explain: Data can sit in a memory buffer; closing flushes it to disk and releases the file for other programs.

questions.q: Running int('abc') raises which kind of error?
options: A syntax error in your source code file
ValueError, because the text cannot become an integer
questions.explain: The code is valid Python, but the value is wrong for the operation, which is exactly what ValueError reports.

questions.q: A program asks users for their age and sometimes crashes on typed words. The best fix is to:
options: Only let the program run once a day
Wrap the conversion in try and except, and ask again when it fails
Store every answer as a picture
questions.explain: Expecting bad input and handling it is the core of error handling: validate, catch, and recover instead of crashing.

rounds.title: Files & Error Handling
rounds.desc: Reading and writing files safely, the with statement, and using try and except so programs do not crash.

title: Object-Oriented Programming
subject: Computer Science Basics
description: Classes as blueprints, objects, attributes, methods, inheritance, and encapsulation at a beginner level.

questions.q: In object-oriented programming, a class is best described as:
options: A single number stored in memory
A blueprint that defines the data and behavior its objects will have
A file on the hard drive
questions.explain: The class describes the pattern; each object created from it is a separate thing built from that pattern.

questions.q: An object created from a class is also called:
questions.explain: Instance and object mean the same thing here: one concrete example made from the class blueprint.

questions.q: In Python, the special method __init__ runs in order to:
options: Set up a new object's starting attributes when it is created
questions.explain: __init__ is the constructor: it runs automatically at creation and usually stores the values passed in as attributes.

questions.q: Inside a class, the name self refers to:
options: The specific object the method is being called on
questions.explain: self lets each object work with its own data, so two dogs can each have their own name attribute.

questions.q: What is the difference between an attribute and a method?
options: Attributes run code; methods store numbers
An attribute is data stored on the object; a method is a function that belongs to the object
questions.explain: Think of a dog object: name is an attribute (data), and bark is a method (behavior).

questions.q: Inheritance lets a new class:
options: Copy a file to another folder
Reuse and extend the attributes and methods of an existing class
questions.explain: A Puppy class can inherit from Dog and gain barking for free, then add its own twists.

questions.q: Given a class Dog, which line creates an object from it?
questions.explain: Calling the class name with parentheses builds a new instance and runs its __init__ method.

questions.q: Encapsulation in OOP mainly means:
options: Writing all code on one line
Keeping an object's internal details bundled and protected, exposing a clear way to use it
questions.explain: Encapsulation hides the messy internals so other code interacts through well-defined methods instead.

questions.q: A Car class and a Boat class both have a move method that works differently in each. This idea is called:
questions.explain: Polymorphism means the same method name can behave appropriately for different kinds of objects.

questions.q: Inside a child class, what does super() let you do?
options: Call methods from the parent class, such as its __init__
questions.explain: super gives the child class a way to reuse parent behavior, for example running the parent's setup before adding its own.

rounds.title: Object-Oriented Programming
rounds.desc: Classes as blueprints, objects, attributes, methods, inheritance, and encapsulation at a beginner level.

title: Algorithms & Big O
subject: Computer Science Basics
description: Searching and sorting step by step, recursion, and reading Big O notation to compare how algorithms scale.

questions.q: An algorithm is best defined as:
options: A random guess at an answer
A clear step-by-step procedure for solving a problem
questions.explain: Algorithms are recipes for computation: finite, ordered steps that turn input into a correct result.

questions.q: Linear search finds a target in a list by:
options: Checking each item in order until it finds the target or runs out
Jumping straight to the middle every time
questions.explain: Linear search is simple and works on any list, but it may have to look at every single item.

questions.q: Binary search only works correctly when the list is:
questions.explain: Binary search discards half the remaining items each step based on comparisons, which only makes sense in sorted order.

questions.q: Big O notation describes:
options: The exact number of seconds a program takes on your laptop
How much the program cost to write
How an algorithm's running time grows as the input gets bigger
The size of the source code file
questions.explain: Big O ignores constant details and focuses on growth, so you can compare algorithms for large inputs.

questions.q: Accessing a list item by its index, like names[5], is an example of:
options: O(n), because the list has n items
O(n squared), because indexes come in pairs
O(1), constant time, because it takes one direct step no matter the list size
questions.explain: Direct index access does not scan the list, so its cost does not grow with the list size.

questions.q: Scanning every item in a list once to find the largest value is:
options: O(n), because the work grows in step with the number of items
O(1), because there is only one largest value
O(log n), because values shrink quickly
questions.explain: One pass over n items means the work is proportional to n, which is linear time.

questions.q: In bubble sort, the basic move is to:
options: Split the list in half forever
Compare neighboring items and swap them if they are in the wrong order, repeating until sorted
Delete the smallest item each round
questions.explain: Repeated neighbor swaps let larger values bubble to the end, pass after pass.

questions.q: A recursive function must have a base case in order to:
options: Stop calling itself and return a result
questions.explain: Without a base case, the function calls itself forever and Python eventually stops it with a recursion error.

questions.q: For a very large sorted list, which search finishes in fewer steps?
options: Reading the list backwards one by one
questions.explain: Halving the search space each step grows incredibly slowly, so binary search wins big on large sorted data.

questions.q: A phone book app checks one name by starting in the middle, then searching only the half that could contain the name, again and again. This is an application of:
questions.explain: The scenario matches binary search exactly: sorted data, compare with the middle, discard the impossible half.

rounds.title: Algorithms & Big O
rounds.desc: Searching and sorting step by step, recursion, and reading Big O notation to compare how algorithms scale.

description: Identify nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, and interjections in context.

questions.explain: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs, and often (but not always) end in -ly. "Swiftly" describes how the dog ran, so it modifies the verb "ran."
questions.q: In the sentence "The quick dog ran swiftly," which word is the adverb?

questions.explain: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. "Happiness" is an abstract idea functioning as the sentence's subject, so it is a noun.
questions.q: In "Happiness filled the room," what part of speech is "happiness"?

questions.explain: Adverbs can modify adjectives, not just verbs. "Extremely" describes the degree of tiredness, so it modifies the adjective "tired."
questions.q: In "She is extremely tired," what part of speech is "extremely"?

questions.explain: A preposition shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and other words in the sentence. "To" links "store" to the verb phrase, showing direction.
questions.q: In "They walked to the store," what part of speech is "to"?

questions.explain: Interjections are exclamations that express strong emotion and stand apart from the sentence's grammar. "Wow!" shows sudden feeling, while the others are a verb, an adjective, and a preposition.
questions.q: Which of these words is an interjection?

questions.explain: Both "quickly" and "unanimously" describe how the members voted, so both modify the verb "voted" — making both adverbs.
questions.q: In "The committee members voted quickly and unanimously," which words are the adverbs?

questions.explain: Conjunctions join words, phrases, or clauses. Coordinating conjunctions — and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet (FANBOYS) — join grammatically equal elements.
questions.q: What part of speech connects two clauses, as "and" does in "I like tea, and she likes coffee"?

questions.explain: "Dramatically" describes the manner of the improvement — how the writing improved — so it modifies the verb "improved."
questions.q: In "Her writing improved dramatically," what does "dramatically" modify?

questions.explain: When "well" follows a linking verb and describes the subject's state (health or condition), it acts as a predicate adjective. In the other sentences it modifies verbs, making it an adverb.
options: She did well on the exam.
questions.q: Which sentence uses "well" as an adjective rather than an adverb?

questions.explain: Correlative conjunctions are pairs that work together — either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also — and must be followed by parallel grammatical structures.
questions.q: In "Either you come with us, or you stay here," what part of speech are "either" and "or"?

subject: English & Grammar
title: Parts of Speech
Capitalization Rules
subject: English & Grammar
description: When to capitalize people, places, days, months, holidays, titles, and the pronoun I.

questions.q: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: We visited the zoo on Saturday.
we visited the zoo on Saturday.
We visited The Zoo on saturday.
We visited the zoo on saturday.
questions.explain: The first word of a sentence and the name of a day both take capital letters.

questions.q: Which word in this list should always be capitalized?
questions.explain: Names of months are proper nouns, so July is capitalized; summer is a common noun and stays lowercase.

questions.q: How should the day be written in a sentence?
options: MONDAY in the middle of a normal sentence
questions.explain: Days of the week are proper nouns and are always capitalized.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the pronoun I correctly?
options: Me and my friend went home early I think.
i went home with my friend.
My friend and me and I went home.
My friend and I went home.
questions.explain: The pronoun I is always written with a capital letter, wherever it appears in the sentence.

questions.q: How should the city name be written?
questions.explain: Both words of the proper name New York are capitalized because it names a specific place.

questions.q: Which book title is capitalized correctly?
options: the lion, the witch and the wardrobe
The lion, The witch And The wardrobe
The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe
THE LION, THE WITCH AND THE WARDROBE
questions.explain: In a title, capitalize the first word and the important words; small words like the and and stay lowercase in the middle.

questions.q: Which name needs capital letters added?
options: the tall woman by the door
questions.explain: A person's name and title are proper nouns, so Mrs. Lee must be capitalized.

questions.q: Which word should be capitalized in a sentence?
questions.explain: Names of holidays are proper nouns; the other words here are common nouns.

questions.q: Which sentence capitalizes the name of a language correctly?
options: She is learning English this year.
She is learning english this year.
she Is learning English this year.
She is learning ENGLISH this year.
questions.explain: Names of languages are proper nouns and are capitalized, just like names of people and places.

questions.q: Which sentence has NO capitalization mistakes?
options: my cousin Ana lives in Texas.
My cousin ana lives in texas.
My cousin Ana lives in Texas.
My Cousin Ana Lives In Texas.
questions.explain: Capitalize the first word, personal names, and place names, but not ordinary words like cousin or lives.

rounds.title: Capitalization Rules
rounds.desc: When to capitalize people, places, days, months, holidays, titles, and the pronoun I.

description: Subjects, predicates, objects, clauses, and the four sentence types.

questions.explain: A complete sentence needs a subject, a predicate (verb), and a complete thought. Only "The dog barked loudly" has all three; the others are fragments.
questions.q: Which is a complete sentence?

questions.explain: The predicate is everything the subject DOES — the verb plus its objects and modifiers. "Answered the question" is the complete predicate; "answered" alone is the simple predicate.
questions.q: What is the predicate in "The tall student answered the question"?

questions.explain: A compound sentence joins TWO or more independent clauses, usually with a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS). "The movie was long" and "the ending was great" could each stand alone.
options: I went home after the game ended.
The movie was long, but the ending was great.
Running every morning, she stayed fit.
The cat that I adopted sleeps all day.
questions.q: Which sentence is a compound sentence?

questions.explain: A complex sentence has one independent clause ("we played anyway") plus at least one dependent clause ("Although it rained," which cannot stand alone).
questions.q: Identify the sentence type: "Although it rained, we played anyway."

questions.explain: "Walking to the store yesterday" is a participial phrase with no subject or finite verb — it cannot stand alone. Add both: "She was walking to the store yesterday."
questions.q: Which is a sentence fragment?

questions.explain: The direct object receives the action of the verb and answers "what?" — She threw WHAT? "The ball." It follows an action verb.
questions.q: What is the direct object in "She threw the ball"?

questions.explain: "When the bell rang" has a subject and verb, but the subordinating conjunction "when" makes it unable to stand alone — that is what makes it a dependent (subordinate) clause.
options: When the bell rang, the students left.
questions.q: Which sentence contains a dependent clause?

questions.explain: The indirect object answers "to whom" or "for whom" — the teacher gave homework TO the students. The direct object (homework) receives the action; the indirect object receives the direct object.
questions.q: "The teacher gave the students homework." What is "the students"?

questions.explain: The first is a comma splice, the fourth is a run-on, and a semicolon cannot precede a conjunction. The subordinating conjunction "because" correctly shows the cause-and-effect relationship in one complex sentence.
options: It was raining, we stayed inside.
It was raining; and we stayed inside.
Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
It was raining we stayed inside.
questions.q: Which correctly combines these sentences: "It was raining. We stayed inside."?

questions.explain: A simple sentence has exactly one independent clause — one subject-predicate pair expressing a complete thought. "Simple" refers to structure, not length; a simple sentence can still be long.
options: One independent and one dependent clause
questions.q: A simple sentence contains:

subject: English & Grammar
title: Sentence Structure

description: Master commas, semicolons, colons, apostrophes, hyphens, and quotation marks.

questions.explain: A semicolon joins two closely related INDEPENDENT clauses. "I studied for weeks" could stand alone as a sentence. Never put a semicolon before a conjunction like "and," and never use one to separate a fragment.
options: The test was hard; I studied for weeks.
My favorite colors; are blue and green.
She ran fast; and won the race.
questions.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?

questions.explain: For irregular plural nouns that do not end in s — children, men, women — form the possessive by adding 's: "the children's toys."
questions.q: Where does the apostrophe go in the possessive of "children"?

questions.explain: In a series of three or more items, place a comma between each item. The Oxford (serial) comma before "and" is standard in formal American writing and prevents ambiguity.
options: Bring a pencil, eraser, and notebook.
Bring a pencil, eraser and, notebook.
Bring, a pencil, eraser, and notebook.
Bring a pencil eraser, and notebook.
questions.q: Which sentence punctuates a list correctly?

questions.explain: A colon must follow a COMPLETE independent clause, and it introduces something that explains or expands on it — a list, a quote, or a clarification.
options: Before any list, even a fragment
To introduce a list, explanation, or quote after a complete clause
Anywhere you would use a period
questions.q: When should you use a colon?

questions.explain: In American English, periods and commas always go INSIDE the closing quotation mark. "She said 'Hello.'" is correct; the period must not sit outside the quotes.
questions.q: Which quotation is punctuated correctly in American English?

questions.explain: Nonrestrictive (nonessential) clauses add extra information and are set off by commas. "Who lives in Denver" can be removed without changing the core meaning, so it takes commas.
options: My brother, who lives in Denver, is visiting.
My brother who lives in Denver is visiting.
The car which is red, is very fast.
questions.q: Which sentence uses commas around a nonrestrictive clause correctly?

questions.explain: A run-on fuses two independent clauses with no punctuation, or with only a comma (a comma splice). Fix it by splitting with a period or semicolon, or by joining with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS).
options: Adding more commas wherever it feels long
Using a semicolon or period to split the clauses, or adding a coordinating conjunction
questions.q: A run-on sentence is best fixed by which method?

questions.explain: For plural nouns ending in s, add only an apostrophe: "the companies' profits." The singular possessive is "the company's profits."
questions.q: Which is the correct plural possessive of "companies"?

questions.explain: Compound adjectives BEFORE a noun are hyphenated: "a well-known author." After the noun, no hyphen is needed: "The author is well known."
options: The author is well - known for her books.
questions.q: Which sentence uses a hyphen correctly?

questions.explain: Use a comma after an introductory phrase or clause. "After the storm" sets up the sentence but is not the main clause, so the comma separates it from "we cleaned the yard."
options: It separates the subject from the verb
questions.q: In "After the storm, we cleaned the yard," why is the comma after "storm" correct?

subject: English & Grammar
title: Punctuation Rules
Verb Tenses
subject: English & Grammar
description: Past, present, and future forms, irregular verbs, and keeping the tense steady inside a sentence.

questions.q: What is the past tense of the verb run?
questions.explain: Run is an irregular verb: its past form is ran, not runned.

questions.q: In the sentence 'She will travel tomorrow,' the verb shows which tense?
questions.explain: The helper will plus a time word like tomorrow points to an action that has not happened yet.

questions.q: In 'He is reading a book right now,' the action is:
options: Happening now and still going on
questions.explain: Is reading is the present progressive form, used for actions in progress at the moment of speaking.

questions.q: What is the past tense of the verb go?
options: Gone yesterday as a plain past form with no helper
questions.explain: Go is irregular: yesterday we went, never goed.

questions.q: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: 'Yesterday, we ___ in the park.'
questions.explain: The time word yesterday requires the past tense form played.

questions.q: The verb form in 'She has eaten lunch already' is an example of:
options: The present perfect, formed with has or have plus a past participle
questions.explain: Has eaten links a completed past action to the present moment, which is the job of the present perfect.

questions.q: The simple future tense is usually formed with:
options: Will plus the base form of the verb
The verb plus -ing and no helper
questions.explain: Will sits in front of the plain base verb: will go, will see, will finish.

questions.q: Identify the tense: 'They walked to school this morning.'
questions.explain: Walked is the past form, and this morning describes a time that has already passed.

questions.q: Which sentence keeps one steady tense without an awkward shift?
options: She opens the door and walked inside.
She opened the door and walks inside yesterday.
She will open the door and walked inside.
She opened the door and walked inside.
questions.explain: Both verbs are in the past tense, so the timeline of the sentence stays consistent.

questions.q: A report is due next week. Which sentence correctly states the plan in the future tense?
options: We finished the report on Friday.
We will finish the report on Friday.
We are finished the report on Friday last week.
We finishes the report on Friday.
questions.explain: Will finish correctly places the planned action in the future.

rounds.title: Verb Tenses
rounds.desc: Past, present, and future forms, irregular verbs, and keeping the tense steady inside a sentence.

title: Pronouns & Agreement
subject: English & Grammar
description: Subject and object pronouns, possessives without apostrophes, reflexives, and matching pronouns to their antecedents.

questions.q: A pronoun is a word that:
options: Takes the place of a noun
questions.explain: Pronouns like he, she, it, and they stand in for nouns so writing does not repeat the same name endlessly.

questions.q: In 'Maria lost her book,' the word her refers back to Maria. Maria is called the pronoun's:
questions.explain: The antecedent is the noun the pronoun stands for; clear antecedents keep sentences understandable.

questions.q: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Please give the ball to ___.'
options: He and I both fill this blank correctly
questions.explain: After the preposition to, an object pronoun is needed, and me is the object form.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a possessive pronoun correctly?
options: That book is their's, not our's.
That book is theirs', not ours'.
That book is they, not we.
That book is theirs, not ours.
questions.explain: Possessive pronouns like theirs and ours never take an apostrophe; apostrophes in pronouns mark contractions instead.

questions.q: Choose the reflexive pronoun: 'He hurt ___ while skating.'
questions.explain: When the subject and object are the same person, use a reflexive pronoun such as himself or herself.

questions.q: Choose the pronouns that complete the sentence: 'The dogs wagged ___ tails when ___ saw us.'
options: His / he for both dogs together
questions.explain: Plural dogs need plural pronouns: their for possession and they as the subject.

questions.q: Which words could replace 'Tom and Sara' as the subject of a sentence?
questions.explain: A subject position needs a subject pronoun, and they replaces a plural subject.

questions.q: What is the problem in this sentence: 'When Sam met Jake after the game, he was smiling.'
options: There is no verb in the sentence
The sentence has too many pronouns to count
It is unclear whether he means Sam or Jake
questions.explain: A pronoun with two possible antecedents confuses the reader; rewriting with a name fixes it.

questions.q: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Neither of the boys brought ___ lunch.'
options: Their as a traditional singular match in formal grammar drills
questions.explain: In traditional agreement, neither is singular, so it pairs with the singular pronoun his.

questions.q: Which sentence uses pronouns correctly from start to finish?
options: Us gave they them coats, and them thanked we.
We gave them their coats, and they thanked us.
We gave they their coats, and them thanked us.
Us gave them they coats, and they thanked we.
questions.explain: Subject pronouns do the action (we, they), object pronouns receive it (them, us), and possessives show ownership (their).

rounds.title: Pronouns & Agreement
rounds.desc: Subject and object pronouns, possessives without apostrophes, reflexives, and matching pronouns to their antecedents.

description: Fix the mistakes everyone makes: their/they're, affect/effect, pronoun cases, and agreement.

questions.explain: They're = they are (a contraction). Their = possessive. There = a place. Only "They're going" expands to "They are going," which is correct here.
options: Their going to the store later.
They're going to loose the game.
There going to win for sure.
They're going to the store later.
questions.q: Choose the correct sentence:

questions.explain: Affect is usually the VERB meaning to influence: "will affect morale." Effect is usually the NOUN meaning a result: "the effect was positive."
options: The new policy will affect morale.
The affect of the storm was severe.
The medicine will effect you strongly.
questions.q: Which sentence uses "affect" and "effect" correctly?

questions.explain: In the subject position, use subject pronouns: "He and I went." Test by removing the other person — "He went to lunch" works, but "Him went" and "Me went" do not.
options: Me and him went to lunch.
Him and I went to lunch.
He and I went to lunch.
Him and me went to lunch.
questions.q: Which sentence uses subject pronouns correctly?

questions.explain: Ignore prepositional phrases ("of students," "on the shelf") when finding the true subject. "Committee" is singular here, so it takes "meets" — and "news" is singular despite ending in s.
options: The group of students are studying.
The books on the shelf is dusty.
questions.q: Choose the sentence with correct subject-verb agreement:

questions.explain: Use "fewer" for countable nouns (people, apples) and "less" for uncountable quantities (water, milk, time). "Fewer people" is correct.
options: There is fewer water in the glass.
There are fewer people in line today.
I have less apples than you do.
Fewer milk is left in the fridge.
questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses "fewer" vs. "less"?

questions.explain: The participial phrase "driving to work" attaches to "deer," implying the deer was driving. Place the modifier next to the word it describes: "Driving to work, I saw a deer."
options: Running late, the bus left without me.
Covered in mud, the dog needed a bath.
Tired and hungry, we ate dinner.
I saw a deer driving to work.
questions.q: Which sentence contains a misplaced modifier?

questions.explain: Parallel structure requires items in a series to share the same grammatical form. All three gerunds — hiking, swimming, biking — match.
options: She likes hiking, swimming, and biking.
She likes hiking, swimming, and to bike.
She likes to hike, swimming, and biking.
She likes hiking, to swim, and biking.
questions.q: Which sentence uses parallel structure correctly?

questions.explain: Prepositions take OBJECT pronouns: "between you and ME." Test by dropping the other person — "between me" works, but "between I" never does.
options: The sentence needs a comma after "I".
The sentence should end with a question mark.
questions.q: "Between you and I, this test is hard." What is wrong?

questions.explain: "Could of" is a mishearing of the contraction "could've" (could HAVE). Always write "could have," "should have," or "would have" — never "of."
questions.q: Which sentence spells the contraction correctly?

questions.explain: Two negatives cancel into a positive in standard English. "Don't need any help" uses one negative with "any" — the correct pattern. The others accidentally say the opposite of what is intended.
questions.q: Which sentence avoids a double negative?

subject: English & Grammar
title: Common Errors
Clauses & Sentence Variety
subject: English & Grammar
description: Phrases versus clauses, relative and adverbial clauses, appositives, and combining choppy sentences.

questions.q: A phrase differs from a clause because a phrase:
options: Is always longer than a clause
Lacks a complete subject and verb pairing
Must begin with a capital letter
questions.explain: A clause has both a subject and a verb; a phrase is a word group without that pairing.

questions.q: In 'The book that I borrowed is overdue,' the clause 'that I borrowed' is a relative clause because it:
options: States the main action of the sentence
Begins with a relative pronoun and describes the noun book
Ends the sentence with a period
questions.explain: Relative clauses start with words like that, who, or which and add detail about a noun.

questions.q: Which word turns an independent clause into a dependent one in '___ the rain stopped, we went out'?
options: And, used as a joining word of equals
When, used as a subordinating conjunction
questions.explain: Subordinating conjunctions such as when, because, and although make a clause depend on the main clause.

questions.q: Which group of words is an independent clause?
options: The sun set behind the hill
questions.explain: An independent clause has a subject and verb and expresses a complete thought that can stand alone.

questions.q: In 'My brother, a talented drummer, practices daily,' the phrase 'a talented drummer' is an appositive because it:
options: Shows the action of the sentence
Renames or explains the noun brother
questions.explain: An appositive sits next to a noun and gives another name or description for it, set off by commas.

questions.q: Writers vary sentence length and openings mainly to:
options: Make every paragraph the same length
Keep the writing flowing and hold the reader's interest
questions.explain: A mix of short punchy sentences and longer flowing ones creates rhythm and emphasis.

questions.q: In 'Swimming is my favorite sport,' the word Swimming functions as:
options: A noun, as the subject of the sentence
questions.explain: Verb forms ending in -ing can act as nouns; these are called gerunds, and here Swimming is what the sentence is about.

questions.q: Which revision best combines these choppy sentences: 'The wind blew. The trees shook. The rain started.'?
options: The wind blew, the trees shook, and the rain started.
The wind blew the trees shook the rain started.
The wind blew. Because trees. Rain.
Blowing wind trees shaking starting rain.
questions.explain: Joining related short sentences with commas and a conjunction removes choppiness while staying grammatical.

questions.q: In 'Running to catch the bus, Lena dropped her notebook,' the opening phrase describes:
options: Lena, the subject it sits next to
questions.explain: An opening participial phrase modifies the subject right after the comma; placing it elsewhere creates a dangling modifier.

questions.q: Identify the adverbial clause in: 'We left the park when the bell rang.'
questions.explain: Adverbial clauses start with words like when, because, or if and tell when, why, or under what condition.

rounds.title: Clauses & Sentence Variety
rounds.desc: Phrases versus clauses, relative and adverbial clauses, appositives, and combining choppy sentences.

title: Paragraph Writing
subject: English & Grammar
description: Topic sentences, supporting details, transitions, conclusions, and keeping every sentence on one main idea.

questions.q: The topic sentence of a paragraph states:
options: A minor detail from the middle
The title of the whole essay
The main idea that the rest of the paragraph supports
A question the writer never answers
questions.explain: A clear topic sentence tells the reader what the paragraph will prove or explain, and details follow from it.

questions.q: Supporting sentences in a paragraph should do which job?
options: Repeat the topic sentence word for word
Give details, examples, and reasons that back up the main idea
questions.explain: Support is evidence for the main idea: facts, examples, and explanations that make it convincing.

questions.q: A concluding sentence in a paragraph should:
options: Wrap up the main idea in fresh words and leave the reader with a finished thought
Be copied from the first sentence exactly
questions.explain: The conclusion closes the loop on the main idea without simply repeating the topic sentence.

questions.q: A paragraph is best defined as:
options: A group of sentences that develop one main idea
The whole essay on one page
questions.explain: Unity is the rule: every sentence in the paragraph serves the same single main idea.

questions.q: The words first, next, and finally in a paragraph are transitions that show:
options: The order in which events or steps happen
questions.explain: Sequence transitions guide the reader through time or through the steps of a process.

questions.q: A paragraph explains why bicycles are good transportation. Which sentence does NOT belong?
options: Bikes cost much less than cars.
Riding a bike is good exercise.
My grandfather grows tomatoes every summer.
questions.explain: Every supporting sentence must connect to the main idea; the tomato sentence wanders off topic.

questions.q: Which order makes a sensible paragraph about making a sandwich?
options: Take out the bread, add the filling, then close and eat the sandwich.
Eat the sandwich, take out the bread, then add the filling.
Add the filling, eat the sandwich, then take out the bread.
Close the sandwich, eat it, then take out the bread.
questions.explain: Process writing follows the real order of steps, usually supported by transitions like first, next, and last.

questions.q: Why should each paragraph have only one main idea?
options: Because essays are limited to one page
So the reader can follow the point clearly and the writer can develop it fully
So the writer can use more periods
questions.explain: Splitting ideas across paragraphs keeps writing organized; a new main idea earns a new paragraph.

questions.q: Which is the strongest topic sentence?
options: Training a puppy takes patience because puppies learn through short, daily practice.
Puppies are cute and that is all.
questions.explain: A strong topic sentence is specific and makes a point the paragraph can actually support with details.

questions.q: How does knowing your audience change a piece of writing?
options: It means you should always write longer
It removes the need for a main idea
It shapes the words, examples, and level of detail you choose
questions.explain: Writing for young children, experts, or friends calls for different vocabulary, tone, and explanations.

rounds.title: Paragraph Writing
rounds.desc: Topic sentences, supporting details, transitions, conclusions, and keeping every sentence on one main idea.

title: Editing & Proofreading
subject: English & Grammar
description: Revising for clarity, catching spelling and punctuation slips, fixing homophones, and the final check before sharing.

questions.q: What is the main difference between editing and proofreading?
options: They are exactly the same step
Proofreading always comes before any drafting
Editing only means changing the title
Editing improves wording, structure, and clarity; proofreading catches final surface errors
questions.explain: Editing is the bigger-picture pass; proofreading is the final polish for spelling, punctuation, and typos.

questions.q: Which sentence contains a capitalization error to fix?
options: We are driving to florida in June.
We are driving to Florida in June.
questions.explain: Florida is a proper noun naming a state, so its lowercase f is the error a proofreader must catch.

questions.q: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explain: Friend follows the pattern i before e in this word; freind is one of the most common misspellings.

questions.q: A draft reads: 'Their going to the park after lunch.' What correction is needed?
options: Change Their to They're, meaning they are
questions.explain: Their shows ownership; the sentence needs the contraction They're for they are.

questions.q: Which edit best fixes this run-on: 'The game ended we went home.'?
options: The game ended we went home happy joyful.
The game ended we, went home.
The game ended. We went home yesterday tomorrow.
The game ended, and we went home.
questions.explain: Joining the two complete thoughts with a comma and and, or splitting them into two sentences, fixes a run-on.

questions.q: Why do writers ask a peer to review a draft?
options: A fresh reader spots confusing spots and errors the writer reads past
So the peer can write the whole paper instead
questions.explain: Writers become blind to their own mistakes; a peer review gives honest outside eyes before the final version.

questions.q: Reading a draft aloud while proofreading helps mainly because it:
options: Makes missing words and awkward phrasing easier to hear and catch
questions.explain: Your ears catch what your eyes skip: dropped words, repeated words, and sentences that do not flow.

questions.q: The final step before sharing a finished piece should be:
options: One last proofread against a checklist for spelling, punctuation, and capitalization
questions.explain: A final checklist pass confirms the piece is clean and complete before it reaches its audience.

questions.q: Which revision makes this wordy sentence clearest: 'Due to the fact that it was raining, we made the decision to stay inside.'?
options: Due to the fact that it was raining outside in the weather, we made the decision to stay inside our house.
Raining, due to the fact, inside we stayed decision.
We stayed inside due to the fact of the rain that was falling down from the sky.
Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
questions.explain: Good editing cuts filler phrases like due to the fact that and says the same meaning in fewer, clearer words.

questions.q: A writer swaps 'the cat chased the mouse' into 'the mouse was chased by the cat' and the sentence feels weaker. The first version is stronger because it uses:
options: Active voice, where the subject performs the action directly
More words than the second version
A question instead of a statement
questions.explain: Active voice is usually clearer and more direct than passive voice, where the subject receives the action.

rounds.title: Editing & Proofreading
rounds.desc: Revising for clarity, catching spelling and punctuation slips, fixing homophones, and the final check before sharing.

description: Malware, phishing, DDoS, social engineering, and the attack types Security+ expects you to recognize.

questions.explain: Phishing tricks users into revealing credentials or data by posing as a trusted sender; it relies on social engineering rather than technical exploits.
options: To steal credentials or sensitive data by impersonating a trusted entity
To slow network traffic with junk data
To legally test a company's defenses
questions.q: What is the primary goal of a phishing attack?

questions.explain: Ransomware encrypts data and extorts payment; worms self-replicate across networks, trojans hide inside legitimate-looking software, and spyware secretly monitors activity.
questions.q: Which type of malware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the decryption key?

questions.explain: A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack floods a target with traffic from many sources (often a botnet) to exhaust its resources.
questions.q: A company's website is overwhelmed by traffic from thousands of compromised devices, making it unavailable to legitimate users. This is a:

questions.explain: Zero-day means defenders have had zero days to prepare — attackers exploit the flaw before a patch exists.
options: A virus that activates on day zero of installation
A password that expires after one day
A backup that is zero days old
A flaw exploited before the vendor knows about it or has a patch
questions.q: What is a zero-day vulnerability?

questions.explain: Pretexting uses a fabricated scenario (a 'pretext') to manipulate someone into giving up information; tailgating is following someone through a secured door.
questions.q: An attacker calls an employee, pretends to be from IT support, and asks for their login credentials. This social engineering technique is called:

questions.explain: SQL injection exploits unsanitized input to run unauthorized database commands; parameterized queries and input validation prevent it.
questions.q: Which attack injects malicious code into a database query through a website's input field?

questions.explain: Worms self-propagate across networks automatically, while viruses need a host file and user action to spread.
options: Spreads on its own without user action
Requires a host program to spread
questions.q: A worm differs from a virus primarily because a worm:

questions.explain: A man-in-the-middle attacker sits between the communicating parties; encryption and mutual authentication (e.g., TLS, certificates) defeat it.
questions.q: An attacker secretly intercepts and relays messages between two parties who believe they are communicating directly. This is a:

questions.explain: Insider threats come from trusted users abusing authorized access; they are hard to detect because the activity often looks legitimate.
questions.q: An employee with legitimate access intentionally steals company data to sell to a competitor. This is an example of:

questions.explain: A watering hole attack poisons a site the victims trust and visit, like predators waiting at a watering hole.
questions.q: Attackers compromise a website that a target group frequently visits, infecting visitors' browsers. This technique is called a:

subject: CompTIA Security+ Prep
title: Threats & Attacks

description: CIA triad, symmetric vs asymmetric encryption, hashing, PKI, and digital signatures.

questions.explain: Confidentiality = authorized access only (encryption helps); integrity = data is unaltered; availability = systems are up; non-repudiation = actions can't be denied.
options: Only authorized parties can access data
questions.q: In the CIA triad, 'confidentiality' means:

questions.explain: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) uses one shared secret key for both encryption and decryption, making it symmetric and fast for bulk data.
questions.q: AES is an example of which type of encryption?

questions.explain: RSA uses mathematically linked public and private keys — great for key exchange and digital signatures, but slower than symmetric ciphers.
options: A symmetric cipher using one shared key
A method of hiding data in images
An asymmetric algorithm using a public/private key pair
questions.q: RSA is best described as:

questions.explain: A hash is one-way: the system compares hashes at login without ever storing the actual password, so a database breach doesn't reveal credentials.
options: To make passwords decryptable by admins
To verify integrity without storing the plaintext
questions.q: What is the primary purpose of hashing a password before storing it?

questions.explain: Signing a hash with a private key proves who sent it (authentication), that it wasn't altered (integrity), and the sender can't deny it (non-repudiation).
questions.q: A digital signature provides which security properties?

questions.explain: A salt is random data added before hashing so identical passwords produce different hashes, defeating precomputed rainbow tables.
questions.q: What does salting a password hash defend against?

questions.explain: The CA is a trusted third party that signs certificates, letting strangers verify each other's public keys.
options: Issues and vouches for digital certificates binding keys to identities
questions.q: In a public key infrastructure (PKI), what does a certificate authority (CA) do?

questions.explain: Diffie-Hellman lets two parties derive the same secret key even while eavesdroppers watch — the foundation of many TLS key exchanges.
options: Securely agree on a shared secret key over an insecure channel
questions.q: The Diffie-Hellman protocol is used to:

questions.explain: In practice they work together: asymmetric crypto exchanges a symmetric session key, then fast symmetric encryption (like AES) protects the data.
options: Symmetric is slower but more secure than asymmetric
Asymmetric uses one shared key; symmetric uses key pairs
Hashing is a type of symmetric encryption
Symmetric is faster and used for bulk data; asymmetric is used for key exchange and signatures
questions.q: Which statement about symmetric vs. asymmetric encryption is TRUE?

questions.explain: Full-disk encryption renders the drive unreadable without the key, so a stolen laptop yields no data — it doesn't help against network or social attacks.
questions.q: Full-disk encryption primarily protects data against:
