title: Cryptography Basics

description: Firewalls, VPNs, DMZs, IDS/IPS, segmentation, and secure wireless.

questions.explain: A firewall enforces an access control policy on network traffic; encryption, DHCP, and endpoint antivirus are separate functions.
options: To filter traffic based on rules, allowing or blocking it
To assign IP addresses to devices
questions.q: What is the primary function of a firewall?

questions.explain: The DMZ hosts public services (web, mail) so if they're compromised, attackers still can't reach the internal network directly.
options: A network segment that isolates public-facing servers from the internal LAN
questions.q: A DMZ (demilitarized zone) in network architecture is:

questions.explain: A VPN encapsulates and encrypts traffic in a tunnel, protecting it from eavesdropping on untrusted networks.
options: Creating an encrypted tunnel between endpoints
questions.q: A VPN protects data in transit primarily by:

questions.explain: Intrusion Detection is passive (alerts), Intrusion Prevention is active (blocks) — the 'P' makes the difference.
options: An IDS blocks threats; an IPS only monitors
An IPS actively blocks threats; an IDS only detects and alerts
An IPS works only on wireless networks
questions.q: How does an IPS differ from an IDS?

questions.explain: VLANs create logical broadcast domains so a breach in one segment (e.g., guest Wi-Fi) can't easily reach others (e.g., finance servers).
options: Limiting lateral movement by isolating traffic between groups
questions.q: Segmenting a network with VLANs improves security mainly by:

questions.explain: WPA3 replaced WPA2 with stronger encryption (SAE handshake) and protection against offline dictionary attacks; WEP is trivially crackable.
questions.q: Which wireless security protocol is currently recommended as the strongest?

questions.explain: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) uses 443; SSH uses 22, FTP uses 21, DNS uses 53 — know the common ports for Security+.
questions.q: Port 443 is the default port for:

questions.explain: A honeypot looks like a valuable target but is isolated and monitored, wasting attacker time and revealing their tactics.
options: Lures attackers to a decoy system to study their methods
questions.q: A honeypot is a security control that:

questions.explain: NAC checks device health and compliance (patches, antivirus) before granting network access — unhealthy devices get quarantined.
options: Enforce policies on devices before allowing them on the network
Cache web content for faster browsing
Translate private IPs to public IPs
questions.q: Network Access Control (NAC) is used to:

questions.explain: A forward proxy / secure web gateway inspects outbound web requests and blocks malicious sites; a hub just repeats traffic to all ports.
options: A secure web gateway / forward proxy
questions.q: Which device is best placed at the network edge to filter malicious web traffic before it reaches users?

subject: CompTIA Security+ Prep
title: Network Security

description: MFA, RBAC, least privilege, SSO, and controlling privileged accounts.

questions.explain: MFA requires two or more different factor types (something you know + something you have); two passwords are still just one factor.
options: Password plus a one-time code from an authenticator app
questions.q: Which of the following is an example of multi-factor authentication (MFA)?

questions.explain: RBAC assigns permissions to roles (e.g., 'Accountant'), and users get permissions through their roles — simpler to manage than per-user rules.
options: The user's job function or role
questions.q: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions based on:

questions.explain: Least privilege limits the damage from compromised accounts and insider misuse by granting only necessary permissions.
options: Have no access to any systems
Share accounts to reduce license costs
Receive only the minimum access needed to do their jobs
questions.q: The principle of least privilege states that users should:

questions.explain: SSO lets users authenticate once to access many apps, reducing password fatigue — but it also makes the SSO credentials a high-value target.
questions.q: Single sign-on (SSO) primarily improves:

questions.explain: Biometrics (fingerprint, face, iris) are 'something you are' — inherence factors. Passwords are 'know', tokens/phones are 'have'.
questions.q: A fingerprint scan is an example of which authentication factor?

questions.explain: Lockouts slow or stop automated password guessing; attackers get only a few tries before the account locks.
questions.q: An account lockout policy (e.g., lock after 5 failed attempts) defends against:

questions.explain: Admin and root accounts have the most power, so PAM vaults their credentials, requires checkout/approval, and logs their sessions.
questions.q: Privileged Access Management (PAM) is most concerned with:

questions.explain: Federation (e.g., SAML, OAuth) lets an identity provider vouch for the user, so the service provider doesn't need its own credentials.
options: Both companies share one password database
The user has two separate accounts
Company B trusts authentication assertions from Company A's identity provider
questions.q: In identity federation, a user from Company A accesses Company B's app using Company A's login. This works because:

questions.explain: Length adds more entropy than complexity rules; each extra character multiplies the guessing space, while frequent forced changes push users toward weak patterns.
options: Requiring the username in the password
questions.q: Which password policy requirement most improves resistance to brute-force attacks?

questions.explain: Prompt deprovisioning closes the window for a disgruntled ex-employee to abuse still-active credentials — part of offboarding.
options: Immediately disable or remove their accounts and access
questions.q: When an employee leaves the company, the FIRST access-control step should be:

description: Risk assessment, BIA, incident response, and GDPR/HIPAA/PCI DSS compliance.

questions.explain: Risk = how likely an event is times how bad it would be; this prioritizes which risks to address first.
questions.q: Risk is commonly calculated as:

questions.explain: Transference shifts the financial impact to a third party (insurer); mitigation reduces the risk, avoidance eliminates the activity, acceptance means living with it.
questions.q: A company buys cyber insurance to cover breach costs instead of fixing every vulnerability. This risk strategy is:

questions.explain: Recovery Time Objective = max tolerable downtime; Recovery Point Objective (RPO) = max tolerable data loss.
options: How quickly systems must be restored after a disruption
How much data loss is acceptable
The cost of downtime per hour
The number of backup copies required
questions.q: In business continuity planning, RTO defines:

questions.explain: The General Data Protection Regulation gives EU residents rights over their personal data and imposes heavy fines for violations.
options: Protecting the privacy and personal data of EU individuals
questions.q: GDPR is a regulation primarily concerned with:

questions.explain: HIPAA safeguards PHI (protected health information) at covered entities like hospitals and insurers; student records fall under FERPA, card data under PCI DSS.
options: Protected health information handled by healthcare entities
questions.q: HIPAA's Security Rule applies to:

questions.explain: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard sets requirements for anyone storing, processing, or transmitting credit card data.
questions.q: PCI DSS exists to protect:

questions.explain: Vulnerability scans list weaknesses; penetration testers exploit them like real attackers to demonstrate actual risk.
options: Scans are manual; pen tests are automated
A pen test actively exploits vulnerabilities to prove impact; a scan only identifies them
questions.q: What is the key difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?

questions.explain: DRP is the IT-focused playbook for getting systems back online; the broader business continuity plan (BCP) keeps the whole business running.
options: Restoring IT systems and operations after a disruption
questions.q: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) focuses on:

questions.explain: Preparation (plans, tools, training, playbooks) comes before detection and analysis — you can't respond well to what you never planned for.
questions.q: Which incident response phase comes FIRST?

questions.explain: Risk acceptance is a valid strategy when mitigation costs more than the risk itself — but it must be a conscious, documented decision.
questions.q: An organization decides a low-impact risk is cheaper to live with than to fix, and documents the decision. This is:

Security Architecture & Design
subject: CompTIA Security+ Prep
description: Zero trust, redundancy, cloud responsibility, and secure design patterns that show up across the Security+ exam.

questions.q: A company stops trusting traffic just because it is inside the office network, and now verifies every user and device on every request. Which model is this?
questions.explain: Zero trust means never trust and always verify: identity, device, and context are checked on every request, wherever it comes from.

questions.q: In a zero trust design, what does microsegmentation do?
options: Encrypts every hard drive by default
Divides the network into small zones so access between workloads can be tightly controlled
Connects branch offices over the public internet
questions.explain: Microsegmentation limits lateral movement: even inside the network, each workload only talks to what it truly needs.

questions.q: A web app runs behind a load balancer with three identical servers, so traffic shifts if one server fails. The main benefit is:
questions.explain: Redundant components remove single points of failure, which protects availability when hardware or software breaks.

questions.q: Why do organizations define a secure baseline for new servers?
options: So administrators never need to patch
So users can choose their own firewall rules
So backups are no longer required
So every server starts from the same hardened, documented configuration
questions.explain: A baseline is a known-good hardened starting point; deviations from it are easy to spot and audit.

questions.q: A company rents IaaS cloud servers. Who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
questions.explain: In IaaS the provider secures the physical host and hypervisor, but the customer owns the guest OS, its patches, and its data.

questions.q: Why do administrators reach a secure server room network through a jump server?
options: It creates a single controlled and logged entry point for administrative sessions
It hides the servers from asset inventory
It replaces the need for backups
questions.explain: A jump server funnels admin access through one hardened, monitored host instead of exposing every system directly.

questions.q: A cloud application must survive the loss of an entire data center building. The best design choice is to:
options: Make one server as powerful as possible
Store backups on the same server
Deploy copies across multiple availability zones
questions.explain: Availability zones are separate facilities in a region, so one building failure does not take the application down.

questions.q: A motherboard chip that stores encryption keys and verifies boot integrity in hardware is a:
questions.explain: A TPM is a hardware security module on the device itself; it protects keys and can measure the boot process for tampering.

questions.q: RAID storage plus redundant power supplies are design choices aimed mainly at which goal?
questions.explain: Redundancy keeps systems and data available through component failures, which serves the availability leg of the CIA triad.

questions.q: A design review finds one firewall is a single point of failure for the whole office. The best fix is:
options: A second firewall in a high-availability pair
Moving the firewall to a closet
questions.explain: Pairing firewalls means one can fail over to the other, removing the single point of failure without weakening filtering.

rounds.title: Security Architecture & Design
rounds.desc: Zero trust, redundancy, cloud responsibility, and secure design patterns that show up across the Security+ exam.

title: PKI & Advanced Cryptography
subject: CompTIA Security+ Prep
description: Certificate life cycles, revocation checking, key stretching, forward secrecy, and the PKI details beyond the basics.

questions.q: A browser needs to check right now whether one specific certificate has been revoked. The fastest targeted method is:
questions.explain: OCSP asks the certificate authority about one certificate in real time, while a CRL is a whole published list of revoked certificates.

questions.q: How does a CRL differ from OCSP?
options: A CRL encrypts traffic; OCSP hashes passwords
They are the same protocol with different names
A CRL is a signed list of revoked certificates; OCSP checks the status of a single certificate on demand
A CRL is used only for email
questions.explain: Both solve revocation checking: the CRL is a downloadable list, and OCSP is a live per-certificate query.

questions.q: Key escrow in a PKI means:
options: Keys are deleted after every session
A trusted third party holds a copy of a private key for controlled recovery
questions.explain: Escrow lets an organization recover encrypted data if a key is lost, but the stored keys need strict controls because they are high value.

questions.q: Perfect forward secrecy protects recorded past sessions mainly because:
options: Each session uses temporary keys, so stealing the long-term key later cannot decrypt old traffic
The server stores no logs at all
questions.explain: With ephemeral session keys, a later compromise of the server private key does not unlock previously captured sessions.

questions.q: Why do phones and small devices often prefer ECC over RSA?
options: ECC gives comparable security with shorter keys and less computing power
RSA cannot be used on the internet
questions.explain: Elliptic curve cryptography reaches RSA-level strength with much smaller keys, which suits constrained devices.

questions.q: bcrypt and PBKDF2 make password guessing expensive because they are:
options: Key stretching functions designed to be slow and adjustable
questions.explain: Key stretching deliberately adds work to every guess; salting stops precomputation, and stretching slows each individual attempt.

questions.q: Certificate pinning helps stop which attack?
options: A phishing email with a spelling error
A man-in-the-middle using a fraudulent certificate that the device would otherwise trust
questions.explain: Pinning ties an app to the expected certificate or public key, so a rogue but valid-looking certificate gets rejected.

questions.q: A wildcard certificate issued for *.example.com covers:
options: One level of subdomains, such as mail.example.com and vpn.example.com
Every domain the company will ever own
Only the bare domain example.com with nothing else
questions.explain: A wildcard matches a single label in place of the asterisk; it does not cover deeper levels or the bare domain by default.

questions.q: Validation of a website certificate fails even though the leaf certificate looks fine. A common cause is:
options: The website uses too many images
A missing or untrusted intermediate certificate, breaking the chain of trust
The user has too many tabs open
The server is in another time zone
questions.explain: Browsers must build an unbroken chain from the leaf through intermediates to a trusted root; a missing intermediate breaks validation.

questions.q: Users report a browser warning that a site certificate has expired. The administrator's first fix is to:
options: Tell users to click through the warning
Renew the certificate and install the valid replacement
questions.explain: Expired certificates must be renewed and installed; training users to bypass warnings destroys the warning's value.

title: Security Operations & Monitoring
subject: CompTIA Security+ Prep
description: SIEM, SOAR, EDR, threat hunting, log analysis, and the day-to-day work of a security operations center.

questions.q: The main job of a SIEM is to:
options: Collect logs from many systems, correlate events, and alert on suspicious patterns
questions.explain: A SIEM centralizes and correlates log data so patterns that are invisible in any single log can trigger alerts.

questions.q: How does a SOAR platform go beyond a SIEM?
options: It runs automated response playbooks, such as disabling an account or isolating a host
questions.explain: SOAR adds orchestration and automation: predefined playbooks carry out response steps quickly and consistently.

questions.q: An EDR tool gives a SOC more than traditional antivirus mainly because it:
options: Monitors endpoint behavior continuously and supports investigation and remote response
questions.explain: EDR watches process and user behavior over time, keeps telemetry for hunting, and can isolate or clean a host remotely.

questions.q: An analyst sees a successful login from the home office, then one from another continent 20 minutes later for the same account. This indicator is called:
questions.explain: Impossible travel flags logins that could not physically happen in sequence, which suggests stolen credentials.

questions.q: NetFlow data is most useful to an analyst because it shows:
options: The exact text of every email
Metadata about traffic flows, such as source, destination, ports, and volume, without full packet contents
Which files are on a hard drive
questions.explain: Flow records reveal who talked to whom, how much, and when, which is ideal for spotting beacons and large transfers.

questions.q: A credentialed vulnerability scan usually finds more than an uncredentialed one because it:
options: Logs in and can check installed software and missing patches directly
questions.explain: With credentials, the scanner inspects the host from the inside instead of guessing from open ports and banners.

questions.q: Threat hunting differs from alert-driven monitoring because hunters:
options: Proactively search for hidden attackers, assuming some threats already got past defenses
Work only after a breach is announced
questions.explain: Hunting is hypothesis-driven searching for stealthy activity that automated alerts did not catch.

questions.q: Anomaly-based detection works by first:
options: Building a baseline of normal behavior, then flagging meaningful deviations
questions.explain: Without a baseline of normal, there is nothing to compare unusual activity against.

questions.q: To investigate repeated failed and successful logins on a Windows domain, the best log source is:
questions.explain: Security event logs record logon successes and failures, account lockouts, and privilege use in one place.

questions.q: A SOC cuts its mean time to detect from days to minutes. The improvement matters because:
options: Attackers have less dwell time to move laterally and steal data
questions.explain: Dwell time is how long an attacker operates undetected; faster detection shrinks the damage window.

rounds.title: Security Operations & Monitoring
rounds.desc: SIEM, SOAR, EDR, threat hunting, log analysis, and the day-to-day work of a security operations center.

title: Incident Response & Digital Forensics
subject: CompTIA Security+ Prep
description: Evidence handling, order of volatility, chain of custody, and the response steps that hold up in real investigations.

questions.q: Following the order of volatility, which evidence should a responder collect first?
questions.explain: Volatile data disappears first: memory and running processes go before disk data, which survives longer.

questions.q: The purpose of a chain of custody form is to:
options: Document everyone who handled evidence and when, so its integrity can be trusted
Assign the incident a ticket number
questions.explain: An unbroken, documented chain shows evidence was protected from tampering from collection to courtroom or review.

questions.q: During disk imaging, a write blocker is used to:
options: Prevent any changes to the original drive while a forensic copy is made
questions.explain: Even mounting a drive can alter timestamps; a write blocker keeps the source evidence pristine.

questions.q: An analyst hashes a drive image right after collection and again before analysis, and the hashes match. This proves:
options: The image has not changed between the two checks
questions.explain: Matching hashes demonstrate integrity: the evidence analyzed is exactly the evidence collected.

questions.q: What is the difference between containment and eradication?
options: They are two words for the same step
Containment limits the spread and damage; eradication removes the root cause and attacker presence
questions.explain: You contain first to stop the bleeding, then eradicate so the attacker cannot simply come back.

questions.q: Ransomware is spreading on a file server. The team unplugs its network cable but leaves it powered on for memory capture. This action is an example of:
questions.explain: Isolating the host stops the spread while preserving volatile evidence, which is classic short-term containment.

questions.q: A legal hold notice during an investigation means employees must:
options: Preserve relevant data and stop normal deletion or rotation of it
questions.explain: Legal hold suspends routine destruction so potentially relevant records survive for legal review.

questions.q: The lessons learned step at the end of incident response exists to:
options: Punish the employee who clicked the link
Close the ticket as fast as possible
Turn what the incident revealed into concrete improvements for people, process, and tools
questions.explain: A blameless review that produces real changes is how one incident makes the next one smaller.

questions.q: A forensic image is more complete than a normal file copy because it:
options: Compresses files so they open faster
Is a bit-for-bit copy that includes deleted data and unallocated space
questions.explain: Bit-for-bit imaging preserves slack and unallocated areas where deleted or hidden evidence often survives.

questions.q: Why must eradication finish before systems return to production?
options: Reconnecting a still-compromised system lets the attacker regain access and restarts the incident
Auditors require a month of downtime
questions.explain: Recovery on top of a surviving foothold just gives the attacker a freshly rebuilt network to re-enter.

rounds.title: Incident Response & Digital Forensics

title: Governance & Audit Programs
subject: CompTIA Security+ Prep
description: Policy hierarchies, frameworks like NIST, control testing, vendor risk, and how governance programs actually run.

questions.q: In the policy document hierarchy, a procedure differs from a policy because a procedure:
options: Gives the step-by-step instructions for carrying out a task
Is written by the board of directors
questions.explain: Policies state mandatory direction at a high level; standards set specifics, and procedures spell out exact steps.

questions.q: The five core functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework are:
options: Plan, Do, Check, Act, and Repeat
Scan, Patch, Test, Deploy, and Monitor
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover
Collect, Store, Analyze, Report, and Archive
questions.explain: The CSF organizes cybersecurity outcomes into Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.

questions.q: An external audit gives a company something an internal audit cannot as easily provide:
options: An independent assessment from outside the organization
questions.explain: Independence is the point of an external audit: outsiders have no stake in hiding the organization's weaknesses.

questions.q: Control testing during an assessment checks whether a control:
options: Has a long enough policy document
Was purchased from an approved vendor
Actually operates effectively in practice, not just on paper
questions.explain: A control that exists in a document but fails in daily operation gives false confidence; testing exposes that gap.

questions.q: Before signing with a new cloud vendor, a governance team reviews the vendor's SOC 2 report mainly to:
options: Evaluate how the vendor's own security controls are designed and operating
questions.explain: Third-party risk management uses attestations like SOC 2 reports to judge a vendor before trusting it with data.

questions.q: Data classification labels such as Public, Internal, and Confidential matter because they:
options: Replace the need for access control
Drive the handling, storage, and sharing rules for each piece of data
questions.explain: Classification connects business value and sensitivity to concrete protections, so sensitive data gets stronger handling.

questions.q: An employee needs a temporary exception to a security policy. A sound exception process requires it to be:
options: Documented, risk-accepted by an appropriate owner, and given an expiry date
Kept secret from the security team
questions.explain: Tracked, time-limited exceptions keep one-off needs from quietly becoming permanent holes in the policy.

questions.q: Separation of duties protects an organization by ensuring:
options: Passwords are shared within a team
No single person controls a sensitive process from start to finish
questions.explain: Splitting a process across people makes fraud and undetected errors much harder, because collusion becomes necessary.

questions.q: A security awareness program is best judged effective when measurements show:
options: Phishing simulation failure rates and reporting rates improving over time
The training video is very long
Employees can recite the policy number
questions.explain: Behavior change is the goal of awareness training, so programs track real behavior trends, not attendance alone.

questions.q: Senior leadership reviews a quarterly risk register. The register's main value is that it:
options: Tracks identified risks, their owners, and treatment status in one accountable place
questions.explain: A living risk register keeps ownership and treatment progress visible so risks are managed, not just listed once.

questions.q: The immediate spark that started World War I in 1914 was:

questions.q: Trench warfare on the Western Front led to:

questions.q: The League of Nations, created after World War I, was weakened most because:

questions.q: The Great Depression spread worldwide in the 1930s partly because:

title: World War II and the Holocaust
subject: World History
description: The causes, turning points, and human cost of World War II, including the Holocaust.

questions.q: World War II in Europe began in 1939 when Germany:
questions.explain: Germany's invasion of Poland on September 1, 1939 prompted Britain and France to declare war.

questions.q: The policy of appeasement in the 1930s meant:
options: Giving in to Hitler's demands to avoid war
questions.explain: Britain and France allowed German expansion, hoping to preserve peace.

questions.q: The Battle of Stalingrad (1942-1943) was a turning point because:
options: Germany's army was destroyed on the Eastern Front and began retreating
The United States left the war
questions.explain: The Soviet victory at Stalingrad shifted momentum against Germany in the east.

questions.q: The Holocaust refers to:
options: The Nazi murder of six million Jews and millions of other victims
questions.explain: The Holocaust was the state-sponsored genocide carried out by Nazi Germany and its collaborators.

questions.q: The Nuremberg Trials after the war established that:
options: Only countries, never individuals, could be punished
All soldiers were guilty of war crimes
Leaders could be held individually responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity
questions.explain: Nuremberg set precedents for international criminal law that still apply today.

questions.q: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941) caused:
options: The United States to enter World War II
The League of Nations to declare war
questions.explain: The U.S. declared war on Japan, and Germany then declared war on the U.S.

questions.q: The Allied strategy of island hopping in the Pacific aimed to:
options: Capture key islands and move closer to Japan, bypassing strongholds
Move the war to South America
questions.explain: Island hopping seized bases for airfields while leaving isolated Japanese garrisons behind.

questions.q: The Manhattan Project was the Allied program to:
questions.explain: The secret U.S.-led project produced the first nuclear weapons, used on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.

questions.q: Civilian populations in World War II were heavily affected because:
options: Most people lived far from any front
Cities were bombed, occupied, and targeted on a massive scale
questions.explain: Total war blurred the line between soldiers and civilians, with bombings, occupation, and genocide.

questions.q: The Yalta and Potsdam Conferences (1945) are important because Allied leaders:
options: Planned the postwar order and divided Germany into occupation zones
questions.explain: These meetings shaped postwar Europe and set up Cold War divisions.

title: Cold War and Decolonization
subject: World History
description: Superpower rivalry, proxy wars, and the end of European empires after 1945.

questions.q: The Cold War was mainly a rivalry between:
options: The United States and the Soviet Union
questions.explain: The two superpowers competed globally without fighting each other directly in a full war.

questions.q: NATO and the Warsaw Pact were:
options: Rival military alliances in the Cold War
questions.explain: NATO grouped the U.S. and Western Europe; the Warsaw Pact grouped the USSR and Eastern Europe.

questions.q: The Korean War (1950-1953) ended with:
options: Korea still divided near the 38th parallel
questions.explain: An armistice left North and South Korea divided roughly where the war began.

questions.q: The Berlin Wall (built 1961) symbolized:
options: The division between communist East and democratic West in Europe
The end of the Cold War
questions.explain: The wall stopped East Germans fleeing to the West and became the Cold War's most visible symbol.

questions.q: Decolonization after World War II refers to:
options: The start of the slave trade
European empires granting independence to colonies in Africa and Asia
questions.explain: Dozens of new nations emerged between the 1940s and 1970s.

questions.q: India gained independence from Britain in 1947 under the leadership of movements associated with:
options: Mohandas Gandhi and the Indian National Congress
questions.explain: Gandhi's nonviolent campaigns pressured Britain to end colonial rule; independence came with partition into India and Pakistan.

questions.q: The Vietnam War reflected Cold War logic because the United States fought to:
options: Stop the spread of communism in Southeast Asia
Defend a NATO member in Europe
questions.explain: Containment and the domino theory drove U.S. intervention in Vietnam.

questions.q: The arms race during the Cold War centered on:
options: Building larger stockpiles of nuclear weapons
questions.explain: Both superpowers built enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other many times over.

questions.q: The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 signaled:
options: The start of World War II
The approaching end of the Cold War and communist rule in Eastern Europe
questions.explain: Within two years Germany reunified and the Soviet Union dissolved.

questions.q: The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, which:
options: Ended the Cold War and left the United States as the sole superpower
questions.explain: Fifteen independent republics emerged from the former USSR.

title: Globalization and the Modern World
subject: World History
description: Interconnection since 1991: trade, technology, environment, and global challenges.

questions.q: Globalization is best defined as:
options: The growing interconnection of economies, cultures, and populations worldwide
questions.explain: Globalization links markets, communication, and culture across borders.

questions.q: The World Trade Organization (WTO), founded in 1995, works to:
options: Set rules for and promote international trade
questions.explain: The WTO provides a forum for trade agreements and dispute settlement.

questions.q: The internet changed globalization most by:
options: Ending all local cultures at once
Making instant global communication and commerce possible
questions.explain: Email, the web, and later smartphones connected billions of people in real time.

questions.q: The European Union is an example of regional integration because its members:
options: Share laws, a common market, and (for many) a single currency
Have no separate governments at all
questions.explain: EU members cooperate deeply while remaining separate nations.

questions.q: Climate change is considered a global challenge mainly because:
options: Its causes and effects cross all national borders
It affects only one small region
Countries can solve it entirely alone
questions.explain: Greenhouse gases mix globally, so solutions require international cooperation like the Paris Agreement.

questions.q: Outsourcing in a globalized economy means companies:
options: Move production or services to other countries, often for lower costs
Hire only local workers by law
questions.explain: Outsourcing lowers prices but can cost jobs in the company's home country.

questions.q: The COVID-19 pandemic (starting 2020) demonstrated globalization's risks by showing how:
options: Isolated countries were hit hardest in trade only
Disease and supply shortages can spread rapidly worldwide
Air travel had no role in spread
questions.explain: A virus spread globally in weeks, and disruptions in one country idled factories in others.

questions.q: A major criticism of globalization is that it can:
options: Make all countries identical in income
Widen inequality and weaken local industries
questions.explain: Critics argue benefits are uneven, while supporters point to lower prices and growth in developing countries.

questions.q: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals aim to:
options: Address global poverty, health, education, and environment by 2030
questions.explain: The 17 goals, adopted in 2015, set shared targets for development worldwide.

questions.q: Social media has changed modern politics mainly by:
options: Removing all misinformation from public debate
Ending the role of newspapers completely
Letting movements organize and spread information rapidly outside traditional media
questions.explain: Platforms speed up organizing and news - and also the spread of misinformation.

title: Counting & Place Value
subject: Elementary Math
description: Counting by 5s and 10s, tens and ones, and what each digit in a number really means.

questions.q: What number comes right after 47?
questions.explain: Counting goes in order, so the number after 47 is 48.

questions.q: How many tens are in the number 60?
questions.explain: The digit 6 sits in the tens place, so 60 is made of 6 tens.

questions.q: In the number 35, what does the digit 3 mean?
questions.explain: Where a digit sits tells its value. The 3 in 35 is in the tens place, so it means 30.

questions.q: Which number is bigger?
questions.explain: 92 has 9 tens and 29 has only 2 tens, so 92 is much bigger.

questions.q: Count by 10s: 10, 20, 30, ... What comes next?
questions.explain: Counting by 10s adds one ten each time: 10, 20, 30, 40.

questions.q: How many tens make 100?
questions.explain: Ten groups of ten make one hundred: 10 x 10 = 100.

questions.q: In the number 84, what is the value of the digit 4?
questions.explain: The 4 is in the ones place, so it is worth 4.

questions.q: Which number has 5 tens and 2 ones?
questions.explain: 5 tens is 50 and 2 ones is 2, and 50 + 2 = 52.

questions.q: Count by 5s: 5, 10, 15, ... What comes next?
questions.explain: Counting by 5s adds five each time: 5, 10, 15, 20.

questions.q: Which of these numbers is an even number?
questions.explain: Even numbers can be split into two equal groups. 14 splits into 7 and 7, so it is even.

questions.q: What is 15 divided by 5?
questions.explain: 15 split into 5 equal groups gives 3 in each group.

questions.q: What is 18 divided by 2?
questions.explain: Half of 18 is 9, and dividing by 2 is the same as finding half.

questions.q: What is 24 divided by 6?
questions.explain: 6 x 4 = 24, so 24 divided by 6 is 4.

questions.q: Division means:
options: Splitting a number into equal groups
Adding the same number many times
questions.explain: Division shares or groups fairly: every group gets the same amount.

questions.q: What is 14 divided by 2?
questions.explain: 14 split into 2 equal groups gives 7 in each group.

questions.q: You put 11 crayons into groups of 2. How many crayons are left over?
questions.explain: Five groups of 2 use 10 crayons, so 1 crayon is left over. That leftover is called a remainder.

questions.q: If 6 x 4 = 24, what is 24 divided by 4?
questions.explain: Multiplication and division are partners. The fact 6 x 4 = 24 tells you 24 divided by 4 is 6.

rounds.title: Division Basics
rounds.desc: Sharing things equally, splitting into groups, and simple division facts with remainders.

description: Learn about halves, thirds, and quarters with yummy examples.

questions.explain: Great job! Half of 8 is 4. If you split 8 into 2 equal groups, each group has 4.
questions.q: What is 1/2 of 8?

questions.explain: Nice work! Half of 10 is 5. Two groups of 5 make 10.
questions.q: What is 1/2 of 10?

questions.explain: Well done! When something is cut into 4 equal parts, each part is called a quarter.
questions.q: If you cut a pizza into 4 equal parts, what is each part called?

questions.explain: Good thinking! A quarter of 12 is 3. Four groups of 3 make 12.
questions.q: What is 1/4 of 12?

questions.explain: Great job! A third of 9 is 3. Three groups of 3 make 9.
questions.q: What is 1/3 of 9?

questions.explain: Nice work! 1/2 is bigger. A pizza cut into 2 parts gives you a bigger slice than one cut into 4 parts.
questions.q: Which fraction is bigger: 1/2 or 1/4?

questions.explain: Well done! Half of 6 is 3. Two groups of 3 make 6.
questions.q: What is 1/2 of 6?

questions.explain: Good job! Two people sharing equally means the cake is split into 2 parts, so each person gets 1/2.
questions.q: You share a cake equally with 1 friend. How much cake does each person get?

questions.explain: Great job! A quarter of 8 is 2. Four groups of 2 make 8.
questions.q: What is 1/4 of 8?

questions.explain: Nice work! Two halves make one whole. Put two half sandwiches together and you get a full sandwich.
questions.q: How many halves make one whole?

subject: Elementary Math
title: Fractions Basics
Decimals & Money Math
subject: Elementary Math
description: Pennies, dimes, and quarters, dollar amounts, and what the numbers after a decimal point mean.

questions.q: How many cents is one dime worth?
questions.explain: A dime is worth 10 cents, so 10 dimes make a dollar.

questions.q: How many quarters make one dollar?
questions.explain: Each quarter is 25 cents, and 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100 cents, which is one dollar.

questions.q: The decimal 0.5 means the same as which fraction?
questions.explain: 0.5 is five tenths, and five tenths is the same amount as one half.

questions.q: A toy costs 30 cents and a sticker costs 20 cents. How much do they cost together?
questions.explain: Add the two prices: 30 + 20 = 50 cents.

questions.q: Which is more money?
questions.explain: 1 dollar is 100 cents, and 100 cents is more than 75 cents.

questions.q: In the amount $3.25, what does the 25 mean?
questions.explain: The numbers after the decimal point are the cents, so $3.25 is 3 dollars and 25 cents.

questions.q: You buy a snack for 40 cents and pay with 1 dollar. How much change do you get?
questions.explain: 100 cents minus 40 cents leaves 60 cents of change.

questions.q: How many pennies make one dollar?
questions.explain: Each penny is 1 cent, and a dollar is 100 cents, so it takes 100 pennies.

questions.q: What is 2 dollars plus 3 dollars?
questions.explain: 2 + 3 = 5, so you have 5 dollars in all.

questions.q: What does the decimal point in a money amount do?
options: It separates the dollars from the cents
questions.explain: Everything before the point is whole dollars, and the two digits after it are the cents.

rounds.title: Decimals & Money Math
rounds.desc: Pennies, dimes, and quarters, dollar amounts, and what the numbers after a decimal point mean.

description: Name basic shapes, count their sides, and learn about centimeters and meters.

questions.explain: Great job! A triangle has 3 sides. The word tri means three, like a tricycle with 3 wheels.
questions.q: How many sides does a triangle have?

questions.explain: Nice work! A square has 4 sides, and they are all the same length.
questions.q: How many sides does a square have?

questions.explain: Well done! A circle is round like a ball or a cookie, and it has no corners at all.
questions.q: Which shape is round and has no corners?

questions.explain: Good thinking! A rectangle has 4 sides. It looks like a long square, like a door.
questions.q: How many sides does a rectangle have?

questions.explain: Great job! 1 meter is much longer. A meter is about as long as a baseball bat, but a centimeter is as small as your fingernail.
questions.q: Which is longer: 1 meter or 1 centimeter?

questions.explain: Nice work! A triangle has 3 corners, one where each pair of sides meet.
questions.q: How many corners does a triangle have?

questions.explain: Well done! A pentagon has 5 sides. A home plate in baseball is shaped like a pentagon.
questions.q: What shape has 5 sides?

questions.explain: Good job! There are 100 centimeters in 1 meter. That is a lot of tiny centimeters in one big meter.
questions.q: How many centimeters are in 1 meter?

questions.explain: Great job! A ruler helps you measure lengths, like how long your pencil is.
questions.q: Which tool do you use to measure how long something is?

questions.explain: Nice work! A hexagon has 6 sides. Bees make hexagon shapes in their honeycombs.
questions.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?

subject: Elementary Math
title: Shapes & Measurement
Telling Time
subject: Elementary Math
description: Reading clocks, hours and minutes, half past and quarter past, and everyday time words.

questions.q: How many minutes are in one hour?
questions.explain: One full trip of the minute hand around the clock is 60 minutes, and that makes one hour.

questions.q: Half past 3 is the same as what time?
questions.explain: Half past means the minute hand has gone halfway around, which is 30 minutes after the hour.

questions.q: On a clock, the minute hand points straight up at the 12 and the hour hand points at the 5. What time is it?
questions.explain: The minute hand at the top means exactly on the hour, and the hour hand tells you it is 5 o'clock.

questions.q: How many hours are in one whole day?
questions.explain: A day runs from midnight to midnight, which is 24 hours.

questions.q: Quarter past 2 means how many minutes after 2?
questions.explain: A quarter of the clock face is 15 minutes, so quarter past 2 is 2:15.

questions.q: On an analog clock, which hand is the short one?
options: They are all the same length
questions.explain: The short hand points to the hour, and the long hand points to the minutes.

questions.q: How many days are in one week?
questions.explain: Monday through Sunday is 7 days, and then the week starts again.

questions.q: Noon is the time in the middle of the day. What time is noon on a clock?
questions.explain: Noon is 12:00 when the sun is high; midnight is also 12:00 but in the middle of the night.

questions.q: The minute hand makes one full trip around the clock. How much time has passed?
questions.explain: One full trip of the minute hand is 60 minutes, which is exactly 1 hour.

questions.q: A digital clock shows 7:30. How do you say this time in words?
questions.explain: Read the hour first, then the minutes: 7:30 is seven thirty.

rounds.title: Telling Time
rounds.desc: Reading clocks, hours and minutes, half past and quarter past, and everyday time words.

title: Graphs, Patterns & Data
subject: Elementary Math
description: Number and shape patterns, tally marks, pictographs, and reading simple bar graphs.

questions.q: What number comes next in this pattern: 2, 4, 6, 8, ...?
questions.explain: The pattern counts by 2s, so after 8 comes 10.

questions.q: A pattern goes red, blue, red, blue, red, ... What color comes next?
questions.explain: The colors take turns, and after red it is blue's turn.

questions.q: On a bar graph, what does a taller bar mean?
options: That the category is first alphabetically
questions.explain: Bar heights stand for amounts, so the tallest bar is the biggest amount.

questions.q: How many tally marks is this: a group of four lines with one line crossed over them?
questions.explain: Tally marks are bundled in groups of five to make them easy to count.

questions.q: In a pictograph, each picture stands for 2 apples. A row has 3 pictures. How many apples is that?
questions.explain: Each picture is worth 2, so 3 pictures are worth 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 apples.

questions.q: What number comes next in this pattern: 100, 90, 80, ...?
questions.explain: The pattern counts down by 10 each time: 100, 90, 80, 70.

questions.q: A class voted for a pet. The bar for dogs is the tallest. What does that tell you?
options: Every pet got the same votes
questions.explain: The tallest bar shows the biggest amount, so dogs were the most popular choice.

questions.q: 3 kids chose cats and 5 kids chose dogs. How many kids voted in all?
questions.explain: Add the two groups together: 3 + 5 = 8 kids voted.

questions.q: What number comes next in this pattern: 3, 6, 9, ...?
questions.explain: The pattern counts by 3s, so after 9 comes 12.

questions.q: On a bar graph, the shortest bar tells you:
options: The category with the biggest amount
The category with the smallest amount
questions.explain: Short means small: the shortest bar is the group with the fewest or smallest amount.

rounds.title: Graphs, Patterns & Data
rounds.desc: Number and shape patterns, tally marks, pictographs, and reading simple bar graphs.

title: Word Problems & Estimation
subject: Elementary Math
description: Story problems that mix adding, subtracting, multiplying, and sharing, plus rounding to make smart guesses.

questions.q: Mia picked 26 apples in the morning and 13 more in the afternoon. How many apples did she pick in all?
questions.explain: This is an adding story: 26 + 13 = 39 apples.

questions.q: A farmer had 45 eggs. He sold 18 of them. How many eggs does he have left?
questions.explain: Selling eggs means taking away: 45 - 18 = 27 eggs left.

questions.q: There are 4 rows of chairs with 6 chairs in each row. How many chairs are there in all?
questions.explain: Equal rows mean multiply: 4 x 6 = 24 chairs.

questions.q: 18 cookies are shared equally by 3 friends. How many cookies does each friend get?
questions.explain: Sharing equally means divide: 18 divided by 3 is 6 cookies each.

questions.q: What is one half of 14?
questions.explain: Half of 14 splits it into two equal parts of 7.

questions.q: About how much is 29 + 31? Use rounding to the nearest ten.
questions.explain: 29 rounds to 30 and 31 rounds to 30, and 30 + 30 = 60, so the answer is about 60.

questions.q: A toy costs 7 dollars. You pay with a 10 dollar bill. How much change should you get?
questions.explain: 10 - 7 = 3, so you get 3 dollars back.

questions.q: Sam has 38 marbles and Ana has 35 marbles. Who has more marbles?
questions.explain: 38 is more than 35, so Sam has more.

questions.q: Play time starts at 4:00 and lasts for 2 hours. What time does it end?
questions.explain: Count 2 hours forward from 4:00: 5:00, then 6:00.

questions.q: Leo saves 5 dollars every week. How much will he save in 4 weeks?
questions.explain: Saving the same amount each week means multiply: 5 x 4 = 20 dollars.

rounds.title: Word Problems & Estimation
rounds.desc: Story problems that mix adding, subtracting, multiplying, and sharing, plus rounding to make smart guesses.

description: Discover where animals live and what they like to eat.

questions.explain: Great job! Fish live in the water and use their gills to breathe under the surface.
questions.q: Where does a fish live?

questions.explain: Nice work! Cows eat grass. They spend lots of the day munching in green fields.
questions.q: What does a cow eat?

questions.explain: Well done! Polar bears live in the cold Arctic, where their white fur helps them blend in with the snow.
questions.q: Where does a polar bear live?

questions.explain: Good thinking! Bees make sweet honey. They collect nectar from flowers to make it.
questions.q: What do bees make?

questions.explain: Great job! Frogs like to live near ponds and water, where they can hop and swim.
questions.q: Where does a frog like to live?

questions.explain: Nice work! Pandas love to eat bamboo. They munch on it almost all day long.
questions.q: What does a panda love to eat?

questions.explain: Well done! Camels live in the desert. They can go a long time without drinking water.
questions.q: Where does a camel live?

questions.explain: Good job! Birds flap their wings to fly through the sky.
questions.q: What do birds use to fly?

questions.explain: Great job! Owls sleep in trees during the day and wake up at night to hunt.
questions.q: Where does an owl sleep during the day?

questions.explain: Nice work! A caterpillar turns into a beautiful butterfly. This big change is called metamorphosis.
questions.q: What does a caterpillar turn into?

subject: Kids Science
title: Animals & Habitats
Plants & Growth
subject: Kids Science
description: What seeds, roots, stems, and leaves do, and what plants need to grow.

questions.q: What does a seed need first to start growing (sprout)?
options: Sunlight only after it is a tree
questions.explain: A seed starts to sprout when it takes in water. Then a tiny root grows out.

questions.q: What part of the plant drinks water from the soil?
questions.explain: Roots grow underground and take in water and nutrients for the plant.

questions.q: What part of the plant makes food using sunlight?
questions.explain: Leaves use sunlight, air, and water to make food for the plant.

questions.q: What grows first from a seed?
questions.explain: A tiny root grows first so the new plant can drink water.

questions.q: Why do plants need sunlight?
questions.explain: Plants use sunlight to make food in a process called photosynthesis.

questions.q: What does the stem do?
options: Holds the plant up and carries water
questions.explain: The stem holds the plant up and carries water from the roots to the leaves.

questions.q: A gardener forgets to water a plant for many days. What will most likely happen?
options: The plant will wilt and droop
The plant will make fruit at once
questions.explain: Without water, a plant wilts because its cells lose the water that helps it stand up.

questions.q: Which of these comes from a plant?
questions.explain: Apples grow on apple trees, so they come from a plant.

questions.q: What do flowers make that can grow into new plants?
questions.explain: Flowers make seeds, and seeds can grow into new plants.

questions.q: Put in order: seed, sprout, big plant with flowers. What is in the middle?
questions.explain: First a seed, then a sprout, then a big plant - so the sprout is in the middle.

rounds.title: Plants & Growth
rounds.desc: What seeds, roots, stems, and leaves do, and what plants need to grow.

title: Five Senses
subject: Kids Science
description: Use sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch to observe the world like a scientist.

questions.q: Which sense do you use to tell that a lemon is sour?
questions.explain: Your tongue tastes sour, sweet, salty, bitter, and savory flavors.

questions.q: Which body part is most important for the sense of hearing?
questions.explain: Sound travels into your ears, which send hearing signals to your brain.

questions.q: You feel that one rock is rough and another is smooth. Which sense is that?
questions.explain: Touch lets you feel roughness, smoothness, temperature, and pressure through your skin.

questions.q: Which sense helps you stay safe by warning you that milk has gone bad?
questions.explain: A bad smell can warn you that food has spoiled before you taste it.

questions.q: A scientist looks closely at a leaf with a magnifying glass. Which sense is she using most?
questions.explain: Looking closely is using sight to observe details.

questions.q: Which taste describes potato chips best?
questions.explain: Potato chips are mainly salty.

questions.q: Why do we have two eyes instead of one?
options: Two eyes let us hear better
Two eyes help us judge how far away things are
One eye is only for sleeping
questions.explain: Two eyes give slightly different views, helping the brain judge distance.

questions.q: Which of these is something you observe with hearing, not sight?
questions.explain: Singing is a sound, so you observe it with hearing.

questions.q: Your skin can feel all of these EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Skin feels temperature and texture. Colors are seen with the eyes, not felt.

questions.q: Touch, taste, smell, sight, and hearing help scientists do what?
questions.explain: Scientists use their senses to make careful observations before drawing conclusions.

rounds.title: Five Senses
rounds.desc: Use sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch to observe the world like a scientist.

description: Learn about rain, snow, rainbows, and why the seasons change.

questions.explain: Great job! Rain is water drops falling from clouds in the sky. Grab an umbrella!
questions.q: What falls from the sky when it rains?

questions.explain: Nice work! In the fall, leaves turn red, orange, and yellow, and then they fall to the ground.
questions.q: In which season do leaves fall off the trees?

questions.explain: Well done! Winter is the coldest season. That is when we might get snow and ice.
questions.q: Which season is the coldest?

questions.explain: Good thinking! A warm coat, hat, and gloves keep you cozy when it snows.
questions.q: What should you wear when it is snowing?

questions.explain: Great job! In spring, the weather warms up and flowers start to bloom.
questions.q: In which season do flowers start to grow?

questions.explain: Nice work! The Earth is tilted, so as it travels around the Sun, different parts get more sunshine at different times of year.
options: Because the Earth is tilted as it goes around the Sun
Because the Sun moves far away
questions.q: Why do we have different seasons?

questions.explain: Well done! A rainbow appears when sunlight shines through raindrops. Look for one after it rains on a sunny day.
questions.q: What makes a rainbow appear in the sky?

questions.explain: Good job! Summer is the hottest season. It is a great time for swimming and ice cream.
questions.q: Which season is the hottest?

questions.explain: Great job! Snow is made of tiny pieces of frozen water called snowflakes. No two snowflakes look exactly the same.
questions.q: What is snow made of?

questions.explain: Nice work! In spring, trees grow fresh new green leaves after their winter rest.
questions.q: What do trees grow in the spring?

subject: Kids Science
title: Weather & Seasons
The Water Cycle
subject: Kids Science
description: Follow water as it evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and collects again.

questions.q: What is it called when the Sun heats water and it rises into the air as an invisible gas?
questions.explain: Evaporation is when liquid water turns into water vapor and rises.

questions.q: Clouds form when water vapor cools and turns back into tiny liquid drops. This is called:
questions.explain: Condensation is gas turning back into liquid - that is how cloud drops form.

questions.q: Rain, snow, sleet, and hail are all forms of:
questions.explain: Precipitation is water falling from clouds to the ground.

questions.q: After rain falls, water collects in lakes, rivers, and oceans. This step is called:
questions.explain: Collection is water gathering in bodies of water, ready to evaporate again.

questions.q: Where does the energy that drives the water cycle come from?
questions.explain: The Sun heats water and powers evaporation, driving the whole cycle.

questions.q: You see drops of water on the outside of a cold glass on a warm day. Those drops formed by:
options: Condensation of water vapor in the air
questions.explain: Water vapor in warm air cooled on the glass and condensed into drops.

questions.q: Snow melts in spring and the water runs into a stream. Melting is water changing from:
questions.explain: Melting changes solid ice or snow into liquid water.

questions.q: What happens to a puddle on a hot, sunny sidewalk?
questions.explain: Heat makes puddle water evaporate, so the puddle shrinks.

questions.q: In the water cycle, water that soaks into the ground is called:
questions.explain: Water stored underground in soil and rock is groundwater.

questions.q: Why is the water cycle called a cycle?
options: Water keeps moving through the steps again and again
questions.explain: A cycle repeats: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection happen over and over.

rounds.title: The Water Cycle
rounds.desc: Follow water as it evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and collects again.

description: Meet the Sun, the Moon, and the eight planets.

questions.explain: Great job! We live on planet Earth, the blue planet full of water and life.
questions.q: Which planet do we live on?

questions.explain: Nice work! The Sun is a star that gives us light and warmth every day.
questions.q: What is the big, hot, bright ball in the sky during the day?

questions.explain: Well done! Mars is called the Red Planet because its rocks and dust look red.
questions.q: Which planet is called the Red Planet?

questions.explain: Good thinking! The Moon travels around the Earth. That is why it looks a little different each night.
questions.q: What travels around the Earth?

questions.explain: Great job! Saturn has big, beautiful rings made of ice and rock.
questions.q: Which planet has big rings around it?

questions.explain: Nice work! There are 8 planets in our solar system, and Earth is one of them.
questions.q: How many planets are in our solar system?

questions.explain: Well done! Jupiter is the biggest planet. More than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.
questions.q: Which planet is the biggest of all?

questions.explain: Good job! A planet's path around the Sun is called its orbit. Earth takes one whole year to go around once.
questions.q: What do we call the path a planet takes around the Sun?

questions.explain: Great job! The Moon shines at night. It does not make its own light; it reflects light from the Sun.
questions.q: At night, what shines in the sky besides the stars?

questions.explain: Nice work! Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, so it is very hot during its day.
questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?

subject: Kids Science
title: The Solar System
Earth & Moon
subject: Kids Science
description: Day and night, the Moon's changing shape, seasons on Earth, and why we see stars at night.

questions.q: What causes day and night on Earth?
options: The Moon blocking the Sun all day
questions.explain: Earth rotates once about every 24 hours, so each side takes turns facing the Sun.

questions.q: How long does it take Earth to go all the way around the Sun once?
questions.explain: One full orbit around the Sun takes about 365 days - one year.

questions.q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape during the month?
options: We see different amounts of its sunlit side
The Moon spins into different shapes
questions.explain: The Moon's phases happen because we see different parts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth.

questions.q: When the whole face of the Moon looks bright and round, it is called a:
questions.explain: A Full Moon is when the whole sunlit face is visible from Earth.

questions.q: What is the Moon?
options: Earth's natural satellite - a rocky body that orbits Earth
questions.explain: The Moon is a rocky natural satellite that orbits Earth.

questions.q: Why can we see the Moon at night even though it does not make its own light?
questions.explain: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight toward Earth.

questions.q: Earth's axis is tilted. That tilt is the main reason we have:
questions.explain: Earth's tilt plus its orbit makes different areas get more direct sunlight at different times of year.

questions.q: How long does the Moon take to orbit Earth once?
questions.explain: The Moon orbits Earth in about 27 to 29 days - roughly one month.

questions.q: When it is daytime where you live, the other side of Earth is having:
questions.explain: Earth's far side faces away from the Sun, so it is nighttime there.

questions.q: A solar eclipse happens when:
options: Earth passes in front of a star
The Moon passes between Earth and the Sun and blocks sunlight
questions.explain: During a solar eclipse, the Moon blocks the Sun's light for a short time in some places.

rounds.title: Earth & Moon
rounds.desc: Day and night, the Moon's changing shape, seasons on Earth, and why we see stars at night.

title: Magnets in Action
subject: Kids Science
description: See what magnets attract, learn about poles, and find magnets in everyday life.

questions.q: A magnet will attract (pull) which of these?
questions.explain: Magnets attract iron and steel. Wood, plastic, and rubber are not attracted.

questions.q: What are the two ends of a magnet called?
questions.explain: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.

questions.q: If you bring the north pole of one magnet near the north pole of another, what happens?
questions.explain: Like poles repel: north pushes north away, and south pushes south away.

questions.q: If you bring a north pole near a south pole, what happens?
questions.explain: Opposite poles attract: north and south pull together.

questions.q: Which tool uses a magnet to always point north?
questions.explain: A compass needle is a small magnet that lines up with Earth and points north.

questions.q: A magnet can pull a paper clip even through a sheet of paper because:
options: Magnetic force can act through some materials
questions.explain: Magnetic force can pass through paper and some other thin materials.

questions.q: If you cut a bar magnet in half, what do you get?
options: One north-only piece and one south-only piece
Two smaller magnets, each with north and south poles
One magnet and one plain bar
questions.explain: Each piece is a complete magnet with its own north and south poles.

questions.q: Which of these would a magnet NOT pick up?
questions.explain: Wood is not magnetic, so a magnet will not pick up a wooden toothpick.

questions.q: Fridge magnets stay on the fridge because the fridge door is usually made of:
questions.explain: Most fridge doors are steel, and magnets attract steel.

questions.q: What happens if you sprinkle iron filings around a magnet on paper?
options: They line up in a pattern showing the magnetic field
They all jump off the paper
questions.explain: Iron filings line up along the invisible magnetic field lines around the magnet.

rounds.title: Magnets in Action
rounds.desc: See what magnets attract, learn about poles, and find magnets in everyday life.

title: Dinosaurs & Fossils
subject: Kids Science
description: Meet plant-eating and meat-eating dinosaurs and learn how fossils tell their story.

questions.q: What is a fossil?
options: Preserved remains or traces of a living thing from long ago
A type of rock with no history
A dinosaur egg that just hatched
questions.explain: Fossils are bones, footprints, or other traces preserved in rock over millions of years.

questions.q: Scientists who study fossils are called:
questions.explain: Paleontologists dig up and study fossils to learn about ancient life.

questions.q: Tyrannosaurus rex ate meat. An animal that eats meat is called a:
questions.explain: Carnivores eat meat. T. rex had sharp teeth for tearing meat.

questions.q: Triceratops ate plants. An animal that eats plants is called a:
questions.explain: Herbivores eat plants. Triceratops had a beak and flat teeth for plants.

questions.q: How do scientists know dinosaurs are extinct?
options: No living dinosaurs (except birds) are found, only fossils
All dinosaurs turned into rocks at once
questions.explain: Dinosaurs other than birds died out about 66 million years ago; we know them from fossils.

questions.q: A dinosaur footprint preserved in rock is a type of fossil that tells scientists:
options: What color the dinosaur was exactly
How the dinosaur walked and how big its feet were
questions.explain: Trace fossils like footprints show behavior, such as walking and stride.

questions.q: Most dinosaur fossils are found in:
options: Ice at the North Pole only
questions.explain: Fossils form when remains are buried in sediment that hardens into rock layers.

questions.q: Which dinosaur had plates on its back and spikes on its tail?
questions.explain: Stegosaurus is known for the bony plates along its back and a spiked tail.

questions.q: Birds are special in the dinosaur story because scientists think:
options: Birds are older than all dinosaurs
Birds descended from small feathered dinosaurs
Birds never lived with dinosaurs at all
questions.explain: Evidence from feathered fossils shows birds evolved from small theropod dinosaurs.

questions.q: If a paleontologist finds a fossil tooth that is sharp and pointed, the dinosaur most likely:
questions.explain: Sharp, pointed teeth are built for cutting meat, suggesting a meat eater.

rounds.title: Dinosaurs & Fossils
rounds.desc: Meet plant-eating and meat-eating dinosaurs and learn how fossils tell their story.

title: Simple Experiments
subject: Kids Science
description: Ask a question, make a prediction, test fairly, observe, and share what you learned.

questions.q: In an experiment, a prediction you can test is called a:
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a testable prediction: what you think will happen and why.

questions.q: You test which plant food works best. To make it a fair test, you should change:
options: Only one thing - the plant food - and keep the rest the same
The plants, water, light, and food all together
questions.explain: In a fair test, change only one variable so you know what caused the result.

questions.q: After an experiment, the part where you explain what you learned is the:
questions.explain: A conclusion sums up whether the results supported your prediction and what you learned.

questions.q: You drop a ball and time how long it takes to fall, three times. Why repeat the test?
options: To check that the result happens again and is not a mistake
To make the ball fall faster
Because one try is always wrong
questions.explain: Repeating trials makes results more trustworthy and catches mistakes.

questions.q: Which is an observation, not an opinion?
options: The plant grew 3 centimeters this week
questions.explain: A measurement like 3 centimeters is an observation; prettiest and best are opinions.

questions.q: A student wants to know if ice melts faster in sun or shade. What is the one thing she should change?
options: The size of the ice, the cup, and the place
The time of day and the ice
Where the ice sits - sun versus shade
questions.explain: She should place matching ice in sun versus shade, changing only the location's light.

questions.q: Recording your measurements in a table helps you:
options: See patterns and compare results clearly
questions.explain: Tables organize data so patterns and comparisons are easy to see.

questions.q: In an experiment on paper planes, the distance each plane flies is the:
questions.explain: The flight distance is the outcome you measure to compare the planes.

questions.q: If your results do NOT match your hypothesis, you should:
options: Report the real results and think about why
Say the experiment did not count
questions.explain: Honest science reports real results; a wrong prediction still teaches you something.

questions.q: Which question can be answered with an experiment?
options: Does a magnet attract a copper penny?
questions.explain: Does a magnet attract a copper penny can be tested directly. Best and fun are opinions.

rounds.title: Simple Experiments
rounds.desc: Ask a question, make a prediction, test fairly, observe, and share what you learned.

description: Beginning sounds and rhyming words for young readers.

questions.explain: Sun and sand both start with the 's' sound.
questions.q: Which word starts with the same sound as 'sun'?

questions.explain: Cat and hat both end with the 'at' sound.
questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'cat'?

questions.explain: Bear starts with 'b', just like ball and book.
questions.q: Which word starts with the 'b' sound?

questions.explain: Pig and wig both end with the 'ig' sound.
questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'pig'?

questions.explain: The letter M says 'mmm', like in moon, mouse, and milk.
questions.q: What sound does the letter M make at the start of 'moon'?

questions.explain: Fish and frog both start with the 'f' sound.
questions.q: Which word starts with the same sound as 'fish'?

questions.explain: Dog and frog both end with the 'og' sound.
questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'dog'?

questions.explain: Top starts with 't', just like tiger and turtle.
questions.q: Which word starts with the 't' sound?

questions.explain: Sun and fun both end with the 'un' sound.
questions.q: Which word rhymes with 'sun'?

questions.explain: Apple and ant both start with the short 'a' sound.
questions.q: Which word starts with the same sound as 'apple'?

subject: Kids Reading
title: Phonics & Sounds
Sight Words
subject: Kids Reading
description: Learn the common little words you see in almost every sentence, like the, and, and was.

questions.q: Which word completes the sentence: ___ dog is brown.
questions.explain: The is a sight word. You learn it by sight because you see it in almost every story.

questions.q: Which word completes the sentence: I ___ a red ball.
questions.explain: See fits the sentence: I see a red ball. Sight words help sentences make sense.

questions.q: Which of these is a sight word you should know by sight?
questions.explain: Was is a common sight word. It does not follow simple sounding-out rules, so you memorize it.

questions.q: Which word completes the sentence: She ___ my friend.
questions.explain: Is completes the sentence: She is my friend.

questions.q: Which word completes the sentence: You and ___ can play.
questions.explain: I completes the sentence: You and I can play.

questions.q: Which sight word means the opposite of out in this sentence: Come ___ the house.
questions.explain: In is the sight word that fits: Come in the house.

questions.q: Which word completes the sentence: He ___ to school every day.
questions.explain: Goes completes the sentence: He goes to school every day.

questions.q: In the sentence 'We like to play,' which word is a sight word that means enjoy?
questions.explain: Like can be a sight word and here it means enjoy. We and to are also sight words, but only like means enjoy.

questions.q: Which word completes the sentence: ___ you ready to go?
questions.explain: Are starts the question: Are you ready to go?

questions.q: Which sight word completes both sentences: ___ is my book. ___ is fun to read.
questions.explain: It completes both: It is my book. It is fun to read.

rounds.title: Sight Words
rounds.desc: Learn the common little words you see in almost every sentence, like the, and, and was.

description: Pick the word that is spelled the right way.

questions.explain: Apple is spelled A-P-P-L-E.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'apple' is correct?

questions.explain: Cat is spelled C-A-T.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'cat' is correct?

questions.explain: Dog is spelled D-O-G.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'dog' is correct?

questions.explain: Fish is spelled F-I-S-H.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'fish' is correct?

questions.explain: Sun is spelled S-U-N.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'sun' is correct?

questions.explain: Bird is spelled B-I-R-D.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'bird' is correct?

questions.explain: Tree is spelled T-R-E-E.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'tree' is correct?

questions.explain: Book is spelled B-O-O-K, with two O's in the middle.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'book' is correct?

questions.explain: Milk is spelled M-I-L-K.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'milk' is correct?

questions.explain: House is spelled H-O-U-S-E.
questions.q: Which spelling of the word 'house' is correct?

subject: Kids Reading
title: Easy Spelling
Rhyming Words
subject: Kids Reading
description: Find words that end with the same sound, group word families, and pick the word that does not rhyme.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with cake?
questions.explain: Cake and make end with the same ake sound, so they rhyme.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with bear?
questions.explain: Bear and chair end with the same air sound.

questions.q: Which word belongs in the -op family with top and hop?
questions.explain: Mop, top, and hop all end in op.

questions.q: Which word does NOT rhyme with light?
questions.explain: Night, bright, and flight rhyme with light. Boat has a different ending sound.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with fox?
questions.explain: Fox and box end with the same ox sound.

questions.q: Which word completes the rhyme: The cat sat, and wore a ___?
questions.explain: Hat rhymes with cat and sat, so it completes the rhyme.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with spoon?
questions.explain: Moon rhymes with spoon. Both end with the oon sound.

questions.q: Which pair are rhyming words?
questions.explain: Rain and train end with the same ain sound, so they rhyme.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with play?
questions.explain: Play and day end with the same ay sound.

questions.q: A poet writes: 'The bee in the tree is free.' Which word rhymes with bee, tree, and free?
questions.explain: Sea ends with the same ee sound as bee, tree, and free.

rounds.title: Rhyming Words
rounds.desc: Find words that end with the same sound, group word families, and pick the word that does not rhyme.

description: Learn what everyday words mean.

questions.explain: Brave means you are not afraid, even when something is hard or scary.
questions.q: What does 'brave' mean?

questions.explain: Tiny means very small. An ant is tiny!
questions.q: What does 'tiny' mean?

questions.explain: Gigantic means very, very big. An elephant is gigantic.
questions.q: What does 'gigantic' mean?

questions.explain: To whisper means to talk very quietly, so only someone close can hear.
questions.q: What does 'whisper' mean?

questions.explain: Happy means you feel glad and good inside.
questions.q: What does 'happy' mean?

questions.explain: To begin means to start something, like beginning a race.
questions.q: What does 'begin' mean?

questions.explain: Rapid means very fast, like a rapid river.
questions.q: What does 'rapid' mean?

questions.explain: To shout means to yell in a loud voice.
questions.q: What does 'shout' mean?

questions.explain: Gentle means soft and kind, like petting a kitten gently.
questions.q: What does 'gentle' mean?

questions.explain: Ancient means very, very old, like ancient castles from long ago.
questions.q: What does 'ancient' mean?

subject: Kids Reading
title: Word Meanings
Building Sentences
subject: Kids Reading
description: Put words in order, find who or what a sentence is about, and choose the sentence that makes sense.

questions.q: Which group of words is a complete sentence?
questions.explain: A complete sentence tells who or what and what happened: The dog runs fast.

questions.q: What is the naming part (who or what) in the sentence: The little frog jumps?
questions.explain: The naming part tells who or what the sentence is about: The little frog.

questions.q: Which words put this sentence in the right order: park / to / went / Sam / the
options: To the park Sam went is wrong order
questions.explain: Words must be in an order that makes sense: Sam went to the park.

questions.q: Which sentence makes sense?
options: The tree flew over the bird.
The bird flew over the tree.
questions.explain: Only the first sentence puts the bird, the action, and the place in a sensible order.

questions.q: What does a sentence always need to begin with?
questions.explain: Every sentence begins with a capital letter.

questions.q: Which word is the action word in: Mia kicks the ball?
questions.explain: Kicks tells what Mia does, so it is the action word.

questions.q: Which is a telling sentence?
questions.explain: A telling sentence gives information and ends with a period.

questions.q: Combine the ideas: Ben has a kite. The kite is red. Which sentence is best?
questions.explain: Combining short ideas can make one clear sentence: Ben has a red kite.

questions.q: Which sentence asks a question?
questions.explain: A question asks something and ends with a question mark.

questions.q: What is missing from this sentence: ___ runs to school.
questions.explain: Runs tells the action, but the sentence does not say who runs, so the naming part is missing.

rounds.title: Building Sentences
rounds.desc: Put words in order, find who or what a sentence is about, and choose the sentence that makes sense.

title: Punctuation for Kids
subject: Kids Reading
description: Learn when to use a period, question mark, exclamation point, capital letter, and comma.

questions.q: Which mark ends this sentence: Where is my hat
questions.explain: Where is my hat asks a question, so it ends with a question mark.

questions.q: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.explain: Names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter: Sam has a pet fish.

questions.q: Which mark shows strong feeling in: Watch out
questions.explain: An exclamation point shows strong feeling or a strong warning: Watch out!

questions.q: Where does a comma belong: I need pencils paper and crayons.
questions.explain: Use commas to separate items in a list: pencils, paper, and crayons.

questions.q: Which mark ends a telling sentence: Birds can fly
questions.explain: A telling sentence ends with a period.

questions.q: Which word should start with a capital letter: I live in texas.
options: texas - it is a place name
questions.explain: Place names like Texas start with a capital letter.

questions.q: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly to show belonging?
options: The dogs' bowl is blue for one dog
questions.explain: Dog's with an apostrophe shows the bowl belongs to one dog.

questions.q: What does the apostrophe do in the word can't?
options: It takes the place of a missing letter
questions.explain: In can't, the apostrophe takes the place of the missing letters in cannot.

questions.q: Which sentence is a question written correctly?
questions.explain: A question starts with a capital letter and ends with a question mark.
