title: Investing Basics
subject: Financial Literacy
description: Discover what stocks, bonds, and index funds are, why investing is long-term, and how risk and reward go together.

questions.q: What does it mean to invest?
options: To put money into something hoping it grows in value over time
To hide cash in a drawer
To lend money and never expect it back
questions.explain: Investing aims to grow money over years by owning things like stocks or funds. It carries risk, unlike insured savings.

questions.q: What is a stock?
options: A small piece of ownership in a company
questions.explain: Buying a stock makes you a part owner of that company. Its value rises and falls with the company and the market.

questions.q: What is a bond?
options: A loan you make to a company or government that pays you interest
A savings certificate you cannot sell
questions.explain: Bond buyers lend money and receive interest payments plus their principal back later. Bonds are usually steadier than stocks but grow more slowly.

questions.q: What is diversification?
options: Putting all money into one stock
Spreading money across different investments so one loss hurts less
questions.explain: Diversification lowers risk because different investments do not all fall at once. It is the idea of not putting all eggs in one basket.

questions.q: What is an index fund?
options: A fund that owns many stocks at once to match a market index
A single stock picked by an expert
A bank account with a fixed rate
A list of companies on paper only
questions.explain: Index funds hold hundreds of companies in one purchase, giving instant diversification. They are a common beginner-friendly choice.

questions.q: Why do long time horizons help investors?
options: Prices can only go up over time
Short-term ups and downs matter less when money stays invested for years
Banks add secret bonuses after ten years
questions.explain: Markets swing in the short run but have historically recovered over long periods. Time does not remove risk, it just smooths the ride.

questions.q: Nia invests 1,000 dollars and it grows 10 percent in a year. How much is it worth before any fees or taxes?
questions.explain: Ten percent of 1,000 is 100, so the value becomes 1,100 dollars. Gains are never guaranteed and values can also fall.

questions.q: What is the relationship between risk and possible reward in investing?
options: More risk always means guaranteed profit
Risk and reward are never related
Safe investments always pay the most
Higher possible rewards usually come with higher risk of loss
questions.explain: Investments promising big returns can also lose big. Match your risk level to your goals and timeline.

questions.q: A friend guarantees an investment will double your money in one month with no risk. What should you think?
options: That is a major warning sign of a scam
It sounds like a normal index fund
Only banks can offer that deal
questions.explain: No legitimate investment guarantees high returns with no risk. Guaranteed quick riches is one of the most common scam signals.

questions.q: What is the best first investing step for most teens with a job?
options: Borrow money to buy one hot stock
Build a small emergency fund, then invest small amounts regularly for the long term
Put rent money into crypto this week
questions.explain: A safety cushion comes before investing so surprises never force you to sell. Then small, steady, diversified investing builds the habit.

title: Insurance Essentials
subject: Financial Literacy
description: Learn how insurance shares risk, what premiums and deductibles mean, and which kinds of coverage protect people every day.

questions.q: What is the basic idea of insurance?
options: One person pays for everyone else
Many people pay into a pool that helps the few who face a big loss
A savings account that doubles yearly
A way to avoid all accidents
questions.explain: Insurance spreads risk across many customers so one emergency does not ruin one family. The company pays covered claims from the pool.

questions.q: What is an insurance premium?
options: The amount the insurer pays you after a claim
A one-time fee for a drivers license
The regular payment you make to keep your coverage active
The total value of your car
questions.explain: Premiums are usually paid monthly or yearly to keep a policy active. Missing payments can cancel your coverage.

questions.q: What is a deductible?
options: The full cost of every repair
A discount the insurer gives you
The amount you pay yourself before insurance starts paying
questions.explain: If your deductible is 500 dollars, you pay the first 500 dollars of a covered loss. Higher deductibles usually mean lower premiums.

questions.q: Your car repair after a covered accident costs 1,800 dollars and your deductible is 500 dollars. How much does insurance pay?
questions.explain: Subtract your deductible from the cost: 1,800 minus 500 equals 1,300 dollars paid by insurance. You pay the 500 dollar deductible.

questions.q: Which type of insurance helps pay medical bills?
questions.explain: Health insurance helps cover doctor visits, hospital care, and prescriptions. Most states also require auto insurance for drivers.

questions.q: Why do states require drivers to carry auto liability insurance?
options: So a driver who causes a crash can help pay for others injuries and damage
questions.explain: Liability coverage protects other people from costs you cause. Driving uninsured can bring fines and personal debt.

questions.q: What does renters insurance typically cover?
options: Your belongings inside a rented home if they are stolen or damaged
questions.explain: Renters insurance is usually inexpensive and protects your clothes, electronics, and furniture. It often includes liability coverage too.

questions.q: Which choice would usually lower an auto insurance premium?
options: Choosing a higher deductible and keeping a clean driving record
Letting coverage lapse for a month
questions.explain: Insurers charge less when you take on more of the risk with a higher deductible and drive safely. Tickets and crashes raise premiums.

questions.q: A phone costs 800 dollars. A protection plan costs 15 dollars a month for 2 years, which totals 360 dollars, plus a 99 dollar claim fee. What is the total cost if you file one claim?
questions.explain: Add 360 plus 99 to get 459 dollars, more than half the phone price. Doing this math helps you judge whether a plan is worth it.

questions.q: When is buying insurance a smart move?
options: When the item is cheap and easy to replace
When a salesperson pressures you for one minute only
When a loss would be too big to pay for on your own
When you do not understand the policy at all
questions.explain: Insurance is for losses that would seriously hurt your finances, like a hospital stay or a totaled car. Small, affordable losses are often cheaper to self-cover.

title: Scams, Fraud and Future Planning
subject: Financial Literacy
description: Spot phishing, fake deals, and identity theft warning signs, then set goals and a simple plan that turns todays habits into future security.

questions.q: What is phishing?
options: A fake message that tries to trick you into sharing passwords or personal data
A safe way to reset passwords
questions.explain: Phishing messages copy real companies to steal logins and card numbers. Always reach the company through its official app or site, not the message link.

questions.q: A text says your bank account is locked and asks you to tap a link and enter your password within one hour. What is the safest response?
options: Tap quickly before time runs out
Reply with your password to prove it is you
Forward the text to friends to warn them by tapping the link
Do not tap the link; contact the bank through its official app or the number on your card
questions.explain: Urgency and surprise links are classic scam tools. Going directly to the official source lets you check safely.

questions.q: What is identity theft?
options: When someone uses your personal information to open accounts or buy things in your name
questions.explain: Identity thieves use stolen details like Social Security numbers to commit fraud. Guarding that data and checking statements helps catch it early.

questions.q: Which password is the strongest?
options: Your pets name and birth year
A long passphrase of random words plus numbers and symbols
The same short password used everywhere
questions.explain: Length and uniqueness make passwords hard to crack. Using a different password for each account limits damage if one leaks.

questions.q: What does two-factor authentication add to an account?
options: A second password you tell friends
A second step, like a code sent to your phone, beyond your password
A backup copy of your password online
questions.explain: Two-factor authentication means a stolen password alone is not enough to break in. Turn it on for email, banking, and social accounts.

questions.q: A stranger online offers to send you a 1,000 dollar check if you send back 200 dollars in gift cards. What is this?
options: A safe way to earn quick money
A scam; the check will bounce and the gift cards will be gone
questions.explain: Fake check scams leave you owing the bank after the check bounces. Gift card payments are untraceable, which is why scammers demand them.

questions.q: What is a smart long-term financial goal for a teen?
options: Saving a set amount each month toward a first car or college costs
Having no plan and spending whatever is left
Keeping all money under a mattress forever
questions.explain: A written goal with a monthly amount turns saving into a habit. Specific goals are easier to reach than vague wishes.

questions.q: You want to save 1,200 dollars for a laptop in 12 months. How much should you set aside each month?
questions.explain: Divide 1,200 by 12 to get 100 dollars per month. Breaking a big goal into monthly steps makes it manageable.

questions.q: What is retirement saving, in simple terms?
options: A fee you pay when you quit a job
A loan you take at age 65
Putting money aside during your working years to live on when you stop working
questions.explain: Retirement accounts grow over decades, which is why starting young is powerful. Compound growth does much of the heavy lifting.

questions.q: Marta gets a call from someone claiming to be tech support who asks her to install software so they can fix her computer. What should she do?
options: Install it quickly so the problem does not spread
Give them her bank details to pay for the fix
Let them stay connected while she shops online
Hang up and contact the real company herself if she is worried
questions.explain: Real tech companies do not cold-call and demand remote access or payment. Hanging up and calling the official number keeps you in control.

title: Measuring Motion
subject: Physics Basics
description: Distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and reading simple motion from numbers and graphs.

questions.q: A runner covers 400 meters in 50 seconds. What is the average speed?
questions.explain: Speed equals distance divided by time: 400 divided by 50 equals 8 meters per second.

questions.q: A student walks 30 meters east, then 10 meters west. What is the displacement?
questions.explain: Displacement is final minus starting position: 30 east minus 10 west equals 20 meters east. Distance walked was 40 meters.

questions.q: Velocity differs from speed because velocity also includes:
questions.explain: Velocity is speed with direction, such as 10 meters per second north.

questions.q: On a distance-time graph, a flat horizontal line means the object is:
questions.explain: If distance does not change as time passes, the object is at rest.

questions.q: A bus travels at a constant 15 meters per second for 20 seconds. How far does it go?
questions.explain: Distance equals speed times time: 15 times 20 equals 300 meters.

questions.q: Which is a vector quantity?
options: Velocity - it has magnitude and direction
questions.explain: Vectors have magnitude and direction. Velocity is a vector; speed, distance, and time are scalars.

questions.q: A cyclist's speed changes from rest in a straight line. Her position graph curves upward more steeply over time. This shows she is:
questions.explain: A distance-time graph that gets steeper shows speed is increasing.

questions.q: Instantaneous speed is:
options: The total distance divided by total time for a whole trip
The speed at one exact moment
The same as average speed on every trip
questions.explain: Instantaneous speed is what a speedometer shows at a single moment.

questions.q: A car goes 120 km in 2 hours, then 60 km in 1 hour. What is its average speed for the whole trip?
questions.explain: Total distance 180 km divided by total time 3 hours equals 60 km per hour.

questions.q: An object moves in a full circle and returns to its start. Its total displacement is:
questions.explain: Displacement depends only on start and end points. Returning to the start makes displacement zero, even though distance is not zero.

questions.explain: Speed = distance / time = 100 / 2 = 50 mph.
questions.q: A car travels 100 miles in 2 hours. What is its average speed?

questions.explain: Gravity is the force that pulls objects toward the center of the Earth.
questions.q: What force pulls objects toward the Earth?

questions.explain: Friction acts between surfaces that touch and always works against sliding motion.
options: A force that opposes motion between touching surfaces
A force that speeds objects up

questions.explain: This is also called the law of inertia: no net force means no change in motion.
options: Every action has an opposite reaction
Objects in motion stay in motion unless a force acts on them
questions.q: Newton's first law says:

questions.explain: F = m x a: force equals mass times acceleration.
questions.q: Newton's second law is written as:
You push a 2 kg box with a force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?

questions.explain: When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with equal force.
options: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
Objects at rest stay at rest

questions.explain: Speed = 60 / 10 = 6 m/s.
questions.q: A skateboarder rolls 60 meters in 10 seconds. What is the average speed?

questions.explain: Inertia is why you lurch forward when a car suddenly brakes.
options: An object's resistance to changes in its motion
questions.q: What is inertia?

questions.explain: Greater mass needs greater force for the same acceleration (F = m x a), and a car has far more mass than a bike.

subject: Physics Basics
title: Motion & Forces
Acceleration & Speed Changes
subject: Physics Basics
description: Acceleration as change in velocity, multi-step problems, and interpreting velocity-time graphs.

questions.q: A car accelerates from 10 meters per second to 30 meters per second in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration?
questions.explain: Acceleration equals change in velocity divided by time: (30 minus 10) divided by 5 equals 4 meters per second squared.

questions.q: A bike slows from 12 meters per second to rest in 4 seconds. Its acceleration is:
options: 3 meters per second squared with speed increasing
questions.explain: Change is 0 minus 12 equals -12. Divided by 4 equals -3 meters per second squared; the negative sign shows slowing in the chosen direction.

questions.q: Starting from rest, an object accelerates at 2 meters per second squared for 6 seconds. Its final velocity is:
questions.explain: Final velocity equals acceleration times time from rest: 2 times 6 equals 12 meters per second.

questions.q: Using v squared style reasoning without symbols: a car at 20 meters per second brakes at 4 meters per second squared. How long until it stops?
questions.explain: Time equals change in velocity divided by deceleration: 20 divided by 4 equals 5 seconds.

questions.q: On a velocity-time graph, the slope of the line tells you the:
questions.explain: Slope of velocity versus time is change in velocity per time, which is acceleration.

questions.q: The area under a velocity-time graph tells you the:
questions.explain: Area under velocity-time (velocity times time) gives displacement.

questions.q: A sprinter reaches 9 meters per second in 3 seconds from rest, then holds that speed for 7 seconds. Total distance is closest to:
options: 76.5 meters - 13.5 during acceleration plus 63 at constant speed
questions.explain: During acceleration average speed is 4.5, times 3 equals 13.5 meters. Then 9 times 7 equals 63 meters. Total equals 76.5 meters.

questions.q: An object in free fall near Earth (ignoring air resistance) accelerates at about:
questions.explain: Gravity accelerates falling objects at about 9.8 meters per second squared near Earth's surface.

questions.q: A dropped ball (from rest, no air resistance) falls for 3 seconds. Its speed is about:
questions.explain: Speed equals g times t: 9.8 times 3 equals 29.4 meters per second.

questions.q: A train moving at 25 meters per second accelerates at 1.5 meters per second squared for 10 seconds. Its final speed is:
questions.explain: Final velocity equals initial plus a times t: 25 plus 1.5 times 10 equals 25 plus 15 equals 40 meters per second.

title: Newton's Laws in Action
subject: Physics Basics
description: Apply inertia, F equals m times a, and action-reaction to everyday scenarios and calculations.

questions.q: A 5 kg object accelerates at 3 meters per second squared. The net force is:
questions.explain: Net force equals mass times acceleration: 5 times 3 equals 15 newtons.

questions.q: A net force of 100 newtons acts on a 20 kg cart. Its acceleration is:
questions.explain: Acceleration equals force divided by mass: 100 divided by 20 equals 5 meters per second squared.

questions.q: A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes hard. This is best explained by:
options: Inertia - the body tends to keep moving (Newton's first law)
questions.explain: Inertia keeps the passenger moving forward while the bus slows - Newton's first law.

questions.q: When a rocket pushes exhaust gases down, the gases push the rocket up. This is:
options: Newton's third law - action and reaction
questions.explain: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction - Newton's third law.

questions.q: Two skaters push off each other. Skater A is 40 kg, skater B is 80 kg. Who accelerates more (same push force)?
options: Skater A - half the mass, so twice the acceleration
questions.explain: With the same force, acceleration equals force divided by mass, so the lighter skater accelerates twice as much.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. The force pair for the book's weight (Earth pulls book down) by Newton's third law is:
options: The table pushes the book up (that is the normal force, a different interaction)
questions.explain: Third-law pairs act between the same two objects: Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls Earth. The table's normal force is a separate pair.

questions.q: What net force is needed to accelerate a 1200 kg car at 2.5 meters per second squared?
questions.explain: Force equals 1200 times 2.5 equals 3000 newtons.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball is thrown and air resistance is ignored after release (only gravity acts, downward). Its acceleration while in flight is:
options: About 9.8 meters per second squared downward the whole flight
Zero at the top only in the sense velocity is zero - acceleration is still downward (this full statement is the correct choice)
Upward on the way up, zero at top, downward on way down
Equal to its throwing force forever
questions.explain: Gravity acts the whole flight, so acceleration stays about 9.8 meters per second squared downward, even at the top where vertical velocity is momentarily zero.

questions.q: If the net force on an object is zero, the object:
options: Keeps its current velocity - at rest or moving steadily (Newton's first law)
questions.explain: Zero net force means no acceleration: velocity stays constant, which includes staying at rest.

questions.q: A 10 N force and a 6 N force act in opposite directions on a 2 kg object. Its acceleration is:
options: 2 meters per second squared in the direction of the 10 N force
questions.explain: Net force is 10 minus 6 equals 4 newtons. Acceleration equals 4 divided by 2 equals 2 meters per second squared.

title: Gravity, Mass & Weight
subject: Physics Basics
description: Distinguish mass from weight, use weight equals m times g, and explain orbits and falling.

questions.q: Mass and weight differ because:
options: Mass changes on the Moon but weight does not
Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with location; weight is a force that depends on gravity
They are exactly the same thing
questions.explain: Mass (in kilograms) is constant. Weight is mass times local gravity, measured in newtons, so it changes on the Moon.

questions.q: A student has a mass of 60 kg. On Earth (g about 10 meters per second squared for estimation), weight is about:
questions.explain: Weight equals m times g: 60 times 10 equals 600 newtons. Using 9.8 gives 588 newtons.

questions.q: On the Moon, gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's. A 60 kg student's Moon weight (using Earth weight 588 N) is about:
questions.explain: 588 divided by 6 equals 98 newtons. Mass stays 60 kg; only weight changes.

questions.q: Why do a hammer and a feather fall together on the Moon (Apollo demonstration) but not on Earth?
options: There is almost no air on the Moon, so no air resistance slows the feather
Gravity is stronger for feathers on the Moon
The hammer becomes lighter than the feather
Feathers do not fall on Earth
questions.explain: Without air resistance, all objects accelerate at the same rate regardless of mass.

questions.q: An astronaut in orbit floats because:
options: There is no gravity in orbit
The astronaut and station are both in continuous free fall around Earth
Gravity is exactly zero at that height
questions.explain: Orbit is free fall: gravity still acts (about 90 percent of surface strength low in orbit) but both fall together around Earth.

questions.q: Which object has more inertia?
options: They are equal if speeds are equal
A loaded truck - more mass means more inertia
questions.explain: Inertia is resistance to changes in motion and increases with mass.

questions.q: A 3 kg object is dropped and a 3 kg object is thrown horizontally at the same instant (same height, no air resistance). Which hits the ground first?
options: Neither - the thrown one never falls
They hit at the same time
questions.explain: Vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both fall the same vertical distance in the same time.

questions.q: Gravitational force between two objects increases when:
options: Their masses increase or they move closer together
questions.explain: Gravity grows with mass and weakens quickly with distance (inverse-square).

questions.q: Weight on Earth of a 2 kg bag of sugar (g = 9.8) is:
questions.explain: Weight equals 2 times 9.8 equals 19.6 newtons. Kilograms measure mass, not weight.

questions.q: If Earth suddenly had twice its mass (same size), your weight would:
questions.explain: Weight is proportional to Earth's mass, so doubling Earth's mass roughly doubles surface gravity and your weight.

Work, Power & Machines
subject: Physics Basics
description: Work as force times distance, power, kinetic and potential energy calculations, and simple machines.

questions.q: You push a box with 50 newtons over 4 meters in the direction of motion. Work done is:
questions.explain: Work equals force times distance: 50 times 4 equals 200 joules.

questions.q: A machine does 600 joules of work in 10 seconds. Its power is:
questions.explain: Power equals work divided by time: 600 divided by 10 equals 60 watts.

questions.q: Kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 meters per second is:
questions.explain: Kinetic energy equals one-half m v squared: 0.5 times 2 times 9 equals 9 joules.

questions.q: Gravitational potential energy of a 5 kg book 2 meters above the floor (g = 10) is:
questions.explain: Potential energy equals m g h: 5 times 10 times 2 equals 100 joules.

questions.q: A lever lets you lift a heavy load with less force because:
options: It trades force for distance - you move the lever farther
It increases both force and distance for free
questions.explain: Simple machines trade force and distance; total work (ignoring friction) is not reduced.

questions.q: Carrying a heavy bag horizontally at constant height while walking at constant speed: work done BY gravity is:
options: Equal to weight times distance walked
Zero - gravity is perpendicular to the motion
questions.explain: Work requires force along the displacement. Gravity acts down, motion is horizontal, so gravity does no work in this ideal case.

questions.q: Two students climb the same stairs. Ana takes 10 seconds, Ben takes 20 seconds. Who developed more power (same weight and height)?
options: Ana - same work in less time means more power
questions.explain: Power equals work divided by time. Half the time means twice the power for the same work.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car at 20 meters per second has kinetic energy:
questions.explain: KE equals 0.5 times 1000 times 400 (20 squared) equals 200,000 joules.

questions.q: If a car's speed doubles, its kinetic energy:
options: Quadruples - it depends on speed squared
questions.explain: KE depends on v squared, so doubling speed multiplies KE by 4. That is why stopping distance grows so fast.

questions.q: Efficiency of a machine that takes in 500 joules and outputs 400 joules of useful work is:
questions.explain: Efficiency equals useful output divided by input times 100: 400 divided by 500 equals 0.8, or 80 percent. The rest is lost mainly as heat from friction.

Waves & Frequency
subject: Physics Basics
description: Wave speed, frequency, wavelength, amplitude, and how light and sound waves differ.

questions.q: A wave has frequency 5 hertz and wavelength 2 meters. Its speed is:
questions.explain: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 5 times 2 equals 10 meters per second.

questions.q: Frequency is measured in hertz, which means:
questions.explain: One hertz equals one cycle per second.

questions.q: A sound wave has speed 340 meters per second and frequency 170 hertz. Its wavelength is:
questions.explain: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency: 340 divided by 170 equals 2 meters.

questions.q: Amplitude of a wave is most related to:
options: How much energy it carries - loudness for sound, brightness for light
questions.explain: Larger amplitude means more energy: louder sounds and brighter light.

questions.q: Which correctly orders parts of the electromagnetic spectrum from longest wavelength to shortest?
options: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
questions.explain: Wavelength decreases (and frequency and energy increase) from radio through gamma rays.

questions.q: A wave's period is 0.25 seconds. Its frequency is:
questions.explain: Frequency equals 1 divided by period: 1 divided by 0.25 equals 4 hertz.

questions.q: When a wave passes from air into water and slows, its wavelength:
questions.explain: Speed equals frequency times wavelength. Frequency is set by the source and stays the same, so slower speed means shorter wavelength (refraction).

questions.q: Ultrasound used in medical imaging is:
options: Sound with frequency too high for humans to hear (above about 20,000 hertz)
questions.explain: Ultrasound means frequencies above human hearing, above about 20,000 hertz. Below 20 hertz is infrasound.

questions.q: Light travels in vacuum at about:
options: 300,000,000 meters per second (3 times 10 to the 8th)
questions.explain: The speed of light in vacuum, c, is about 3 times 10 to the 8th meters per second. 340 is the speed of sound in air.

questions.q: Two waves have the same speed. Wave A has twice the frequency of wave B. Wave A's wavelength is:
questions.explain: At fixed speed, wavelength equals speed divided by frequency, so doubling frequency halves wavelength.

title: Electricity & Circuits
subject: Physics Basics
description: Voltage, current, resistance with Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, and electrical power - with multi-step problems.

questions.q: Ohm's law states voltage equals:
options: Current times resistance (V = I times R)
questions.explain: Ohm's law: V equals I times R. Rearrange to find current or resistance as needed.

questions.q: A 12 volt battery is connected to a 4 ohm resistor. The current is:
questions.explain: Current equals voltage divided by resistance: 12 divided by 4 equals 3 amperes.

questions.q: A circuit has current 2 amperes and resistance 10 ohms. The voltage needed is:
questions.explain: Voltage equals current times resistance: 2 times 10 equals 20 volts.

questions.q: Two 6 ohm resistors in series have a total resistance of:
questions.explain: Series resistances add: 6 plus 6 equals 12 ohms.

questions.q: Two 6 ohm resistors in parallel have a total resistance of:
questions.explain: For two equal resistors in parallel, total is half of one: 6 divided by 2 equals 3 ohms. In general 1 over R total equals sum of 1 over each.

questions.q: A 9 volt battery drives a series circuit with a 2 ohm and a 7 ohm resistor. Current everywhere in the series loop is:
questions.explain: Total resistance is 2 plus 7 equals 9 ohms. Current equals 9 divided by 9 equals 1 ampere, the same at every point in series.

questions.q: Electrical power for a device with voltage 120 volts and current 5 amperes is:
questions.explain: Power equals voltage times current: 120 times 5 equals 600 watts.

questions.q: A 100 watt bulb runs for 3 hours. Energy used (in kilowatt-hours) is:
questions.explain: Energy equals power in kilowatts times hours: 0.1 kW times 3 equals 0.3 kilowatt-hours.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit, if one branch bulb burns out, the other branches:
options: Stay lit - each branch has its own path
questions.explain: Parallel branches are independent paths, so one open branch does not break the others. Voltage across each branch stays the same (ideal).

questions.q: Multi-step: A 24 volt source connects to a parallel pair: branch 1 is 8 ohms, branch 2 is 24 ohms. Total current from the source is:
options: 4 amperes - 3 A through 8 ohms plus 1 A through 24 ohms
questions.explain: Branch currents: 24 divided by 8 equals 3 A, and 24 divided by 24 equals 1 A. Parallel currents add: 3 plus 1 equals 4 amperes.
